Photograph: Dimitrios Kambouris/Getty Images Los Angeles This article is more than 5 months old How Spencer Pratt’s ‘patently absurd’ bid for Los Angeles mayor fell flat This article is more than 5 months old The ex-reality TV star, who lost his home in the Pacific Palisades fire, cast himself as the antidote to the city’s woes Dani Anguiano and Uwa Ede-Osifo Tue 9 Jun 2026 20.26 EDT First published on Tue 9 Jun 2026 18.52 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Spencer Pratt, an ex-reality TV star, cast himself as the antidote to Los Angeles’s woes as he campaigned to be the city’s next mayor. He curried favor with swaths of disillusioned voters who related to his diatribes against city leadership. His fervent social media posts, including reshares of AI-generated campaign ads showing LA in an apocalyptic light, garnered national attention. But when voters got to the polls, ultimately the online virality was not enough to boost a registered Republican, who is best known for his villainous turn on MTV’s The Hills and has zero experience in governing, in a deep blue city embroiled in debate over its future. Why the California vote count is slow – and Trump’s fraud claims are bogus Read more The progressive city councilor Nithya Raman edged out Pratt, according to results called by the Associated Press on Monday night. Raman will face the incumbent Karen Bass in November’s race. Pratt has not yet conceded the election. In a break from his usually prolific online presence, he has issued few remarks about the election on social media since the 2 June primary, save for an X post in which he suggested without evidence that Raman rounded up a cohort of unhoused people to vote for her. He broke his social media silence on Tuesday when he tweeted a photo of a duck on a body of water, apparently referring to Bass as a lame duck. Donald Trump , who backed Pratt’s bid, has offered up his own assessment on the race and California primaries at large: “crooked”. The state’s slow ballot-counting process has drawn unfounded conspiracy theories from the right about voter fraud. But Pratt, who first appeared on Americans’ TV screens in the late aughts as Heidi Montag’s infamously bad boyfriend on The Hills, had been set for an uphill battle on several fronts. For one, his lack of government experience drew questions about his exact plans for the city. He was quick to dismiss concerns about his capability. “I’m a lifelong Angeleno who’s seen my home city waste away under poor leadership. THAT is my experience,” he recently said on social media. View image in fullscreen A ‘Pratt for Mayor’ billboard in Los Angeles before election day. Photograph: Highfive/Bauer-Griffin/GC Images Pratt, who said he voted for Trump in 2024, was also running in a largely Democratic city. Los Angeles has not been led by a Republican since Richard Riordan, who served from 1993 to 2001. The endorsement from Trump, who is deeply unpopular among Los Angeles voters, was also viewed as a hindrance. On the campaign trail, Pratt largely distanced himself from partisan allegiances and emphasized that the election for Los Angeles mayor is non-partisan. He focused his attacks on city leadership, tapping into sources of resentment beyond party lines. Before last year, Pratt was an unlikely candidate for mayor. Born to a dentist and a homemaker in the Pacific Palisades, he was best known for his reality TV antics and as a tabloid fixture, with covers documenting his wedding and his relationship with now-wife Montag. But the public perception of Pratt softened in recent years as he shared self-deprecating jokes on social media and frequently posted adoringly about the hummingbirds outside his home. Nithya Raman: progressive who bested Spencer Pratt eyes Hollywood ending Read more In January 2025, Pratt was one of thousands of Angelenos to lose their homes in the deadly wildfires that tore through the city. He shared emotional videos showing the remnants of his destroyed home in the Palisades and the toll of displacement on him, his wife and their two small children. Pratt frequently amplified the challenges faced by fire victims, and soon became one of the most visible and vocal critics of the city’s response to the disaster and Bass’s leadership. He argued that Los Angeles did not do enough to prepare for the fire and was falling short in helping residents with recovery. He launched his campaign in January, putting wildfire frustrations front and center, while also harnessing anger over longstanding issues in the city, including the cost-of-living crisis and an enduring homelessness emergency. Polling has found that the majority of Los Angeles residents feel the city is headed in the wrong direction. Los Angeles remains one of the most expensive cities in the US, and is short of 270,000 affordable housing units . While Bass has overseen a 17.5% reduction in people living on the streets, many Angelenos remain frustrated at the staggering scale of the crisis, with nearly 44,000 unhoused people in the city. According to the Associated Press , as of Monday, Pratt had secured 25.8% of the vote, trailing behind Raman, who received 28.6% and Bass, who was at 34.3%. “It says something – or should say something – to leaders of Los Angeles that roughly a third of the city’s voters are so unhappy with life as it is that they are willing to back a patently absurd candidate to run the place,” Jim Newton, a veteran Los Angeles journalist, wrote last week in a column for CalMatters . Zev Yaroslavsky, director of the Los Angeles initiative at the UCLA Luskin school of public affairs, said Pratt was effective in channeling the frustration of many voters. But, there was a ceiling to how many votes he would receive in the Democratic stronghold, even among those undecided about whether to re-elect Bass, Yaroslavsky said. “Most people in Los Angeles are moderate-liberal or progressive people. There’s only so many votes a Maga Republican is going to get,” Yaroslavsky said, referring to a comment Trump made about Pratt. Pratt’s campaign underperformed in comparison with Rick Caruso, a centrist real estate mogul, who lost to Bass in the 2022 mayoral race. Caruso, at that time, received about 36% of votes in the primary. Raman and Bass, former allies, will square off in a race regarded as a symbol of internal tensions roiling the Democratic party – veteran, center-left Democrats being challenged by younger, progressive candidates. Raman is a Democratic socialist. It’s unclear whether Pratt’s political ambitions will continue. He vowed to leave the city if he lost the race. His campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment on his next chapter. During a lengthy interview in Wisconsin that aired on “Meet the Press” on Sunday, Trump echoed claims he made in recent days — without providing evidence — that officials in California were “cheating,” because after four days, they “aren’t even close” to finishing the ballot counting. With more than 70% of the vote in on Sunday, veteran Democratic politician Xavier Becerra was about a percentage point ahead of Republican Steve Hilton in the governor’s race. In the Los Angeles mayoral race, City Councilmember Nithya Raman moved ahead of former reality TV personality Spencer Pratt by less than a percentage point as of Sunday afternoon. Advertisement × “Do you have evidence to support that?” Welker asked Trump about his cheating claims. “All I have to do is look,” he said. “But sir, that’s not evidence. That’s how they count the votes in California,” Welker said. She added that state and local officials acknowledge they are slow. “No, they’re crooked … just like you’re crooked. Your press is crooked and ‘Meet the Press’ is crooked,” Trump said. “You’re either crooked or you’re stupid,” he went on. “You know that these elections are rigged. Your network knows that they’re rigged.” Advertisement The back-and-forth continued until Trump decided to “call it quits.” “I’ve had enough,” he said, removing the microphone from his lapel and tossing it to the floor. “Thank you, darling, have a good time.” As Welker tried to convince him to finish the interview, he added: “A country can never be great with a dishonest press.” And eventually he walked off. A misreading of voting data in the Los Angeles mayoral race late on election night has fueled the false narrative that Trump and other Republicans have pushed in recent days that California Democrats were cheating. The claim was that in one vote count update, one candidate received zero votes. First Assistant U.S. Atty. Bill Essayli said on X that the claim was false, and “each candidate received votes in every update.” Essayli has confirmed on X that his office “has multiple election fraud investigations underway,” in coordination with the FBI in Los Angeles. title: Johnson Says California Election Fraud Is So Bad It Can’t Be Proven | The New Republic
desc: Apparently it’s more of a vibes-based thing for Mike Johnson.
body: Johnson Says California Election Fraud Is So Bad It Can’t Be Proven | The New Republic Skip Navigation The New Republic The New Republic LATEST BREAKING NEWS POLITICS CULTURE MAGAZINE THE TNR BLUE BOOK PODCASTS VIDEO The New Republic The New Republic The New Republic The New Republic The New Republic LATEST BREAKING NEWS POLITICS CULTURE MAGAZINE THE TNR BLUE BOOK PODCASTS VIDEO The New Republic The New Republic The New Republic Breaking News Breaking News from Washington and beyond Most Recent Post Finn Hartnett / June 9, 2026 / 11:14 a.m. ET Share This Story Johnson Says California Election Fraud Is So Bad It Can’t Be Proven Apparently it’s more of a vibes-based thing for Mike Johnson. Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg/Getty Images Asked whether he thought the Los Angeles mayoral election was rigged, House Speaker Mike Johnson did what he does best: steer away from facts and embrace nebulous speculation. “I’m not saying it’s rigged, I’m saying it stinks to high heaven, and everybody knows that,” Johnson said to a gaggle of reporters Monday evening. “Let’s remove the appearance of impropriety—what a concept. Let’s have votes on an election the day of the election.” CNN correspondent Manu Raju asked Johnson what evidence there was to support his vague complaints. Unsurprisingly, the Louisiana politician couldn’t provide a whiff of it. “Look, some of these efforts are so diabolical and so far upstream it’s impossible to prove,” Johnson said. “But I think everybody knows instinctively something is wrong here.” RAJU: But what evidence is there to prove the California election is rigged? MIKE JOHNSON: Look, some of these efforts are so diabolical and so far upstream it's impossible to prove. But I think everybody knows instinctively that something is wrong here. pic.twitter.com/gJIYChtG0X — Aaron Rupar (@atrupar) June 8, 2026 The incumbent mayor of Los Angeles, Democrat Karen Bass, advanced to the general election with 34.3 percent of the vote on Monday. A progressive Democrat, Nithya Raman, beat Republican Spencer Pratt for second place, with 28.5 to 25.8 percent. Raman will now take on Bass in the general election, in a leftist-versus-moderate clash similar to last year’s New York City mayoral race. The battle between Raman and Pratt is what Johnson was moaning about. Pratt, a former reality-TV personality, led early on Monday before Raman took the lead as more mail-in ballots were processed. Pratt offered some typically Trumpian fearmongering by alleging that the homeless were illegally voting for Raman. The president himself also claimed , again without evidence, that the vote was “crooked.” Even longtime Republican legislators like House Majority Leader Steve Scalise are baselessly insinuating voter fraud. It is strange that Republicans are unable to accept that they lost a mayoral race in one of the bluest cities in the country. Then again, this is the party whose leader attempted to stage a coup after losing a presidential election, who kicked off a mid-decade gerrymandering war in order to consolidate power, and whose disciples have literally tampered with voting machines in order to hijack elections. With the GOP desperate to cling to power, and lacking the morality to accept defeat, the midterms should be a ball. Share This Story Read more about the election: MAGA Is Melting Down Over the Results From L.A.’s Mayoral Primary Most Recent Post Edith Olmsted / June 9, 2026 / 10:23 a.m. ET Share This Story Trump Ruins Knicks Game for Everyone—Then Falls Asleep in Middle of It Donald Trump forced foot traffic and the official Knicks watch party to close—and then didn’t even watch the game. SAUL LOEB/AFP/Getty Images President Donald Trump shut down Midtown Manhattan Monday so he could take a nap at the NBA Finals. After getting loudly booed by attendees at Madison Square Garden, Trump was spotted snoozing in his box seats next to Knicks owner James Dolan and his granddaughter Kai Trump. DONALD TRUMP HAS FALLEN ASLEEP AT THE NBA FINALS IN MADISON SQUARE GARDEN. pic.twitter.com/rFrW6c4cME — CALL TO ACTIVISM (@CalltoActivism) June 9, 2026 It seems that a tense Game 3 between the New York Knicks and the San Antonio Spurs wasn’t enough to pique the president’s interest. It’s not particularly surprising, considering that Trump has repeatedly been seen dozing off during press conferences , bill signings , and Cabinet meetings , among other apparent instances of cognitive decline . Trump’s nap came amid his highly disruptive trip to Midtown at the taxpayer’s expense and New Yorkers’ apparent dismay . Authorities closed 10 blocks around Madison Square Garden to traffic and pedestrians ahead of Trump’s arrival. The Secret Service and TSA, along with the NYPD, heightened security protocols at MSG. Attendees were forced to arrive hours early, and without any bags. And perhaps worst of all, the New York Knicks were forced to cancel their rambunctious watch party outside the stadium. Clearly the vibes were off: The Knicks lost by four points, ending a 13-game winning streak. Share This Story Read more about Trump’s game attendance: Trump Makes Pathetic Claim About His Reception at Knicks Game Most Recent Post Hafiz Rashid / June 9, 2026 / 10:17 a.m. ET Share This Story How One Indian Billionaire Bought Off Trump by Investing in His Son A new report reveals how Anant Ambani won favors from the Trump administration. Reliance Industries Chairman Mukesh Ambani and his son Anant Ambani show their ink-marked fingers after casting their vote for the Maharashtra Assembly elections, November 20, 2024. Milind Shelte/ The India Today Group/Getty Images Reliance Industries Chairman Mukesh Ambani and his son Anant Ambani show their ink-marked fingers after casting their vote for the Maharashtra Assembly elections, November 20, 2024. An Indian billionaire paid millions of dollars to Donald Trump Jr. and later won major concessions from the Trump administration. Anant Ambani, 30, is a member of the richest family in India, and his family’s energy business was in the White House’s crosshairs as part of President Trump’s tariffs against India. But when Trump Jr. visited India in November, he met with Ambani and everything changed. Ambani wined and dined Trump Jr., taking him to the family’s private zoo and performing a Gujarati folk dance together. Only four months later, a Texas start-up aiming to build the first major oil refinery in 50 years in the U.S. announced it had received a nine-figure investment from the Ambanis’s company, Reliance Energy. The deal was facilitated by Trump Jr., who secretly bought a stake in the new venture, ProPublica reports . View this post on Instagram A post shared by Shubham. (@shubham.daveeee) Prior to Trump Jr.’s involvement, the Texas company had failed several times to raise money, missing deadlines and rebranding again and again. Its founder had been repeatedly sued for fraud and had a history of bankruptcy. But with Trump Jr.’s help, America First Refining not only secured funding from Ambani but has also met with investors from foreign countries such as Saudi Arabia. One foreign government official told ProPublica that the company’s team said they were backed by the Trump family, and that an investment would open doors in the White House. That appears to be accurate, with President Trump gleefully posting about America First Refining’s oil refinery project in March . Reliance Energy also paid the Trump Organization $10 million as a “development fee” in 2024, although no project has ever been announced. Ivanka Trump was a guest at Anant Ambani’s lavish wedding that year, and Anant’s father, Mukhesh Ambani (worth close to $90 billion), attended Trump’s second inauguration. In February, the Ambanis’ efforts paid off for all of India, with the country striking a trade deal with the United States. Reliance, meanwhile, got a license to buy Venezuelan oil. After the Iran war, India got an early sanctions waiver to buy Russian crude oil. All of this goes to show that in Trump’s second term, it’s impossible to tell when Trump’s personal business ends and U.S. policy begins. It’s increasingly apparent that cutting deals with and paying money to the Trump family means that you’ll get benefits from the federal government. Share This Story Most Recent Post Malcolm Ferguson / June 9, 2026 / 10:10 a.m. ET Share This Story JD Vance Isn’t Handling Republicans’ Defeat in Los Angeles Very Well The vice president is boosting a MAGA conspiracy theory after Spencer Pratt failed to advance in the race for L.A. mayor. Matt Rourke/Pool/Getty Images Vice President JD Vance is echoing his president’s false claims of election fraud in the Los Angeles mayoral race. Vance went on Fox News to carry water for the baseless theory after Republican Spencer Pratt was defeated by progressive Los Angeles City Councilmember Nithya Raman, who will face incumbent Karen Bass in the general election. “They are still counting the votes [in California]. Do you trust this election?” Fox News host Jesse Waters asked the vice president on Monday night. “Fundamentally the problem here with this whole thing is: How is it that you had Karen Bass was in first place, Spencer Pratt was in second place, and then this other woman was in third place. You would expect these mail-in ballots to kind of meet that same basic pattern,” Vance said. “But somehow we find ourselves in a situation where number one—they’re still receiving ballots, not just counting ballots. And number two—the way they’re coming in just so happens to work out such that the Republican is getting kicked out of the final two, so it’s a Democrat-versus-Democrat runoff. “That seems pretty shady to me, especially when you add on top of the fact that in California you are prohibited from asking for somebody’s identification before they vote,” he added. JD Vance says it's "shady" for California to count all of the legally cast ballots pic.twitter.com/zCjQ5yRgvA — Aaron Rupar (@atrupar) June 9, 2026 This is the vice president of one of the most corrupt administrations in history talking about what’s “shady.” Los Angeles has over two more million more registered Democrats than Republicans. It is also common knowledge at this point that liberal and progressive voters are more likely to vote by mail than conservatives, especially since President Trump has wrongly railed against it as corrupt for years. Now, Republicans are reverting back to this tired argument because their chosen candidate lost—not because of fraud, but because voters rejected him. title: Spencer Pratt responds to L.A. mayoral race loss, says 'it's war' in new video - ABC7 Los Angeles
desc: Spencer Pratt responded to his loss in the Los Angeles mayoral race in a video posted Friday, saying "you have no idea how bad things are about to get for the city."
body: Spencer Pratt responds to L.A. mayoral race loss, says 'it's war' in new video - ABC7 Los Angeles 24/7 Live Los Angeles Orange County Inland Empire Ventura County California POLITICS Spencer Pratt responds to L.A. mayoral race loss, says 'it's war' in new video Spencer Pratt responded to his loss in the Los Angeles mayoral race in a video posted Friday, saying "you have no idea how bad things are about to get for the city." Saturday, June 13, 2026 Share Este artículo se ofrece en Español LOS ANGELES (KABC) -- The Republican and former reality television personality Spencer Pratt responded to his loss in the Los Angeles mayoral primary in a video posted Friday morning, saying "you have no idea how bad things are about to get for the city." In the video captioned "Saving LA-Phase III" posted on his social media, Pratt said he is not leaving town and is going to stay active in local politics. "You thought you could get rid of me that easily?" Pratt said. "I didn't get in this for political power, I got in this to expose this corrupt machine and nothing's changed." "And now I don't have to worry about offending CNN viewers. I don't have a campaign to hamstring me now. It's war," he added. The three-minute video featured clips from movies, news broadcasts and even a UFC fight. Much of it consists of Pratt painting Los Angeles as a negative place to live. Pratt criticized the remaining candidates, City Councilwoman Nithya Raman and Mayor Karen Bass. "Angelenos are now stuck with two morons responsible for all their problems and now have to choose between dumb and dumber," Pratt said, as images of Raman and Bass appeared. He also said that "every problem that plagues Los Angeles because of these two corrupt communists is going to accelerate" under their leadership. Pratt's goal has not changed, he said, and he remains focused on stopping "these commie animals." "If you think we uncovered a lot of fraud and evil in the campaign, just wait," Pratt said. He went on to say that they have a recording of one of the candidates "doing or saying something that would make her resign in shame," but did not directly say whether it was of Bass or Raman. He calls them both out while looking directly at the camera, saying, "So, Karen, Nithya, ask yourself. Is it possible that one of your employees may have a recording of you doing or saying something that would force you to resign in disgrace?" Pratt used the opportunity to discuss the Palisades Fire, which destroyed his home and was a recurring topic during his campaign. "Hope you sleep well at night over the next five months, because you know who hasn't slept well at all for the last 17 months? My mom. All my neighbors in the Palisades,'' he said. Top Stories California DMV bans Waymos from operating on state freeways after series of traffic incidents; Waymo temporarily suspends freeway operations nationwide 3 hours ago Explosion at Chiquita Canyon Landfill capped, but smell lingers in Castaic Nithya Raman will be sworn in next month. Here's a breakdown of her campaign promises 2 hours ago He also claimed major developers, hoteliers, business owners and entrepreneurs have told him they are leaving the city, which he argued would lead to more restaurant closures and less tax revenue. "That means the city has to cut services. More potholes, less firefighters, less police patrols, more criminals, more drug addicts terrorizing your communities," Pratt said. "You have no idea how bad things are about to get for the city, look at this place already," he added. "The city is a mess and you're about to reward the arsonist who torched the place with four more years of destruction." Pratt competed against Bass and Raman in the primary election for a spot in the November runoff. He was eliminated after failing to secure enough votes to advance. His video message comes just one day after Raman made a pledge to his supporters to deliver on the change they want in an effort to be their candidate come November. The election was not a vote of confidence in Bass, who, according to incomplete returns, received under 35% of the vote, a vulnerable position for an incumbent. Still, she remains ahead of Raman with a more than 44,000 vote difference. Raman holds a lead of more than 29,000 votes over Pratt in the latest election results , with 246,333 votes to Pratt's 216,783. Raman, who previously endorsed Bass for reelection, had been running in third until Sunday, but she gained more votes with every update provided by election officials in Los Angeles since June 2, primary day. Eyewitness News reached out to Raman's campaign, who had no comment about Pratt's video. The Bass campaign did not respond to our request for comment. Pratt's candidacy drew national attention due to his celebrity status and outspoken criticism of liberal leadership in a heavily Democratic city, but that attention did not translate into sufficient support at the polls. Angelenos will decide in November whether Bass keeps her position as mayor or if voters turn the page and elect Raman as the new leader for the city. Published October 3, 2026 9:58 PM L.A. City Councilmember Nithya Raman (left) and L.A. Mayor Karen Bass both appeared separately at a mayoral forum Sept. 29. ( Eric Thayer / Los Angeles Times via Getty Images ) Topline: Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass and her challenger, City Councilmember Nithya Raman, appeared at a South L.A. forum Saturday, where they agreed on some aspects of the city’s approach to homelessness, but offered different ideas on addressing housing costs. On police: Raman criticized LAPD for its crowd control tactics during protests around ICE facilities and said Bass has allowed the department to not enforce a state law banning federal agents from wearing masks. Bass defended LAPD’s actions during ICE operations and said she would order the police chief to enforce the state mask ban if a judicial order blocking it is lifted. On homelessness: Bass called the current approach “completely disfunctional” and called for a new system under the control of the city. Raman has said she also supports leaving the region’s troubled lead homelessness agency and investing in a new city homelessness bureau. On housing: Raman criticized the mayor’s opposition to building more densely in residential neighborhoods near transit centers. She said the result has been more building in the city’s poorer council districts, including the South L.A. district that hosted Saturday’s forum. Bass has said density doesn’t belong in some neighborhoods. She opposed a state law, SB 79, that will force cities to allow apartment buildings up to nine stories tall near rail transit stations. Read on… to learn how the candidates are promising to help South L.A. Full Story Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass and her challenger, City Councilmember Nithya Raman, appeared at a South L.A. forum Saturday, where they agreed on some aspects of the city’s approach to reducing homelessness, but offered different ideas on addressing housing costs. The two appeared separately in conversations with Brenda Verano of CALO News at A Place Called Home, a youth services community organization. Bass went first, saying she grew up just 20 blocks south of the venue. “South L.A. has been a big part of my life and what I have done,” said Bass, who in 1991 helped start Community Coalition, which fights for racial and economic justice in that part of the city. Each candidate was asked how they would build trust in City Hall among Black and Latino residents in South L.A. “Black and brown poor folks the most have been central in my administration and will continue to be so,” Bass said. “But to me, representation is not just about faces in a room. It's about collaborating on everything you're doing.” Raman said the establishment “has taken the people of Los Angeles for granted.” “I’m running for mayor because I don’t want to ignore any part of this city,” she said. “I want to make sure we are people who know these communities not just in the mayor's office but across the many commissions, across the many departments that are designed to oversee these neighborhoods.” How the candidates would work with LAPD Both vowed to expand pilot programs where unarmed social workers respond to certain non-emergency 911 calls instead of the police department. “Law enforcement should not be dealing with homelessness and substance abuse and mental health,” Bass said. “Those are public health issues.” But Bass said it's doubtful the police department’s budget will be cut before the 2028 Olympics. The mayor in the past has expressed support for growing the number of police officers. Raman has said the department is about the right size. She expressed concern about the police department’s cooperation with ICE during recent federal immigration raids. Raman also criticized the department for its crowd control tactics during protests around ICE facilities. Police used tear gas and rubber bullets against some protestors. “This mayor did not speak out against those actions by LAPD, appointed a chief who has not met this moment, who said he would not enforce laws put in by the state to protect us,” Raman said. Chief Jim McDonnell has previously said his department would not enforce California's state law banning federal immigration and law enforcement agents from wearing masks on duty. A federal appeals court in February blocked enforcement of the law. Bass said if the judicial ban is lifted, she would order McDonnell to enforce the state law. The mayor also defended the department’s use of police officers for crowd control during ICE operations. “If there is a crowd around an arrest, then LAPD is involved because we don’t want to have the federal government doing that,” she said. Both say city should exit troubled homelessness agency On the city’s response to homelessness, Bass called the current system “completely disfunctional” and called for a new system under the control of the city. Currently, the Los Angeles Homeless Services Authority oversees the city’s delivery of homeless services. Numerous audits have found poor accounting of taxpayer money at the agency — which spent nearly $830 million in public funds last fiscal year. The county has already pulled its funding from the agency in favor of standing up a new county-run Department of Homeless Services and Housing. Bass said unhoused people are not getting enough care once they leave the streets. “It is insufficient. They are not taken care of in terms of their health, education, etc. A new system would enable us to do that,” Bass said. Raman has said she also supports leaving LAHSA and investing in a new homelessness bureau. She noted that street homelessness fell in her council district while numbers across the city went up, according to this year’s homeless count . “In the past few years, this mayor has refused to audit our homelessness response,” Raman said. “I am very committed to doing that, and I'll request that audit on day one.” Sharp divides on housing development, renter protections On housing, Raman criticized the mayor’s opposition to building more densely in residential neighborhoods near transit centers. She said the result has been more building in the city’s poorer council districts, including the South L.A. district that hosted Saturday’s forum. “Wealthier neighborhoods, less diverse neighborhoods, whiter neighborhoods have actually pushed back on affordable housing, on greater density,” Raman said. More of the city, said Raman, should bear the burden of greater density. “We need to build more housing in Los Angeles, but we need to build it across every single neighborhood,” Raman added. Bass has said density doesn’t belong in some neighborhoods. She opposed a state law, SB 79, that will force cities to allow apartment buildings up to nine stories tall near rail transit stations. Bass said her administration has fast-tracked new income-restricted housing. But she argued that certain development restrictions are necessary to prevent gentrification. “We need housing, but we cannot displace Black and Brown people,” Bass said. “If you have housing that is just built anywhere and everywhere, they're coming for us.” Raman also criticized Bass’ move to temporarily lift restrictions on short-term rentals in preparation for an influx of visitors during the 2028 Olympics. “I want to make sure that this mayor’s push for deregulating short-term rental during this time, in ways that are harmful to renters, don’t go through,” Raman said. She said tenants could be displaced as landlords turn long-term rentals into short-term accommodations. Airbnb and business groups back the proposal, saying it will fill a visitor lodging gap for the Olympics and that it would generate significant municipal revenue. Airbnb has put more than $4 million toward backing Bass and three other city candidates, according to the latest campaign finance reports . Published November 17, 2026 5:59 PM Darren Kettle has led Metrolink since September 202 ( Phillip Faraone / Getty Images ) Topline: Metrolink’s chief executive officer, Darren Kettle, will leave the agency early next year, following his retirement. Tuesday’s announcement comes days after the nation’s third-largest commuter rail agency closed this year’s fiscal budget with help from a $20 million lifeline state grant. Why it matters: Kettle’s exit comes after Metrolink earlier this month closed its $420 million budget for this fiscal year . It received a $20 million bailout from the California State Transportation Agency to maintain its current services. The agency faced harsh criticism after it previously proposed cutting about a third of weekday trains and 40% of weekend trains in order to close its books. In his own words : “As a regular Metrolink rider, I've especially enjoyed getting to know fellow passengers, hearing their stories and learning about how public transportation can better serve their needs,” Kettle said in a statement. “As I prepare to step away from the public sector, I can make our customers a familiar promise: I will continue to see you on the train.” Kettle’s career at Metrolink : Kettle has led the agency since September 2021 as Metrolink worked to recover from the impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic. He is retiring after 37 years in public service, according to a Metrolink statement . What’s next: Kettle’s last day with Metrolink will be Feb. 26, 2027. The Metrolink Board of Directors will oversee the leadership transition and executive search for Kettle’s successor, according to Tuesday’s release. Go deeper … California grants Metrolink a $20M lifeline to avoid major service cuts Sponsored message LAist watchdog reporting Homeless money Judge finalizes LAHSA handoff to county Nick Gerda is an accountability reporter who has covered local government in Southern California for more than a decade. Published November 17, 2026 5:01 PM Makeshift shelters line a sidewalk in Los Angeles. ( Apu Gomes / AFP via Getty Images ) Topline: The troubled Los Angeles Homeless Services Authority, known as LAHSA, is now officially losing control of the L.A. region's federal money for homeless services. A federal judge on Monday finalized a deal that hands control of that money — and the region’s annual homeless count — to the county government in phases. The timing: The handoff starts next month and wraps up by the end of 2027. It's the first time in decades that a different agency will manage this federal tax money, which totals hundreds of millions of dollars per year. Criticism from judge: At a hearing Friday on the deal, U.S. District Judge David O. Carter had harsh words for what he called decades of failure by the federal and local governments to fix oversight problems with L.A.’s homelessness dollars. “This has been an absolute past dereliction of duty,” he said. “What is so sad and disappointing is these funds were meant to serve the absolute most vulnerable in our society.” Full Story The troubled Los Angeles Homeless Services Authority, known as LAHSA, is now officially losing control of the L.A. region's federal money for homeless services. A federal judge on Monday finalized a deal that hands control of that money — and the region’s annual homeless count — to the county government in phases. The handoff starts next month and wraps up by the end of 2027. It's the first time in decades that a different agency will manage this federal tax money, which totals hundreds of millions of dollars per year. The switch is designed so that people who rely on shelters, outreach teams and housing programs don't see their services disrupted, attorneys said at a hearing Friday. The same nonprofits will keep doing that work. What changes is that the county — promising more transparency and accountability — will pay the nonprofits and check their work, instead of LAHSA. U.S. District Judge David O. Carter signed the deal Monday , ending a lawsuit LAHSA filed after the Trump administration suspended the agency in June. The settlement says the court will have the power to enforce the agreement. The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, or HUD, which was the defendant, said in a statement that the deal ensures LAHSA “never receives another dollar of HUD funding.” Gita O’Neill, LAHSA's interim CEO, said the agency has maintained throughout the lawsuit “that LAHSA did not engage in wrongdoing and that HUD's suspension lacked a legal foundation.” Gita O'Neill, LAHSA's interim CEO, at the 2026 Homeless Count launch in January. ( Jordan Rynning / LAist ) The deal also keeps on track the region's annual request for federal funding — about $240 million this year. And it adds tighter checks on how that money is spent. When does the money move? Starting Dec. 1: Grants for programs that begin on or after that date move to the county before they start. January 2027: LAHSA — which has overseen the L.A. region’s annual homeless counts since 2005 when they were first required by the federal government — runs the annual homeless count one last time. The county runs it after that. By March 1, 2027: The county becomes the agency that asks the federal government for homeless money on behalf of the whole region. By April 1, 2027: The county takes over management of many federal grants from LAHSA for programs already running and continuing past June 2027. June 30, 2027: Grants that end by this date finish under LAHSA. By Dec. 31, 2027: The county takes over two key systems. One is a database called HMIS that tracks which services are provided to each person experiencing homelessness. The other, called CES, matches people with housing. LAHSA's federal role then ends, except for closing out old grants. January 2028: The county runs the region’s yearly homeless count for the first time. Criticism from judge At a hearing Friday on the deal, Carter had harsh words for what he called decades of failure by the federal and local governments to fix oversight problems with L.A.’s homelessness dollars. “This has been an absolute past dereliction of duty,” he said. “Please, this can never happen again." “I termed it a partnership in failure,” he added. “Local government turned an absolute blind eye to the distribution of these funds and transparency and accountability for these funds.” “And what is so sad and disappointing is these funds were meant to serve the absolute most vulnerable in our society,” the judge added. Problems at LAHSA LAHSA — which is overseen by L.A. Mayor Karen Bass and the county Board of Supervisors — has faced major problems in recent years. Last year, an LAist investigation found the signature of LAHSA’s then-CEO, Va Lecia Adams Kellum, finalized a $2.1 million contract with the nonprofit where her husband was working in senior leadership, despite previously telling LAist she was “completely recused.” LAist also found the agency kept awarding millions in contract renewals to another nonprofit even after LAHSA’s own compliance team labeled it “high-risk” for, among other things, billing for services while reporting no enrolled participants. That group’s leader, Alex Soofer, recently pleaded guilty to diverting $2 million. Another nonprofit operator contracted with LAHSA, Michael Young, was arrested and charged by federal prosecutors with misappropriating millions of tax dollars, including allegedly siphoning $1 million into a high-end nightclub. Additionally, a 2024 L.A. County audit found LAHSA had mismanaged hundreds of millions in contracts for homeless services, often paying service providers late and failing to track whether services were provided. Under the settlement deal signed Monday, Carter will receive quarterly reports on progress and can intervene if one of the parties asks him to resolve a dispute. New safeguards For taxpayers, the deal adds safeguards on spending Carter has demanded for years. LAHSA must send invoices and spending records to HUD before drawing grant money, and submit receipts afterward. A HUD contractor, Guidehouse, will review its books, and the county must follow the same rules for older grants it inherits. The parties will report to Carter every three months, until LAHSA no longer has any federal roles overseen by HUD. How the case got here HUD suspended LAHSA from federal funds on June 11, citing alleged failures in the agency’s financial management and conflict-of-interest safeguards. The move put roughly $240 million in expected federal homelessness funding for the region in limbo and held up federal funding HUD had already awarded. In a statement Tuesday about the settlement, HUD Secretary Scott Turner said the suspension followed findings by the agency's inspector general of “fraud, failure and flagrant mismanagement.” “Taxpayers will no longer bankroll an organization that fails to deliver for the Americans it was created to serve,” Turner said. Scott Turner, U.S. Housing and Urban Development secretary, testifies before the Senate Appropriations Subcommittee on Transportation, Housing and Urban Development on May 14, 2026 in Washington, D.C. ( Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images / Getty Images North America ) After HUD’s suspension, LAHSA sued, calling it an unlawful federal overreach. In August, Carter blocked the suspension, writing that LAHSA and HUD had been in “a joint partnership in failure.” The judge ordered a competition for LAHSA's federal roles, deferring the selection decision to the L.A. Continuum of Care — the regional group designated by federal law to make that choice. In October, the continuum chose the county for all four federal roles — applying for funds, managing grants and running the two systems for tracking services and matching people with housing. It did so over objections from L.A. Mayor Karen Bass and several City Council members , who wanted the city to share control. The city then reached a tentative side deal giving it access to data on unhoused residents and a role placing people in city-funded housing. Shayla Myers, lead attorney for the Continuum of Care, said the deal restores local say over the money. “Congress created the Continuum of Care system to empower local stakeholders to set the priorities for how federal funding is spent in their communities,” she said in a statement. “HUD’s actions took that away from Los Angeles. This settlement brings it back home.” What’s next? The county's new Department of Homeless Services and Housing, which will take over duties from LAHSA, has set up an internal transition team and will make sure the department has the “staffing, systems, and resources necessary” to meet the settlement's deadlines, spokesperson Rachel Kassenbrock said in a statement. The department will give the continuum's board regular updates on its transition plan, she said. The federal funding shift is now locked in with a deal that a judge can enforce. That leaves just one major LAHSA funder remaining — the city of L.A. Mayor-elect Nithya Raman, who takes office next month, has promised to pull the city out of LAHSA within her first year. It’s a faster timeline than the one suggested by Bass, who said during the mayoral campaign it would take a “couple of years.” How to reach me If you have a tip, you can reach me on Signal. My username is ngerda.47. You can follow this link to reach me there or type my username in the search bar after starting a new chat. For instructions on getting started with Signal, see the app's support page. And if you're comfortable just reaching out to my email, I'm at ngerda@laist.com . Paul Rubenstein, LAHSA’s chief of staff, said in a statement that LAHSA will work with the city and county on job opportunities for its staff at the agencies taking over its work. In late October , Rubenstein said LAHSA had 326 employees and 59 vacant positions. He said it takes the equivalent of about 120 full-time staff to support the federal roles that will transition to the county. The handoff begins as LAHSA has been dealing with an ongoing disruption for the past week and a half. On Nov. 6, the agency identified “suspicious activity” on its network and took its internal computer and email systems offline as a precaution , according to an email Rubenstein sent city officials Monday. Many of LAHSA’s systems are still down this week, as the agency starts a multi-day process of restoring employee access, his email said. Outreach teams and interim housing programs kept operating during the outage, Rubenstein wrote, adding that the outage has affected “certain administrative functions and communications.” The email noted the importance of protecting information about employees and the people LAHSA serves, without saying whether it was improperly accessed. Rubenstein and O’Neill had not responded to LAist's questions since Friday about whether the systems were still down, and replied on Tuesday after LAist contacted multiple elected officials’ offices about the lack of response. Subscribe Civics & Democracy Olympics human rights LA Civil Rights dept says it needs more funding Libby Rainey has been tracking how L.A. is preparing for the 2028 Olympic Games. Published November 17, 2026 4:21 PM The Olympics and Paralympics have been described as the biggest sporting event in the world. One major venue in the city of L.A. is the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum. ( Brian Feinzimer / LAist ) Topline: After multiple years of budget cuts, L.A.’s Civil Rights Department says it needs more staff and funding to respond to an expected spike in human rights issues during the Olympic and Paralympic Games. The latest: City staff said it needed $696,000 at a city council ad hoc Olympics committee meeting Monday, warning that without additional resources they would not be able to adequately enforce L.A.’s civil and human rights ordinance or investigate complaints. Diminished staffing: The ask comes as the civil rights department operates with fewer staff after more than two years of budget reductions. The recent cuts meant they couldn't hire for vacant positions, according to the department's General Manager Capri Maddox. Why 2028 is a concern: The department is down to 26 employees from 44 and currently has no Spanish-speaking special investigator, Claudia Luna, assistant general manager for the Office of Civil Rights, told the council on Monday. Luna laid out a spate of potential issues that her office could have to address during the summer of 2028, including increased employment and disability discrimination complaints. Read on... for the city council's response to the department's request, and where the money might come from. Full Story After multiple years of budget cuts, L.A.’s Civil Rights Department says it needs more staff and funding to respond to an expected spike in human rights issues during the Olympic and Paralympic Games. City staff said it needed $696,000 at a City Council ad hoc Olympics committee meeting Monday, warning that without additional resources it would not be able to adequately enforce L.A.’s civil and human rights ordinance or investigate complaints. The ask comes as the civil rights department operates with fewer staff after more than two years of budget reductions. The recent cuts meant the department couldn't hire for vacant positions, according to the department's general manager, Capri Maddox. The department is down to 26 employees from 44 and currently has no Spanish-speaking special investigator, Claudia Luna, assistant general manager for the Office of Civil Rights, told the council on Monday. Luna laid out a spate of potential concerns that her office could have to address during the summer of 2028. “We anticipate an increase in discrimination complaints in the area of commerce, involving hotels, restaurants, retail establishments and other public accommodations,” she told the council. “We also expect employment discrimination involving temporary workers, housing-related complaints and disability discrimination concerns, particularly during the Paralympics.” The department wants to hire five temporary staffers and fund three additional part-time roles, including two special investigators and positions to expand community outreach. The department also seeks to increase its operating budget to do more multilingual communication, according to an August letter filed with the City Council. The asks come as private Olympics organizing committee LA28 faces ongoing pressure from advocates to beef up its own human rights strategy , which includes plans for a human rights hotline people can call throughout the Games. On Monday, Luna said that the hotline will refer civil rights complaints to the city. “Establishing a report mechanism is only half the equation,” she said. “We must ensure the agencies receiving those complaints have the resources to investigate and respond.” World Cup test run The 2026 World Cup offers a window into the challenges the department may face in less than two years’ time. The city saw a modest uptick in complaints during the two months when the city was hosting matches, Luna told the council on Monday. It received 78 calls overall, and 1 in 4 was in Spanish. Without a Spanish-speaking special investigator, staff had to scramble to provide translation, Luna said. “The big challenge was multilingual access,” Luna said. The World Cup was just a blip compared to the Olympics and Paralympics, which will bring millions to Los Angeles. Organizers have compared the event to hosting seven Super Bowls a day for a month. Where will the money come from? The civil rights department plans to submit its funding request to expand its staff in the upcoming budget cycle for fiscal year 2028, Luna said on Monday. That process begins with city departments submitting budget requests to Mayor-elect Nithya Raman, who will present her budget proposal in April. Councilmember Monica Rodriguez, who represents Council District 7, pointed to the city’s strapped finances, saying the department should start planning for how it will adjust if it doesn’t get the money. “We have to be realistic,” Rodriguez said, suggesting the city look into how it could lean on partners, such as L.A. County. The committee also instructed the city administrative officer to look into the department’s request and determine potential funding sources, including the federal government. Less clear is whether the city might ask LA28 to contribute to temporarily expanding the city’s civil rights enforcement staff. LA28 is obligated to pay for city services related to the Games outside what is “normal and customary,” according to a contract with the city and an agreement approved by the City Council earlier this year. That agreement focuses on city resources at venues, and specifies that reimbursement will be for services in “direct support of the 2028 Games.” LA28 has also announced a “ Human Rights Grants Program ” to award individual groups $50,000 to $100,000 for human rights work in the L.A. region. It’s not clear if the city could apply for some of that cash. LAist posed those questions to LA28 on Tuesday but did not hear back in time for publication. Rodriguez said Monday she did not expect help from the Olympics organizers to arrive. “We're certainly not getting anything from LA28,” she said. Editor's note: Capri Maddox sits on the Board of Trustees for Southern California Public Radio, which publishes LAist.com. Published November 17, 2026 4:07 PM The first winter storm of the season is expected to bring heavy rain to Southern California this week. ( Apu Gomes / AFP via Getty Images ) Topline: The first major storm of the winter season is expected to bring widespread rain to Southern California this week. It’s also coming with a dose of chilly weather. The rain: The storm is expected to arrive Wednesday night or Thursday morning, with the heaviest showers coming Thursday afternoon or evening. Parts of the L.A. Basin could get up to 3 inches, with more possible in the hills and mountains. The weather pattern is also expected to bring snow to the mountains. Up to 8 inches of snow could accumulate at high elevations. Flood risk: Forecasters are warning that a high risk of significant road flooding will come with this week’s storm. The National Weather Service will have a flood watch in effect on Thursday. There will also be a moderate risk of debris flows, mudslides and rockslides, especially around recent wildfire burn scars. The risk of coastal hazards will be moderate and include large waves, flooding, rip currents and beach erosion. The temperature: This week will see some of the coolest conditions of the season so far in Southern California. Highs will be in the mid-60s for most of the region, with overnight lows getting down to the 40s. Temperatures will drop even lower at high elevations. The cool period is expected to last at least through the weekend. Is this El Niño? The storm arrives as Southern Californians are bracing for what’s expected to be a historically strong El Niño . But National Weather Service meteorologist Ryan Kittell said it’s hard to pinpoint a starting moment for effects of a global climate pattern. "It's a little fuzzy to call this the start of our rain El Niño signal," he said in an NWS briefing Tuesday, "but this is our first healthy storm of the season." Loading... Listen 0:41 How big money is impacting the LA mayor's race The deadline for the first round of pre-election campaign spending filings was Sep. 24. LAist watchdog correspondent Nick Gerda shares some of the findings. A hedge fund manager who wants more bike lanes and a construction workers' union are the biggest donors in L.A. city elections over the past two months. They put a total of $7 million behind City Councilmember Nithya Raman’s run for mayor, according to the latest campaign filings submitted by Thursday to meet a state deadline. Aaron Sosnick, a hedge fund founder, and the construction workers union — the Western States Regional Council of Carpenters — each gave $3 million to the same committee backing Raman, city filings show. Sosnick gave another $1 million to the pro–Raman political committee of the street-safety group Streets for All. Airbnb has pumped in more than $4 million into backing Mayor Karen Bass and three other city candidates. The filings also show the LAPD officers' union has spent nearly $3 million, money that went to oppose Raman, city attorney candidate Marissa Roy and city council candidate Estuardo Mazariegos, and to support council candidate Tim Gaspar. Most of that Airbnb and police union spending was before the June primary election, though police union spending against Raman has picked up recently. Overall, the filings show Raman’s significant earlier disadvantage in outside dollars has narrowed significantly in recent weeks. So far, the amount of ad spending by outside groups for the general election is similar between the two candidates, with a total of $1.57 million supporting Bass and against Raman, versus $1.53 million supporting Raman and against Bass. Those groups still have millions of donor dollars on hand for future ads. Ballots are set to start hitting voters’ mailboxes by the week of Oct. 5. Sponsored message What to know about the mayor’s race Sosnick runs the New York-based hedge fund A.R.T. Advisors, which uses computer programs to quickly buy and sell stock, to make money from short-term price changes. He is based in Reno, according to campaign filings, and splits his time between New York and L.A.’s Los Feliz neighborhood, according to Michael Schneider, Streets for All’s founder . Sosnick has been a major donor to prior streets-focused campaigns in L.A., including 2024’s Measure HLA. That voter-approved initiative requires the city to add planned bike lanes, bus lanes and pedestrian upgrades when it repaves major streets. Two years after voters approved it, the city had completed only about 300 feet of HLA improvements as of March, Streetsblog L.A. reported at the time . The city paused some repaving and shifted to smaller repairs that stay under the measure's trigger, Streetsblog reported. The construction workers union — which has said most of its nearly 100,000 members are in Southern California — endorsed Bass in 2022, before switching to Raman in August. The union broke with Bass over her affordable-housing directive, ED1, which doesn't require union wages. Another donor to pro-Raman ads, through the Streets for All committee, is real estate developer Todd Wexman, who gave $50,000 . Last year the state issued a $2.3 million wage theft fine to him and other developers over allegations about 124 construction workers. The LAPD officers' union has put more than $2 million into groups opposing Raman. A recent ad funded by the union highlights Raman’s remarks about opposing a city ban on homeless encampments near schools. In the ad, Raman is shown saying she doesn’t "think a kid’s gonna be safer because a tent is 500 feet away from a school." Sponsored message The police union committee also received $525,000 from Douglas Emmett Inc., the landlord behind the largest attempted eviction from rent-controlled housing in the city in decades. The city declined to legally intervene on behalf of the renters, who ended up suing and winning a 2024 court ruling that found the evictions were illegal. Airbnb has given more than $4 million to groups backing Bass, city attorney candidate John McKinney and City Council candidates Jose Ugarte and Gaspar. The city attorney's office has a current lawsuit against Airbnb over alleged price gouging after the January 2025 fires. Whoever wins in November will inherit the case. This year, Bass advanced a proposal backed by Airbnb to relax city regulations by letting Airbnb hosts rent out second homes and investment properties through 2028. Dodger Stadium parking-lot co-owner Frank McCourt's real estate firm also gave $25,000 to a group backing Bass. McCourt needs approvals from the Metro board, which Bass chairs, for a proposed gondola project. Much of Bass' other outside support comes from unions, including the SEIU union that represents most city government staff, whose pay is negotiated by the mayor and approved by the city council. City attorney Beyond $2 million from an Airbnb-backed committee supporting McKinney, the police union’s committee has spent $357,000 against city attorney candidate Roy. Smart Justice California, a criminal-justice-reform advocacy group that wants to reduce incarceration, and a group of trial lawyers are major backers of a committee supporting Roy. The city attorney oversees the city’s misdemeanor prosecutions and defends the city against lawsuits, including those brought by plaintiffs' firms. Sponsored message More LAist watchdog reporting Judge makes it official: LAHSA loses control of LA’s federal homeless money to the county A federal judge has signed off on a step-by-step handoff. Here’s a breakdown of when the switch happens, what it means for shelters and outreach, and who will watch the money. LAUSD spent more than $6 million on its phone ban. Survey data show mixed results In the first district-wide survey since the policy began, students and staff did agree that engagement has improved. New California hospice rules target fraud. Will they fix LA County’s problems? State regulators say the rules can help end billing fraud in the end-of-life care industry. City Council: Gaspar and Ugarte far ahead in outside money In Council District 3, Gaspar’s biggest outside supporters include about $550,000 from an Airbnb-backed group, around $230,000 from a major association for apartment landlords and $136,000 from the police union. His opponent, Barri Worth Girvan, has received a much smaller amount of outside backing, largely from unions, including one that represents construction workers. In Council District 9, outside spending for Ugarte includes about $300,000 by Airbnb and about $230,000 by the landlords association. Among their many responsibilities, the city council votes on rent rules. Ugarte’s opponent, Estuardo Mazariegos, has received much less outside support, largely from the main union for L.A. Unified School District teachers and a tenant organizing group known as ACCE. How the biggest donations flow Direct giving to the candidates’ campaigns is legally restricted to $1,800 per donor each election cycle for L.A. mayor and city attorney, and $1,000 for city council. So the biggest donors instead spend through “independent expenditure” committees, or “IEs.” Donors can give unlimited amounts to these committees, as long as the spending isn't coordinated with the candidates' campaigns. Sponsored message That IE money often flows through multiple committees — many of which combine money meant for candidates in multiple races — on its way to election ads, which can make the money hard for the public to easily track. Set us as preferred p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> Former Los Angeles mayoral candidate Rick Caruso declined once again to endorse either incumbent Mayor Karen Bass or challenger Nithya Raman in the Nov. 3 runoff election, but expressed what he called “extreme concern” about Raman’s plans to remove Police Chief Jim McDonnell. The billionaire developer lost to Bass in the 2022 election, and was a staunch critic of the mayor for her response to the 2025 Palisades fire. Even so, he appeared with the mayor at his upscale Palisades Village shopping center Tuesday to promote a new program to streamline city utility services. While declining to endorse Bass, Caruso commended the mayor by saying “she’s done her work, and she’s worked with the team, and I compliment this.” Advertisement “In comparison, Councilwoman Raman has made statements that we should all ask for an explanation to,” Caruso said, citing her plans to replace McDonnell. “I do show extreme concern when a candidate is talking about firing a chief of police.” Raman’s campaign didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. At last week’s televised mayoral debate, Raman said that if elected mayor, she would replace McDonnell, saying the LAPD appeared to be protecting federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents during their operations in L.A. Raman didn’t give a clear timeline of when she would act. Bass has publicly backed the chief she hired two years ago, and warned that the Police Department could be thrown into disarray if he is removed before the 2028 Olympic Games. Advertisement Caruso applauded Bass’ support for McDonnell at Tuesday’s event. “I don’t think we need LAPD being a lab experiment for the DSA,” Caruso said, referring to the Democratic Socialists of America, which has endorsed Raman. “It’s going to take L.A. in the wrong direction, and we should all be concerned about the direction she wants to take LAPD.” When pressed by reporters about a possible endorsement, Caruso said, “I can’t answer that tonight or today. I’ll let you know.” Caruso also declined to make an endorsement at a groundbreaking he attended with the mayor last month for the new Palisades Recreation Center, calling both Bass and Raman “tough choices.” Bass also sidestepped questions from The Times at the September event about whether she’d welcome Caruso’s endorsement. Caruso funneled more than $100 million of his own fortune into his 2022 mayoral campaign, outspending Bass 11 to 1. Bass defeated Caruso by nearly 10 percentage points. Caruso didn’t run for the 2026 race, despite many expecting him to challenge Bass again. Caruso said Tuesday that he and Bass haven’t always agreed on policy, but came together to help Pacific Palisades in a time of crisis. Caruso has played a prominent role in helping rebuild Pacific Palisades and Altadena following the fires. The 67-year-old developer is behind popular L.A. malls, including the Grove and the Americana at Brand. He also owns Palisades Village, which first opened in 2018 and closed down after the fires destroyed much of downtown. Palisades Village reopened on Aug. 15, after 19 months and more than $100 million in renovations, Caruso said. Advertisement “I know what I’ve seen in the last year and a half, and the help she’s leaned in and given to this community,” Caruso said of Bass. “So, we did get together because it has to transcend politics, and we have to do the right thing.” Bass and Caruso both acknowledged their longstanding relationship, dating back to Bass’ days in Sacramento, she said. The pair have been in constant communication since the 2022 mayoral race and started directly collaborating immediately after the Palisades fire, she said. “My love for the city transcends politics, and I’m going to stand behind people that are doing right for the city and doing right for the people of the city that need the help the most,” Caruso said. “That’s why I’m standing here today.” Caruso joined Bass Tuesday to announce Power Ready LA — an initiative that will streamline how the Department of Water and Power delivers utility services to commercial and residential projects. The effort will result in lower upfront costs for eligible housing and commercial projects, Bass said. It builds on an executive directive the mayor signed in April, which aims to cut delays, introduce tech automation and speed up building permits for residential and commercial development. title: In ABC7 exclusive, Rick Caruso says he's voting for Karen Bass in Los Angeles mayoral race - ABC7 Los Angeles
desc: Former mayoral candidate Rick Caruso says he's voting for the person who defeated him four years ago, Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass.
body: In ABC7 exclusive, Rick Caruso says he's voting for Karen Bass in Los Angeles mayoral race - ABC7 Los Angeles 24/7 Live Los Angeles Orange County Inland Empire Ventura County California POLITICS In ABC7 exclusive, Rick Caruso says he's voting for Karen Bass in Los Angeles mayoral race With eight days left to vote, former mayoral candidate Rick Caruso says he's voting for the person who defeated him four years ago, Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass. By Josh Haskell Tuesday, October 27, 2026 Share LOS ANGELES (KABC) -- With eight days left to vote, former mayoral candidate Rick Caruso says he's voting for the person who defeated him four years ago, Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass. "I think like most Angelenos, I've struggled with the choices that we have, but I've given it a lot of thought, especially a lot thought over the weekend," Caruso told ABC7 Political Reporter Josh Haskell in an exclusive interview. "I've looked at the records and I've made a clear decision of who I'm going to vote for...And that's going to be Mayor Bass," Caruso said. Speaking about Mayor Bass, Caruso said "The last few months, almost a year, we've worked together and I saw a change. She has worked hard to learn from the mistakes of the past. I feel very strongly, because of my love for Los Angeles, I had to put the past behind me. This election, I believe, should not be a referendum of the past. It should be looking for the future of Los Angeles. And I think she's the most prepared to take us into the future of L.A." RELATED: LA mayor race: Bass admits to mistakes on homelessness, slams Raman for wavering on key positions Caruso praised Bass' support of rebuilding Pacific Palisades, expediting permitting and bringing in city resources, specifically to help Caruso open his Palisades Village shopping mall back in August. FULL INTERVIEW: Rick Caruso explains why he's voting for Bass over Raman for LA mayor Rick Caruso explains why he's voting for Karen Bass over Nithya Raman for Los Angeles mayor in an exclusive interview with ABC7 Political Reporter Josh Haskell. Mayor Bass responded to Caruso's support , saying in part, "Rick and I have a long history of working together to solve big problems... I'm honored to receive his support and look forward to working with him over the next four years to solve major problems in our city." Top Stories Storm expected to bring heavy rain, flood risk to SoCal. Here's the timeline 18 minutes ago 'Miracle': All rescued from capsized New Orleans riverboat in tanker collision Landfill geyser erupts at Chiquita Canyon in Castaic, prompts evacuation advisory Caruso has been critical of Bass' first term which has seen homelessness rise, crime fluctuate and experienced the devastating Palisades Fire . But, Caruso says he loves this city and has been impressed recently with Bass and her team. "The mayor has had four years of learning on the job and she's made a lot of mistakes. I've been critical of her. I've been honest, but I'm also honest when she's tried to do the right things and she has done the right thing," said Caruso. "It's not just about helping me. I've asked for no personal help. It's about helping these communities that were so devastated. And she's been open-minded to the suggestions how to get help and public-private partnerships and working together. So, I've been impressed with that. She hasn't been stubborn about it," he added. RELATED: LA Mayor Karen Bass, Rick Caruso come together for Palisades Recreation Center groundbreaking Caruso, a former LAPD Police Commissioner, said he has concerns about Bass' opponent in the race, LA city councilmember Nithya Raman. Caruso said that's a big reason why he's speaking out now. "I also feel strongly that Councilwoman Raman is not ready for the job. She's not prepared for the jobs. I think the positions she's taken with Chief McDonnell are reckless. I think it shows from my point of view as a former police commissioner and the president of the commission, the importance of that job cannot be overstated. And Jimmy McDonnell is regarded as one of the best chiefs of police in this country. The mayor made the right choice, appointing him. And Nithya Raman has continued to double down, saying she's going to remove him," Caruso said. "It will not be good for the city. It will take us back years, which we don't want to do. Not good for LAPD morale. And we're an appointed LAPD that we need to build up the force, and it's been tough recruiting. And so when you have these kind of proposed changes at the top, you're just making it that much more difficult to keep our city safe, especially in light of the Olympics." Although Caruso wouldn't call this an endorsement, he said he wanted to be clear about who he's supporting. title: BEA PAC Endorses Eight Candidates to Win Key Seats as Voters Head to the Polls - Black Economic Alliance PAC
desc: Black Economic Alliance is a coalition of business leaders and aligned advocates committed to economic progress and prosperity in the Black community with a specific focus on work, wages, and wealth. We are using our collective power and business acumen to advance policies that can and will create economic empowerment in our community.
body: BEA PAC Endorses Eight Candidates to Win Key Seats as Voters Head to the Polls - Black Economic Alliance PAC BEA PAC Candidates Research and Polling News Contact Visit BEA Sign Up Donate Press Release BEA PAC Endorses Eight Candidates to Win Key Seats as Voters Head to the Polls By Black Economic Alliance PAC | October 20, 2026 FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE CONTACT: BEA@skdknick.com From Michigan to Nevada, BEA PAC-endFrom Michigan to Nevada, BEA PAC-endorsed candidates are putting Work, Wages, and Wealth on the ballot November 3rd. WASHINGTON, DC – Black Economic Alliance PAC (BEA PAC) – a nonpartisan coalition of Black business leaders and allies supporting candidates who advance Black economic progress and thereby grow the entire economy – today announced its latest round of 2026 endorsed candidates. Through a rigorous vetting process, BEA PAC has determined that these candidates in critical districts and states are committed to advancing a Work, Wages, Wealth agenda that will expand Black economic progress. The endorsed candidates for the U.S. House and Senate include William Lawrence (D-MI-07), Denise Powell (D-NE-02), and Abdul El-Sayed (D-MI). The endorsed candidates for Governor include Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson (D-MI), former Atlanta Mayor and Senior Advisor to President Biden Keisha Lance Bottoms (D-GA), Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley (D-WI), and Attorney General Aaron Ford (D-NV). The endorsed mayoral candidate is Mayor Karen Bass (D-CA) for Mayor of Los Angeles. “BEA PAC is proud to endorse this new slate of candidates because they are committed to advancing policies that strengthen our economy, ensure opportunity, and expand Black Americans’ pathways to work, wages, and wealth,” said BEA CEO Samantha Tweedy . “Voters are looking for leaders with real, achievable solutions that provide an economic vision to help them get ahead, which our rigorous endorsement process ensures each of these candidates has.” BEA’s own polling and research has made clear that rising costs matter to Americans not simply because they are making life more expensive, but because they are making it harder to achieve economic mobility . Voters are looking to candidates who present concrete, achievable solutions to lower costs and build wealth. BEA PAC’s endorsements highlight the importance of electing leaders who will advance policies that expand economic opportunity and strengthen the ability of Americans to work, earn, and build wealth. From state and local investments in workers and families to federal policies that shape access to critical economic resources, leaders at every level of government have a role to play in building an economy that creates opportunity, rather than taking it away. This latest slate builds on BEA PAC’s previous 2026 endorsements, including Governor Wes Moore (D-MD); Senators Cory Booker (D-NJ), Jon Ossoff (D-GA), and Mark Warner (D-VA); Representatives Don Davis (D-NC-01), Lizzie Fletcher (D-TX-07), Steven Horsford (D-NV-04), Lucy McBath (D-GA-06), Kristen McDonald Rivet (D-MI-08), Deborah Ross (D-NC-02), Hillary Scholten (D-MI-03), Marilyn Strickland (D-WA-10), and Lauren Underwood (D-IL-14); Illinois Lieutenant Governor Juliana Stratton (D-IL); District Attorney Scott Colom (D-MS); and former Governor Roy Cooper (D-NC). ### About the Black Economic Alliance PAC Black Economic Alliance PAC is a coalition of business leaders and aligned allies committed to expanding economic progress and prosperity in the Black community — and in so doing, growing the entire U.S economy. We are using our collective power and business acumen to advance candidates of all backgrounds committed to advancing a Black work, wages, and wealth agenda. If you’d like to support BEA PAC’s advocacy for Black economic progress and support candidates for office who are committed to improving work, wages, and wealth for Black Americans, visit https://pac.blackeconomicalliance.org/ .
