The endorsement also gives Raman newfound clout in an area where her campaign has struggled: securing support from her fellow elected officials. Thirteen of her council colleagues have endorsed her opponent, Mayor Karen Bass, while a fourteenth — Councilmember Traci Park — said she is voting for the incumbent despite reservations. Horvath, whose district takes in 2 million people, said Raman will shake up the status quo, bringing a new approach to homelessness, housing affordability, emergency preparedness and other issues. Advertisement “It’s been said that she doesn’t have many friends at City Hall, and I know what that feels like,” Horvath told The Times. “When you take on institutional inertia and decades of refusal to change, that kind of shake-up can feel disruptive to people. But I think that’s the kind of leadership people are clamoring for in Los Angeles right now.” Bass’ campaign declined to comment. The endorsement could give Raman a new rejoinder to Bass’ assertions that she struggles to work well with other political leaders. It also could give Raman new inroads in Horvath’s district, which takes in large portions of the Westside and Valley, including strongholds for onetime mayoral candidate Spencer Pratt, who placed third in the June 2 primary. Horvath, standing next to Raman in Grand Park downtown on Tuesday, issued a lengthy broadside against Bass, blasting the mayor over her record on the 2025 Palisades fire, the Lineage warehouse fire that burned in Boyle Heights this year, the exodus of entertainment industry jobs and other issues. Advertisement “We need a mayor who knows how to make a difference,” Horvath said. “Enough of the excuses. Enough of blaming everyone else. Enough of the Basslighting.” Even with Horvath’s announcement, Bass will have the lion’s share of local political endorsements, including those of the four other county supervisors and county Sheriff Robert Luna. Horvath’s endorsement was not unexpected, given the recent history of acrimony between the two. Still, she and the mayor were not always at odds. Horvath initially supported the mayor’s response to the homelessness crisis, introducing her at the mayor’s State of the City address in 2024. But the two eventually became antagonists, a split that broke into public view in the aftermath of the Palisades fire, which destroyed thousands of homes and left 12 people dead. Horvath, who represents the Palisades burn area, sent Bass multiple text messages in the weeks that followed the fire expressing frustration over her handling of communications and other issues. Later on, Horvath took aim at Bass’ work on homelessness, calling the city’s record “indefensible.” Advertisement Bass, in turn, has criticized county officials for pulling more than $300 million out of the Los Angeles Homeless Services Authority — a move largely spearheaded by Horvath — and into a new county agency focused on homelessness. “Once you create a department, once you create a bureaucracy, it never goes away. And then where’s the incentive to actually end homelessness?” Bass told The Times last month. Bass wasn’t alone in fighting the county over that issue. Last year, Bass and Raman co-signed a letter warning the supervisors the county pullout would create a “monumental disruption” in the city’s fight against homelessness. Raman and four other council members also appeared personally before the county supervisors asking them to hold off. The supervisors approved the plan anyway. Shortly before launching her mayoral bid, Raman also voiced frustration over the county’s handling of mental health services for the city’s homeless residents, and what she described as a lack of data. Horvath said she and her colleagues have responded to the critiques from Raman and other city leaders by working to improve the system. “It’s no secret that Nithya and I don’t agree on everything,” she said. “But we do have respect and regard for one another in our respective positions, and a commitment to make sure that the county and city overcome the mistakes and failures of the past.” Advertisement Horvath is still one of just a handful of L.A.-area elected officials lining up behind Raman. City Controller Kenneth Mejia and school board member Rocio Rivas have endorsed her, appearing with her at campaign events. Several former elected officials, including former Councilmember Bernard C. Parks and former City Controller Laura Chick, have also endorsed Raman’s mayoral bid. More to Read Raman’s colleagues all opposed her run for mayor. Raman received more than $500,000 in matching funds in the period. p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass outraised her challenger, Councilmember Nithya Raman, by more than $300,000 in the first fundraising period of the general election, new campaign finance reports show. The mayor took in more than $510,000 in June, which her campaign said was the most they had raised in a single month throughout her campaign for reelection. Raman raised just over $170,000 in the same reporting period, which covers contributions through June 30 and were filed late Friday. For the record: 1:28 p.m. Aug. 1, 2026 An earlier version of this article said Karen Bass’ team said she had qualified for about $576,000 in matching funds. Nithya Raman’s team said Raman had qualified for those matching funds. 3:20 p.m. Aug. 3, 2026 An earlier version of this article said Nithya Raman raised just under $1 million during the primary campaign. Raman raised just over $1 million. The mayor’s campaign also said that Bass qualified for more than $675,000 in publicly funded matching funds from the city, bringing her total to more than $1.1 million raised in June. Raman’s team said she had qualified for about $576,000 in matching funds, making her total just under $750,000. Advertisement “It’s no accident that June was our strongest month of the entire campaign. It shows that Angelenos understand the stakes of this election and are fully invested in winning this race in November,” the mayor said in a statement. Bass and Raman emerged as the top two vote-getters in the city’s June 2 mayoral primary, setting up the Nov. 3 general election runoff. Former reality TV star Spencer Pratt was in second place on election night, but Raman gained as mail-in ballots were counted and was declared the second-place finisher by the Associated Press on June 8. Bass advanced to the Nov. 3 runoff after taking first place in the June 2 primary, winning about 34% of the vote in the primary. Raman secured the second spot with 29%. Pratt got about 26%. In a statement Friday, Raman said that much of Bass’ financial support comes from vested interests. Bass has obtained financial support from companies including Airbnb and Douglas Emmett Properties. Advertisement “Corporate landlords and other powerful interests are spending record sums to preserve the status quo,” Raman said in the statement, referring to millions in independent expenditures spent during the mayoral primary in support of Bass. “But Los Angeles is not for sale — and our grassroots campaign, powered by thousands of small-dollar donors, will continue to ramp up to deliver the change Angelenos are demanding.” Then Los Angeles mayoral candidate Spencer Pratt speaking to the media June 2 outside of a election night party at Don Antonio’s Mexican restaurant in Los Angeles. (Ronaldo Bolanos/Los Angeles Times) Bass’ fundraising haul came from celebrities, politicians and business leaders. Director J.J. Abrams gave the maximum $1,800, as did Debra Lee, the former chairman and CEO of BET, the parent company of Black Entertainment Television. L.A. City Councilmembers Imelda Padilla and Heather Hutt also contributed, though in smaller denominations. Hutt gave $500 and Padilla gave $100. On Raman’s side, some contributors came from the left flank of Los Angeles while others were more establishment. Advertisement She took in the maximum from Rick Cole, a former aide to City Controller Kenneth Mejia who serves as a council member in Pasadena and has been actively supporting Raman’s campaign. Raman also picked up a donation from former City Controller Laura Chick, who gained a reputation as a sharp critic of the status quo during her time at City Hall. She also raised $100 from Jillian Burgos, who ran for L.A. City Council endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America, but lost. The funds raised by the campaigns will be critical for spending on television and social media ads, direct mailers to houses and apartments and other campaign essentials. Candidates cannot use funds they raised in the primary to pay for general election expenditures. In the primary, Bass raised more than $3.2 million, while Raman raised just over $1 million. Both received the maximum amount of matching funds, $1,257,000, during the primary. Advertisement Bass had much longer to fundraise. The mayor announced her reelection bid in July 2024, while Raman joined the race on the filing deadline in February of this year. The mayor was also heavily favored by independent expenditure groups, which are required to be unafilliated with the campaigns, that spent more than $2.5 million in support of Bass. Independent expenditure groups also spent $1.2 million opposing Raman, while only $88,000 was spent in support of Raman. Times staff writer David Zahniser contributed to this report. Nithya Raman City Councilwoman Nithya Raman, who is challenging Mayor Karen Bass in the Nov. 3 election, was endorsed on Sept. 10 by former City Controller Laura Chick. Raman also announced the launch of a mobile billboard campaign and interactive website showing the cost to communities of the city’s Convention Center expansion. During a news conference at Balboa Park in the San Fernando Valley, Chick said she supported Raman’s bid for mayor, citing the councilwoman’s vote against a “personnel contract” and the convention center project “despite enormous pressure by powerful players at City Hall.” Between 1993 and 2001, Chick represented the Third Council District, encompassing communities in the western San Fernando Valley, and later became the first woman to hold citywide office as the L.A. City Controller from 2001 to 2009. During her tenure as controller, she released more than 170 audits and reports. The Newsletter That Gets It Every Thursday morning, Our Weekly connects you to what’s happening—from city developments to cultural trends—all through the lens of Los Angeles’ African-American experience. Sign up Raman also discussed her campaign’s newest website, Convention.NithyaForTheCity.com, which allows residents to decide how they would have invested the approximately $100 million the convention center expansion project is estimated to take from the city’s General Fund each year. The website calculates how many firefighters, 911 dispatchers, bus shelters, street lanes, curb ramps, sidewalk repairs and resurfaced streets that money could provide, according to Raman. “I want to be absolutely clear: I wholeheartedly support infrastructure projects and downtown revitalization,” Raman said in her remarks. “But our city’s major investments have to be financially sustainable, and they can never come at the expense of keeping basic city services running, especially when many of those services are currently hanging by a thread.” “This irresponsible and politically motivated spending is robbing communities, like here in the Valley, of the kind of services our tax dollars should be paying for, that would improve everyone’s quality of life,” Raman added. In 2015, the convention center expansion project was estimated at $470 million. Approved in 2025, the financing plan calls for $2.68 billion in borrowing and $5.39 billion in total debt service. Alex Stack, spokesman for Bass’ campaign, responded with a statement saying, “Raman is again lying about this being politically motivated – this convention center is something that was agreed upon by business, labor, community groups and just about all of her colleagues. It’s creating thousands of jobs, is already leading to more convention bookings and will benefit local businesses with more people coming to L.A. to spend at restaurants, hotels and other iconic locations. Raman is anti-business and anti-jobs.” The expansion project is being built through a phased delivery, with construction leading up to the 2028 Olympic Games, pausing for that event, then continuing through completion as soon as 2029. Once complete, the project will connect the South and West Exhibit Halls above Pico Boulevard, adding 190,000 square feet of exhibit hall space, nearly 40,000 square feet of meeting room space and 95,000 square feet for a multi-service room. “The expansion of the L.A. Convention Center is crucial to our effort to revitalize the downtown area, create new economic opportunities and send a message to the world that L.A. is ready to compete and win on the global stage,” Bass said in a previous statement, marking a groundbreaking ceremony for the project on Oct. 1, 2025. Since then, 16 large organizations have announced they will be holding major events at the expanded space starting in 2029. LA City Tourism officials have stated that those events will bring more than 100,000 people to the city and provide a boost to the local economy. Even after the projected revenue is counted, the project is expected to cost the General Fund about $100 million annually for decades, according to Raman. Raman and City Councilwoman Katy Yaroslavsky, chair of the Budget and Finance Committee, voted against the expansion, citing concerns with fiscal management. “Modernizing the Convention Center and revitalizing Downtown are important – but no responsible mayor would pursue them through a financing plan that drains essential services for decades,” Nithya said in a statement. “This was a politically motivated deal negotiated for the interests with the most influence at City Hall, not for the residents being told to accept broken streets, dark street lights and bus stops without shade.” “Mayor Bass sided with powerful interests that wanted this project regardless of its cost – and some of those same interests are now spending to keep her in office,” Nithya added. “Valley residents and residents across the city deserve to know what that political bargain is costing them.” The mobile digital billboard began traveling across the San Fernando Valley displaying the website’s comparisons. It’s a “moving receipt for the services City Hall chose to push aside,” according to Raman’s campaign. At Balboa Park, the billboard showed that $100 million could provide 1,066 shaded bus shelters or plant and establish more than 38,000 street trees. It will travel to the North Hollywood Arts District, Ventura Boulevard through Studio City, and to the Universal City/Studio City Metro Station. The billboard will highlight that $100 million could have been used to repair more than 1.3 million square feet of sidewalk or install more than 2,200 ADA curb ramps, or for 400 lane-miles of streets or operate and maintain nearly 176,000 streetlights for a year, or fund approximately 625 firefighter and paramedic positions, or more than 700 civilian 911 dispatchers for a year. “Angelenos deserve independent, fiscally responsible leadership that puts their essential services ahead of politically connected interests,” Raman said in a statement. “As mayor, I will never gamble with the city’s future while urgent needs in our communities go unmet.” Cassandra Horton, a co-founder of the DTLA Residents Association, said her organization voted last year to take a position of support for the convention center expansion. The non-partisan organization does not endorse candidates and work with all elected officials to advocate on quality of life issues, specifically for downtown residents. Horton described the expansion project as a big investment in downtown with the potential of reverberating across the city. “The convention center isn’t even finished yet. We’re kind of very much midstream on a project that’s moving forward, and we already have seen a huge shift in terms of investment around that space – with the investment on behalf of AEG at LA Live, with Oceanwide (Plaza) moving in a positive direction, and that’s been nearly a decade of not having the forward progress that we need for our community there,” Horton told City News Service in a telephone interview. Horton said, as a downtown resident, the organization understands that their community has a responsibility to generate revenue for the city. Downtown also takes on a lot more dense housing, and supportive services in Skid Row. “I think it’s fair for people to ask questions about how the city’s money is being spent. Our hope, like why we really wanted to advocate for this, is to certainly benefit for the neighborhood, but for the whole city too,” Horton said. Horton explained the convention center expansion is happening and quickly, and the question at hand is how the city will move forward with the investment they made. “What are we going to do to make this investment that the city already chose to make as fruitful and as effective, and as catalytic as possible? So, I’d be curious about that from both of them because I don’t really know that there’s a way for us to put that toothpaste in the tube, you know,” Horton added. In a video posted Thursday, the duo criticized City Hall's spending choices, highlighting Mejia's warnings over a $1 billion LAPD contract they claim triggered a local fiscal crisis. Raman pledged to fully fund and restore Mejia's oversight authority, which both claim politically powerful interest groups have actively tried to strip away. LOS ANGELES - In a joint campaign announcement on Thursday, Los Angeles City Controller Kenneth Mejia threw his support behind City Councilmember Nithya Raman's bid for Mayor of Los Angeles. What we know: Both politicians have aligned against what they describe as a broken City Hall establishment, with Mejia highlighting his 2023 warnings that a $1 billion contract for the Los Angeles Police Department would plunge the city into a fiscal crisis. Raman, who voted against that controversial police contract, pledged that if she is elected mayor, she will protect, fully fund, and empower the City Controller's Office. This promise comes in response to what both leaders call efforts by powerful interest groups to systematically neuter Mejia's oversight authority. Mejia also praised Raman's legislative record, pointing directly to her work as the primary force behind the city's largest increase in rental protections in forty years, her advocacy for building new housing, and her role in co-writing the Century City Law to protect immigrant communities. What they're saying: "Los Angeles is not just broke, it's broken. Streets are busted, animal shelters underfunded, childcare centers closed... I warned that the LAPD's $1 billion contract would put us into a fiscal crisis. And guess what? It did," Mejia said. "For too long, powerful interest groups have influenced City Hall, forcing us into impossible spending decisions. As mayor, I'll break from the pay-to-play system that has broken the city," Raman said. "Kenneth has been one of the clearest, most powerful voices for fiscal transparency LA has ever had, and the politically powerful have worked to defang his office and cut into his oversight authority as a result. When I'm mayor, I'll empower and fully fund the Comptroller's Office to make sure that he has the resources to do his job," Raman added. The Source: This report is based on the transcript of a joint campaign announcement released by LA City Controller Kenneth Mejia and Councilmember Nithya Raman. title: Nithya Raman Says She'll Do More For Hollywood than Karen Bass
desc: Addressing a showbiz crowd, the mayoral candidate says she’s uniquely positioned to represent the industry.
body: Nithya Raman Says She'll Do More For Hollywood than Karen Bass × Skip to main content Plus Icon Click to expand the Mega Menu Click to expand search form Got a tip? By Steven Zeitchik Plus Icon Steven Zeitchik Senior Editor, Technology and Politics More Stories by Steven David Ayer to Become a Partner at Ryan Kavanaugh’s New Location-Defying AI Company (Exclusive) The Real Reason Producers Are Fleeing California You Can’t See Everything: The Sneaky Problem With the Elizabeth Holmes Documentary View All October 1, 2026 1:39pm Share on Facebook Share on X Show additional share options Share on LinkedIn Share on Pinterest Share on Reddit Share on Tumblr Share on Whats App Send an Email Print the Article Post a Comment Add us as a Google Preferred Source Nithya Raman spoke at a campaign celebration with volunteers and supporters marking her advance into the general election on June 13, 2026, in North Hollywood, California. Mario Tama/Getty Images Share on Facebook Share on X Show additional share options Share on LinkedIn Share on Pinterest Share on Reddit Share on Tumblr Share on Whats App Send an Email Print the Article Post a Comment Political rhetoric aside, Nithya Raman comes by her Hollywood bona fides honestly. Her husband, after all, is Vali Chandrasekaran, writer on Modern Family, 30 Rock and other TV hits. On Thursday Raman went in front of the industry’s biggest names to argue that her professional credentials were on par with her personal ones and that she’s the candidate who will do the most for the entertainment business. “There’s a lot that mayor could do, and if I’m mayor I’m going to do it,” she told the Bloomberg Screentime conference, suggesting that her rival, incumbent Karen Bass , has fallen short in this (and other) regards. Raman promised to be a “relentless advocate” for better tax credits in Sacramento, though informed observers might note that California’s tax-credit program is among the most generous; it’s the cost of food and housing that drives production costs so high. Related Stories Midterms 2026 Nithya Raman Wins Los Angeles Mayor's Race, Defeating Karen Bass Midterms 2026 Nithya Raman and Karen Bass Head to Costner 'Swing Vote' Territory The City Councilmember also talked up her idea for an L.A. film commissioner to ease the path for shooting, citing a high-profile recent example of a … less smooth road. “Baywatch had problems becayse the city and the county were two different jurisdictions,” she said, referring to the spring kerfuffle . A commissioner could help in situations like that, even if Bass, after a delay, also hired a film liaison last year. Los Angeles runaway production and the subsequent drying up of jobs has become one of many hot-button issues in the election given how many voters work in the entertainment business. Raman says she’s see the effects in her personal life. Speaking to moderator Sarah McGregor and a room packed with luminaries (she followed Casey Bloys two speakers earlier), the candidate said, “We feel lucky but we’ve seen in our friend network how jobs are fewer,” adding, “People that my husband has worked with deciding the industry uncertainty is so much that they’re either leaving the industry or Los Angeles entirely. That’s really painful to watch play out.” After being in a nip-and-tuck race with Spencer Pratt for a second-place qualifying spot for a week following June’s primary, Raman has now surged in the head-to-head general election and leads incumbent Karen Bass by at least 15 points according to most surveys. The City Council member seems to be drawing Spencer Pratt voters (there were nearly 220,000 of them) far more successfully than her opponent, a point she sought to make in Thursday’s talk. “To every voter who voted for Spencer Pratt in the primary who’s disappointed that he’s not in the general election,” she said, “I share your frustration.” As part of that tack to the center, Raman also sought to distance herself from the DSA after McGregor asked her about her feelings for the organization. “I’ve spent most of my talk talking about how we need to give tax credits, which is very much at odds with what Democratic Socialists are to most people,” she said. Raman is a longstanding member of the organization dating back to 2019 and was the first DSA member in the L.A. City Council. Bass and Raman have largely split Hollywood support since the race began earlier this year, with a younger-skewing creative set including Adam Scott and Mindy Kaling supporting Raman while Bass has attracted the likes of JJ Abrams and Samuel L. Jackson. Raman doubled down on issues of interest to the entertainment business when asked about the Paramount Warner Bros. merger. “The deal is essentially done, and don’t want to be re-litigating this into eternity,” she said. “[But] what I would really say to David Ellison is I want those dollars that you’ve committed to production not just to be spent in America — I want them to be spent in Los Angeles.” Read More About: Karen Bass nithya raman Spencer Pratt THR Newsletters Sign up for THR news straight to your inbox every day Subscribe Sign Up More from The Hollywood Reporter Florence Pugh Carrie Coon Calls for Women to Start Their Own Studio as Elle Women in Hollywood Honorees Push for Change Instagram Instagram Testing Joke-Stealing Detection to Crack Down on Fake AI Comics Kane Parsons ‘Heated Rivalry’ Star Connor Storrie, ‘Obsession’ Ingenue Inde Navarette and ‘Backrooms’ Filmmaker Kane Parsons Set as BAFTA U.S. Breakouts Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival From Westeros and Venice Festival Winner ‘Woman Unknown’ to ‘Star City’: Meet Baltic Craft Specialists Who’ve Worked on Int’l Productions Russell Brand Over 400 U.K. Industry Figures Demand End to “Culture of Open Secrets” After Russell Brand Trial Stephen Colbert John Oliver Fills in for Tom Papa at Michael J. body: Political Endorsements – Committee of Interns and Residents Skip to content About Priorities Organize Media Delegate Hub Search let’s Elect Healthcare Champions in 2026 From reproductive rights, resident well-being, healthcare, housing, wages, and more, CIR members have secured major victories. CIR members’ stories were included in the filed complaint (see it HERE ). After the lawsuit was filed, USCIS published new guidelines that limited who is subject to the $100,000 fee, a signal that our lawsuit is making a difference. CIR will continue its lawsuit until the Proclamation is fully blocked. Return to this page for updates. × × Not yet a member of CIR/SEIU? Join today! Find your UC hospital on the map on this page to view your organizer information and member sign-up form. Thank you! × Click to order your insurance card: (800) 541-7846 – Group # G-417732 (877) 923-2847 – Client code: 2200 × Visit Executive Committee page for a larger view × Understanding S.P.I.T. What are the benefits of forming a union? When we come together as housestaff, we have a unified voice for safe working conditions and better patient outcomes. This pandemic has demonstrated that having workplace representation is urgent and necessary. Thousands of residents across the country have organized union chapters and have won historic improvements for housestaff and patients through collective bargaining agreements. What’s legal? What’s not? The laws vary from state to state as well as the type of employer you are paid by – private or public.Generally, however, most laws give employees the right to act together to try and improve their working conditions, with or without a union.It is illegal for employees to be fired, suspended, or otherwise penalized for taking part in protected group activity. Generally, it is illegal for employers to S.P.I.T.: (Document any activity that may look like this) S urveil Administration and department leadership may not conduct unlawful surveillance of employees’ union activity. Identifying, tracking and surveillance of employee discussions about the union or union meetings is illegal. Examples: Supervisors cannot inquire about what goes on at union meetings, ask which employees attend the meeting, or even give the impression of such surveillance. P romise Administration and department leadership must not directly or indirectly promise any benefits or reward employees for refusing to sign a union card, or for voting against your union. They may not promise a wage increase or give preferential treatment in exchange for refraining from union activity. Encouraging employees to withdraw or repudiate union authorization cards is also unlawful. They may not solicit grievances about working conditions while expressly or impliedly promising corrections if residents do not form a union. Examples: “I can get you a job here or give you a good recommendation letter if you don’t get involved.” Reminder: There is nothing holding management accountable to any promises they make and they do not have to follow through. I nterrogate Administration and department leadership should not interrogate , or ask, any employee whether or not he or she favors the union, has signed a union card, or has gone to a union meeting. You can always say you’re not comfortable answering their questions. Remember to ask whether they’ve talked to others, whether they know if they’re allowed to ask, and if they have concerns about residents forming a union and what they are. Questions they may ask: Have you heard of a union being formed? Are you involved? Have you been asked to sign a card? Do any of your colleagues have interest in forming a union? Who have you heard union talk from? Do you think you’ll join? T hreaten Administration and program leadership must not threaten employees with harm or reprisals (economic or otherwise) if they decide to get involved with the union or sign a union card. Examples: Administration may not threaten to take away residency spots or current department benefits if the residents decide to form or join a union. What can we do to protect ourselves? Despite being generally protected, it is always a good idea to be extra careful: Remember to be discrete and never seek advice or reveal to management/administration that you are considering unionizing Refrain from using hospital property – both physical (printers, computers, phones) – and intellectual (email, paging/messaging systems) – in communicating regarding union matters Be mindful of where and when you discuss unionization with your colleagues – being overheard talking about unions in the hospital “on company time” can be considered “solicitation,” so exercise caution and discretion As long as you are using personal means of communication such as personal phones, emails, and only talking to other interns, residents, or fellows, the hospital cannot discipline you Reminder: Forming a union is 100% our legal right and our vote is anonymous. × Click to order your insurance card: (877) 923-2847 – Client code: 3614 × Click to order your insurance card: (800) 541-7846 – Group # G-417732 (877) 923-2847 – Client code: 2200 × Click to order your insurance card: (800) 553-9603 – Group # 720070 (800) 541-7846 – Group # G-417733 (877) 923-2847 – Client code: 2189 (866) 865-4070 – Group # K4DA × Click to order your insurance card: (800) 541-7846 – Group # G-417732 (877) 923-2847 – Client code: 2200 (866) 865-4070 – Group # JRGA × Secret Link

Alliance of South Asian American Labor (ASAAL) Alliance of South Asian American Labor (ASAAL) ensure fairness, respect, dignity, and opportunity in every sphere of life — including the workplace — for all South Asian workers. Transportation Communications Union/IAM The Transportation Communications Union/IAM proudly represents 25,000 members across the U.S., primarily in the railroad industry. TCU merged with the IAM in 2012 and has remained a powerful force for workers’ rights. Climate Action California Climate Action California is an active community of individuals, organizations, and groups—working together to promote science-based climate solutions. California Environmental Voters California Environmental Voters (EnviroVoters) exists to build the political will and power to solve the climate crisis, use climate action to advance justice, and create a global roadmap of innovative solutions that can be exported globally. Project ID Action Fund Over 26 million Americans lack the ID they need to live full lives. At Project ID Action Fund, we advocate for laws and policies to help our communities obtain the IDs they need for jobs, housing, health care, and, most importantly, identity. NEW AMERICAN LEADERS ACTION FUND New American Leaders Action Fund (NALAF) is building a democracy that represents and includes all people by engaging new voters, supporting New Americans as they run for office, and expanding civic engagement. CALIFORNIA WOMEN'S LIST California Women’s List (CWL) is a Political Action Committee that endorses, fundraises for, and elects women to public office in California. Our volunteer board runs the organization and each board member is committed to the mission and values of CWL. East Area Progressive Democrats East Area Progressive Democrats is a vibrant and diverse organization formed to influence lawmakers, candidates, elections, and policies that affect our communities and daily lives. MIRACLE MILE DEMOCRATIC CLUB The Miracle Mile Democratic Club represents the Miracle Mile, Fairfax District, Mid-Wilshire, Hancock Park, Park La Brea, and Greater Wilshire neighborhoods. We are chartered with the Los Angeles County Democratic Party. CAIR ACTION CALIFORNIA Cair Action California’s mission is to engage, educate, and mobilize Muslim voters, train emerging leaders, and champion policy priorities that enhance the well-being and representation of Muslim communities. KOREAN AMERICAN DEMOCRATIC COMMITTEE The Korean American Democratic Committee (KADC) was created to promote the political empowerment, advocacy, and civic participation of the Korean American community within the framework of Democratic Party principles. Democrats for the Protection of Animals Democrats for Protection of Animals promotes the humane treatment of animals by promoting the institution of humane legislation and governmental policy and by increasing public awareness of animal protection issues at city, county, state and federal levels. UELA UELA’S mission is to advocate for policies that promote housing abundance, advance sustainable mobility options, and center environmental stewardship, ensuring that our city remains a thriving and inclusive community for generations to come. WESTSIDE FOR EVERYONE Westside for Everyone is a community of neighbors on the westside fighting for real solutions to our housing crisis. PRO-HOUSING DEMOCRATIC CAUCUS ASIAN DEMS OF LA COUNTY Empowering Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander (AANHPI) communities, supporting leaders who champion our priorities, and advancing policies that deliver real results are central to the future of Los Angeles County. Established in 1985, it focuses on renter rights, community communication, and local quality of life. INDIAN AMERICAN IMPACT Indian American Impact is a national civic and political organization focused on building political power, mobilizing voters, and electing South Asian Americans to public office. FOOD & WATER ACTION Food & Water Action works to protect people’s health, communities and democracy from the growing destructive power of the most powerful economic interests. InlandBoatmen's Union (ILWU) The Inlandboatmen’s Union of Pacific, Marine Division of ILWU, represents workers on the west coast including Alaska and Hawaii. ILWU Local 56 ILWU Local 56 has a long, proud history of fighting for worker’s rights and providing critical services to the Southern California waterfront for over 80 years. TRANSPORT WORKERS UNION OF AMERICA The Transport Workers Union of America, AFL-CIO represents more than 160,000 members across the airline, railroad, transit, university, utility, and service sectors of the economy. SMART-TD Local 1674 The International Association of Sheet Metal, Air, Rail and Transportation Workers (SMART) is a 21st century labor union serving, protecting and raising the living standards of women and men working in the sheet metal, shipyard, manufacturing/production and transportation industries throughout the United States and Canada. California College Democrats Students mobilizing for progressive change in the Golden State . Personal Endorsements KENNETH MEJIA *LA CITY CONTROLLER “You only have two options. That’s it. We can continue the status-quo or not. Many of you asked me who will support the Controller’s Office so we can do our job in overseeing $45 billion annually! That person is Nithya Raman. During her tenure, she was one of the few who: Voted against cutting the Controller’s budget, motioned to get the Controller’s Office more auditors, fought back against eliminating the Controller’s Office, supported an independent protected budget for the Controller’s Office. No matter your politics, we all agree that we need more transparency and accountability over your tax dollars.” WATCH ENDORSEMENT VIDEO LINDSEY HORVATH *LOS ANGELES COUNTY SUPERVISOR , 3rd District “Los Angeles deserves leadership that delivers real results, brings people together, and puts Angelenos first. Nithya Raman has shown the courage to challenge the status quo, fight for affordable housing, champion safer streets, and demand greater transparency and accountability in City Hall. I believe our city needs a mayor focused on data-driven solutions, and progress over politics. I’m proud to endorse Nithya because she has a vision for a more affordable, livable, and equitable Los Angeles — and the determination to turn that vision into reality.” DR. ROCIO RIVAS *BOARD MEMBER, District 2 · Los Angeles Unified School District “As an educator, immigrant, and mother, I’m proud to endorse Nithya Raman. I’ve seen firsthand how hard families work to build a better future, and I believe we need leaders who understand those experiences and will fight for them. Nithya listens, leads with heart, and fights for a Los Angeles that works for everyone.” WATCH ENDORSEMENT VIDEO RICK COLE *PASADENA CITY COUNCIL MEMBER , Former Mayor of Pasadena, Former City Manager of Azusa, Ventura and Santa Monica; and Former Deputy Mayor and Chief Deputy Controller for the City of LA “Everyone except the incumbent Mayor can see that LA is in decline – even if they are afraid to say so out loud. Los Angeles desperately needs leadership focused on making the city work for its residents with the competence and intelligence to produce tangible results. Nithya Raman can provide that crucial leadership. No one else who is running can.” KELLY GONEZ *BOARD MEMBER, Los Angeles Unified School District “Families across Los Angeles, including the students and families I represent in the East San Fernando Valley, are facing enormous challenges, from the rising cost of living and lack of affordable housing to ICE raids that have created fear and uncertainty in our communities. Nithya Raman understands these challenges. She has worked to prevent LAPD collaboration with ICE and expand protections and resources for low income tenants. We need her leadership to address the urgent challenges impacting our students and families so they can feel safe at school and have a real opportunity for a healthy future. I look forward to working together to advance these efforts and ensure our students and families have the resources and opportunities they deserve.” David Hogg *President and Co-Founder: March for Our Lives, Co-Founder: Leaders We Deserve "I had the chance to meet with Nithya Raman and was blown away by her care, fight, and urgency to make LA affordable. She is working to keep families like mine in LA and to deliver for working Angelenos — not billionaire donors. Just like what we’re seeing in NYC with Mayor Mamdani, we can beat the status quo and elect someone who can and will deliver better things." Chelsea Lee Byers *WEST HOLLYWOOD CITYCOUNCILMEMBER "Nithya’s Council District borders West Hollywood and I’ve seen how she has shown up and worked as a good neighbor and partner, proving to me that she is not only serious about her vision for shared prosperity across the region, but she is tireless when it comes to her investment in the work required to make it happen. Solving the most pressing challenges and real needs we have in this region — our affordability crisis, our housing shortage, the gaps in our transportation infrastructure, and our climate crisis — requires deep collaboration and bold action and this is not possible if the City of Los Angeles continues its current trajectory. This region needs courageous leadership to break through and it’s why I’m so excited to support Nithya." LAURA CHICK *FORMER LA CITY CONTROLLER , Former LA City Council Member “Nithya Raman was one of only two people who had the courage to vote against the [boondoggle convention center]. She's accountable, and she's responsible, and she's courageous. Nithya Raman is the mayor the city of Los Angeles has been yearning for. Join me in voting for the leader this city needs. Nithya Raman for Mayor.” WATCH ENDORSEMENT VIDEO KEVIN PEREZ *EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR, Somos Familia Valle “Nithya’s leadership reflects a deep understanding that our communities do not live single-issue lives. We move through the world as Latino, queer, immigrant, working-class, and Valley residents all at once. She understands how those intersecting identities shape the challenges faced by queer community members in the San Fernando Valley. Nithya is willing to push boundaries and stand with our communities to make sure government works for everyone, especially those who have too often been left out of the conversation.” HANS JOHNSON *PRESIDENT, East Area Progressive Democrats “Proud to endorse Nithya Raman for LA Mayor. This hardworking, big-hearted, battle-tested Councilmember & public school parent has a broad coalition & superior plan to solve the biggest problems that bedevil our City of Angels: unhoused residents; unsafe streets & sidewalks due to broken street lights, many with their wires stolen (go solar!) & unaffordable costs of living, including housing, energy, utilities, & transit. Nithya Raman voices nonstop, genuine devotion to the can-do, altruistic, love-thy-neighbor lifeblood of L.A. Her personal involvement in humane lifelines of safety & sustenance for homeless people has served thousands, activated hundreds of volunteers, & built bridges of trust citywide. Hope & optimism rooted in teamwork & leadership by example like hers, are force multipliers. That's exactly what Angelenos say we want now to overcome the rudderlessness afflicting our city. She is ready to serve us ALL as Mayor. Let's GO, LA!” BERNARD C. PARKS *FORMER LA CITY COUNCIL MEMBER (8th District) & Chief of Police, Los Angeles Police Department “I’m proud to endorse Nithya Raman to be the next Mayor of Los Angeles. I admire her courage, independence, and fiscal responsibility, as she is the only councilmember to vote against the city’s most expensive contract and project to balance our budget. I trust Nithya as LA Mayor to protect our tax dollars so that our city can finally restore basic services, increase public safety, and re-evaluate how our officers are deployed. Nithya is the candidate who is ready to accept the challenge of improving our quality of life. I urge all Angelenos to vote for Nithya on June 2nd.” SUJU VIJAYAN *CO-LEADER, East Valley Indivisibles “My Indivisible group endorsed Nithya for City Council in 2020 and 2024. Over the years, she has joined us for backyard chats, Zoom meetings, rallies, and more, making herself accessible to our group in myriad ways. She is also my councilmember, and thanks to her work in the district, we have seen homelessness - in my opinion, the number one challenge facing Los Angeles - drop sharply. Nithya is a pragmatic progressive who cares deeply about our city and wants to make it work better for more people. I am proud to support her bid to become our mayor.” MAGYBET MENDEZ *CHIEF EXECUTIVE OFFICER, Immigo “I’m proud to endorse Nithya Raman because she understands immigrant families not just as a policymaker, but through lived experience. I immigrated to the San Fernando Valley with my family when I was three years old, and for several years, my parents and I were undocumented. I know the fear, uncertainty, and barriers that immigrant families face when trying to access basic city services. My family also experienced immigration fraud, which showed me how vulnerable our communities can be when they do not have strong protections and trusted support.” DAVID KIM *BOARD MEMBER, Korean American Democratic Committee “Nithya Raman brings thoughtfulness, compassion, and a deep commitment to public service to Los Angeles politics. Even in difficult political environments as an elected official, she has continued pushing conversations around housing, affordability, accountability, and making city government more responsive to everyday Angelenos. I believe she has the elected experience, vision, and integrity to help move Los Angeles forward at a time when our city needs serious and people-centered leadership.” AMOS MARVEL *VICE PRESIDENT, Reseda Neighborhood Council “She's smart as a whip, and she's listening and trying to work on things that are pragmatic and have a real impact on people in our community." *Title for identification purposes only. Airbnb is backing Bass. p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> Organized labor is heavily favoring incumbent Karen Bass, but Los Angeles mayoral challenger Nithya Raman scored a key endorsement Tuesday from Unite Here Local 11, the powerful union representing hospitality workers in hotels and airports. Unite Here has emerged as a major player at City Hall, successfully pushing the Los Angeles City Council last year to pass a $30 hourly minimum wage for hotel and airport workers ahead of the 2028 Olympics, although the council later delayed implementation. In endorsing Raman, union President Kurt Petersen said the group believed in the City Council member’s commitment to fighting L.A.’s housing crisis, supporting the minimum wage hike and willingness to oppose short-term rental giant Airbnb — a key rival of Unite Here. Bass has supported delaying the minimum wage hike and expanding the short-term rental market, saying more beds will be needed for the 2028 Summer Olympics. Advertisement “Nithya has stood with us and our members through many fights,” Petersen said, noting that Raman was arrested as she protested with Unite Here workers in 2023 during their contract negotiations. “We believe [she] is the right person to help us solve the city’s problems.” Petersen said Unite Here had the largest ground operation of any union in the state during primaries in June and knocked on more than 300,000 doors. “Our endorsement means a lot more than a press release,” he said. Raman still trails Bass significantly when it comes to the city’s major unions. Bass has more than 30 endorsements from unions across the region while Raman now has five, according to the candidates’ websites. Labor groups backing Bass include local chapters of the Teamsters, the International Longshore and Warehouse Union, L.A. County Federation of Labor and the Police Protective League. The PPL, which represents Los Angeles police officers, has already spent more than $2.5 million against the mayor’s opponents. Advertisement But over the last month, the battle between Bass and Raman for union support has tightened somewhat. In addition to Unite Here, Raman scooped up the endorsement of the Western States Regional Council of Carpenters . The carpenters plan to provide a much-needed bankroll boost of $3 million for an independent expenditure group backing Raman’s campaign. In its campaign for the $30 hourly minimum wage, Unite Here was up against hotels, airlines and other business groups that argued the wage hike would trigger layoffs and closures of restaurants, hotels and airport concession stands. Supporters dubbed it the “Olympic wage,” saying the measure was aimed at allowing workers to share in the expected economic boom that will accompany the 2028 Summer Games in Los Angeles. The council passed the measure but the fight didn’t end there, evolving into a war of dueling ballot measures between Unite Here and a coalition of business groups. The business groups initially filed paperwork to have Angelenos vote on a referendum on the $30 per hour minimum wage for hotel and airport workers. Then Unite Here fired back with a package of ballot proposals , including a plan that would have forced a citywide election on development of all new large hotels and other facilities — including some 2028 Olympic venues. The union also included a proposed ballot measure that would have extended a $30 minimum wage to all workers in L.A. Then business leaders went for the jugular, turning in a proposed measure to repeal the city’s gross receipts business tax , which could have lost the city hundreds of millions annually in revenue. Advertisement The council eventually agreed in May to delay implementation of the minimum wage increase by 18 months in exchange for the business coalition withdrawing the gross receipts measure. Raman and three other council members initially voted against the delay, but Raman later supported it in a City Council vote, saying it provided “greater fiscal certainty” for the city. Bass supported the compromise. Petersen said at the time that the city was giving in to blackmail from the business community. Business leaders said they had simply beat Unite Here at its own game. In 2022, the hotel workers union qualified a measure for the city ballot that would have required L.A. hotels to lease their vacant rooms to homeless people. The union later withdrew that measure, but only after the council struck a deal to require new hotel projects to go through a more extensive approval process at City Hall. Unite Here has also been politically at odds with Airbnb. The union has fiercely opposed allowing Angelenos to rent out their second homes as short-term rentals on sites like Airbnb — something Airbnb has been pushing for years. Bass proposed legalizing vacation rentals in her budget this year, though the proposal was removed from the budget by the City Council. Raman opposed the mayor’s proposal as did Unite Here. Airbnb, meanwhile, has supported the mayor in her reelection bid, pouring nearly $2 million into an independent expenditure group on the mayor’s behalf in the primary. Advertisement Petersen said that Raman’s “unwavering” support of the minimum wage increase for hotel and airport workers, along with her opposition to the vacation rental expansion, were key to her receiving the union’s endorsement. If Raman becomes mayor, he said, he would like to see her enforce wage theft laws as well as laws currently on the books to make sure short-term rental owners are paying required taxes to the city. Times staff writer David Zahniser contributed to this report. Share on Facebook Post Show more sharing options Email Share on LinkedIn Pin it Submit to Reddit Post to Tumblr Share on WhatsApp Print This Page Nithya Raman Getty The Writers Guild of America West has endorsed Nithya Raman in the Los Angeles mayor ‘s race over incumbent Karen Bass . The WGAW PAC cited her “consistent record supporting organized labor and increased local film and television production.” Board member Michele Mulroney said in a statement, “With organized labor under attack nationally, and television and film production leaving Hollywood, LA must elect a mayor who is committed to supporting entertainment workers. That’s why WGAW is proudly backing Nithya Raman, who has a real vision for protecting jobs and supporting the entertainment industry.” Bass’ campaign has highlighted her support among Hollywood labor groups, including IATSE Local 33 and Teamsters 399. Watch on Deadline In their statement, the WGAW highlighted Raman’s walking of the picket lines during the strike of 2023, as well as a Save Hollywood Jobs plan. Raman said in a statement, “Writers are the foundation of this industry, and Los Angeles cannot remain the world’s creative capital if the people who tell our stories can’t build stable careers or afford to live here.” The WGAW PAC endorsed Raman in her 2024 City Council race. Set us as preferred p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> The Los Angeles chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America endorsed Councilmember Nithya Raman for mayor Wednesday, giving the challenger a boost of left-wing, door-knocking energy as she challenges incumbent Karen Bass in the Nov. 3 election. The endorsement came after Raman secured more than 60% of the vote in an online election among the more than 6,000 DSA members in the Los Angeles region, the group said. With nearly 1,500 votes cast, the tally was 937 to endorse Raman and 484 against, with 52 abstentions, according to a screenshot of the vote viewed by The Times. The DSA is known for espousing controversial positions including defunding the police and abolishing prisons — stances that have drawn scorn from conservatives and put it at odds with the Democratic Party establishment. Advertisement The group has notched major electoral victories across the country over the last year, however, most significantly with the election of Zohran Mamdani as mayor of New York. “The growth of DSA has shown a clear movement to the left nationally,” said Sara Sadhwani, a professor of politics at Pomona College. “A DSA endorsement will be shorthand for how to define Nithya Raman as a candidate both for the establishment in Los Angeles and for Republicans nationally.” Raman, herself a DSA member since before her first run for council in 2020, will top a slate of nine candidates backed by DSA-LA in local and federal races Nov. 3. Advertisement “Our base of left-leaning demo socialists are fed up with the status quo and really want to see a significant change in how the city is run,” said Tal Levy, a member of DSA-LA’s electoral politics committee, which voted 3 to 2 to recommend the endorsement of Raman before the organization-wide vote. Levy noted concerns about Raman’s endorsement, conceding she has been a less reliable vote on DSA issues than three other DSA-backed council members in L.A. “That said, I think there is near-unanimity that she is the better candidate in the race in the general election,” he said. In a statement, Raman said she was “proud that DSA-LA is joining our broad coalition of Angelenos working to make Los Angeles a city that works — and where everyone can afford to build a life.” Bass campaign representative Alex Stack declined to comment directly on the endorsement, although he criticized Raman for her stances on public safety and homelessness. Michael Trujillo, a Democratic political consultant who plans to work on an independent expenditure group supporting the incumbent mayor, suggested the DSA endorsement may be more curse than blessing. Advertisement “As more normal Democrats learn about their weird uncle DSA at the dinner table the less and less they’re liking them,” Trujillo said. “Democrats are finding that their weird uncle is belligerent, definitely not normal and has wacky ideas on how the world and cities should operate.” Raman was endorsed by the Los Angeles chapter of DSA in her two council runs as well, and she has passed major legislation supported by the group during her time on the council, including strengthening renter protections and reforming the city’s rent stabilization ordinance for the first time in decades. Raman and the DSA have also had numerous public disagreements that have led some in the group to question whether she would be a good candidate to endorse for such an important role in local government. Her approval of budgets that increased police spending as well as her move earlier this year to revise Measure ULA — also known as the “mansion tax” — to offer an exemption to developers of multifamily and commercial projects drew the ire of many in the group. Her biggest split with the group came after the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack that killed more than 1,200 people in Israel. DSA released a statement saying the attack “was not unprovoked.” Raman called the group’s statement “unacceptably devoid of empathy for communities in Israel.” Advertisement Then, in early 2024, Raman was censured by DSA for seeking and accepting an endorsement from Democrats for Israel-Los Angeles, a liberal Zionist group. Raman was the first L.A. elected official backed by DSA to win office. Since her election, the group has endorsed three more candidates for City Council who have won: Hugo Soto-Martínez, Ysabel Jurado and Eunisses Hernandez. All three of those council members have endorsed Bass. In addition to Raman, the DSA slate for the Nov. 3 election includes Marissa Roy, a candidate for city attorney, and Estuardo Mazariegos, who is running for council in South L.A. The DSA, which dubbed its list of endorsements the “Shake Up LA” slate, said it will also back Angela Gonzales-Torres, who is challenging Rep. Jimmy Gomez (D-Los Angeles) in the 34th Congressional District runoff. The group endorsed two candidates — Nolan Southerland and Mike Van Gorder — for Burbank City Council, and Stephen Post for West Hollywood City Council. In local school board races, the DSA has endorsed Estefany Castañeda in the Centinela Valley Union High School District and Yaritza González in the Inglewood Unified School District. title: LALCV Endorses Nithya Raman for Mayor of Los Angeles | LALCV
body: LALCV Endorses Nithya Raman for Mayor of Los Angeles | LALCV Donate Now × Home About Us About Us Board Members Former Board Members Sponsors Media Latest News Press Releases Videos Endorsements Current Endorsements Past Endorsements Endorsement Process Elections Voter Information LALCV in Los Angeles County Awards & Events Upcoming Past Awards & Events Support LALCV Donate Now Featured News News Press Releases LALCV Endorses Nithya Raman for Mayor of Los Angeles September 21, 2026 The Los Angeles League of Conservation Voters (LALCV) announced its endorsement of Councilmember Nithya Raman for Mayor of Los Angeles, citing her city council record as a champion of critical climate and environmental justice policies, and her environmental priorities for the city’s future. “Los Angeles League of Conservation Voters is proud to endorse Councilmember Nithya Raman for Mayor of Los Angeles. She brings a strong track record on advancing environmental and climate policies and a clear vision to advance urgent climate action as Mayor,” said Maro Kakoussian, President, Los Angeles League of Conservation Voters. “As the City faces significant environmental challenges, from extreme heat, wildfires, air pollution, and neighborhood oil drilling, we need executive leadership that will move an agenda with the urgency these issues require to protect communities and our environment.” During her time on the Los Angeles City Council, Raman has developed a record on issues that improve the health of LA families and protect valuable habitat. These include: building decarbonization, improving air quality, expanding zero-emission transportation, building climate resilience, curtailing neighborhood oil drilling, protecting our urban forestry, and improvements to native habitat. “I’m honored to earn the powerful endorsement of the LA League of Conservation Voters,” said Raman . “Los Angeles should be leading the nation on climate action, but too much of that work remains unfinished. As mayor, I will work with LALCV and environmental justice leaders across the city to clean our air, accelerate the closure of neighborhood drilling sites, decarbonize buildings, create good green jobs and prepare every community for extreme heat and wildfire. Together, we will restore Los Angeles as a national climate leader and make sure every community shares in that progress.” Raman’s mayoral agenda places climate and environmental policy among her priorities and emphasizes greater urgency in responding to climate change. Learn more about Councilmember Nithya Raman and her campaign priorites HERE. About LALCV LALCV is the only environmental Political Action Committee (PAC) in Los Angeles County. LALCV’s mission is to endorse and support candidates in Los Angeles County and its 88 cities for Mayor, City Council, and County Supervisor who exhibit a knowledge of, and commitment to, preserving and protecting the environment. title: Nithya Raman for Mayor of Los Angeles - Our Revolution
desc: Our Revolution is proud to endorse Brad Lander for Congress in New York’s 1st Congressional District, a proven progressive leader with a track record of delivering for working people and standing up to corporate power.
body: Nithya Raman for Mayor of Los Angeles - Our Revolution Skip to main content Close Search Menu ABOUT ENDORSEMENTS ACTION MERCH DEFUND OLIGARCHY D O N A T E twitter facebook youtube instagram Nithya Raman for Mayor of Los Angeles By Our Revolution ALL , CA , Endorsement No Comments Home » Nithya Raman for Mayor of Los Angeles Nithya Raman for Mayor of Los Angeles Nithya Raman has shown what progressive leadership looks like, and Our Revolution is proud to endorse her for Mayor of Los Angeles. As a City Councilmember, Nithya has served as Chair of the Housing and Homelessness Committee — focused on tackling the crisis in LA while working to make city government more responsive to the people it serves. Before running for office, Nithya spent years working alongside communities across Los Angeles to address homelessness and expand access to affordable housing. An urban planner with degrees from Harvard and MIT, she co-founded the SELAH Neighborhood Homeless Coalition, bringing together volunteers to connect unhoused neighbors with housing, services, and support. Nithya’s campaign is rooted in the belief that solving our biggest challenges requires both compassion and effective government. And she is clear that Angelenos deserve a city that delivers for them. Her campaign is focused on addressing the housing affordability crisis by building more homes, making it easier to produce affordable housing, and ensuring that working families aren’t priced out of the communities they call home. Los Angeles voters have repeatedly approved funding to address the crisis, and Nithya believes City Hall has a responsibility to ensure those investments produce measurable results—moving more people into permanent housing while making government more transparent and effective. Throughout her time in office, Nithya has championed a vision of local government that listens to residents, invests in neighborhoods, and makes it easier—not harder—for people to access city services. Those priorities reflect the values that have always driven Our Revolution: building power from the grassroots, making government accountable to ordinary people, and ensuring public institutions serve the public—not special interests. At a time when too many politicians accept the status quo, Nithya continues to demonstrate that bold, people-powered leadership can deliver real change. Our Revolution is proud to endorse Nithya Raman for Mayor of Los Angeles. Together, we can continue building a government that works for working people, not the powerful—and prove once again that when grassroots movements organize, we win. title: Karen Bass, Nithya Raman in dead heat in race for LA mayor – NBC Los Angeles
desc: The UC Berkeley Institute of Government Studies poll co-sponsored by the LA Times indicates a dramatic change among voters who supported third-place finisher Spencer Pratt in the June primary.
body: Karen Bass, Nithya Raman in dead heat in race for LA mayor – NBC Los Angeles Skip to content Main Navigation Search Search for: Local NBC4 Investigates Weather U.S. & World Entertainment Stream NBC LA News 24/7 Watch 24/7 Create profile / Log in Dashboard Email preferences Sign out Trending Dolores Huerta 🗳️Elections 📍Problem Properties 👀 NBCLA on YouTube 🔍 NBC4 Investigates Tips Expand Decision 2026 Karen Bass, Nithya Raman in dead heat in race for LA mayor, poll says The UC Berkeley Institute of Government Studies poll co-sponsored by the LA Times indicates a dramatic change among voters who supported third-place finisher Spencer Pratt in the June primary. By Jonathan Lloyd • Published October 28, 2026 • Updated on October 28, 2026 at 8:06 pm BOOKMARKER NBC Universal, Inc. The latest poll showed that nearly 20% of eligible voters were undecided, while each candidate received 40% support. Conan Nolan reports for the NBC4 News at 4 p.m. on Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. A new poll shows the race for Los Angeles mayor in a dead heat with less than one week before Election Day in California. The UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies poll co-sponsored by The Los Angeles Times released Wednesday shows incumbent Karen Bass and challenger Nithya Raman both with support at 40% from likely Los Angeles voters. Nineteen percent remain undecided, according to the poll. Stream Los Angeles News for free, 24/7, wherever you are. WATCH HERE Decision 2026 Oct 14 Fact-checking the LA mayoral debate between Karen Bass and Nithya Raman Los Angeles Oct 13 Karen Bass vs. Nithya Raman: 5 key takeaways from LA mayoral debate The figures represent a dramatic turnaround from the last Berkeley IGS/LA Times poll in the closely watched mayoral race, which showed Councilmember Raman, a former Bass ally, with a double-digit lead. A sizeable 33% of likely voters were undecided in the previous poll published in late September. Raman, who placed second to Bass in the June primary, was favored by 39% of likely Los Angeles voters with Bass at 28% in the September poll. The drop-off in undecided voters since then likely contributed to the comeback for Bass, who has never lost an election for public office, according to the poll's director. That decline in undecided voters was significant among conservative voters who supported reality TV star Spencer Pratt in the June primary, director Mark DiCamillo told the Times. In the September poll, 22% of Pratt voters indicated they planned to vote for Bass and 16% said they would vote for Raman. That left 63% of Pratt voters undecided. In the latest poll, 41% of Pratt voters said they plan to back Bass over the candidate endorsed by the Los Angeles chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America. Raman's support among Pratt voters was at 14% in the October poll. Forty-five percent of Pratt voters remained undecided, according to the poll. The poll released Wednesday was conducted online Oct. 19 and Oct. 25 in English and Spanish with a sample of 2,197 likely city of Los Angeles voters. The margin of error is about 3 percentage points, according to the Times. "If you to end street homelessness, if you want the city to be more affordable, if you want the city to be more safe, then vote for Karen Bass for mayor," Bass said Wednesday morning. The mayor's favorable ratings, which took a significant decline after the January 2025 wildfires, remained low with 65% of respondents viewing her unfavorably. That figure was at 64% in the September poll. Thirty-two percent had a positive view of the mayor, according to the latest poll, up from 28% in the earlier poll. In a statement, Raman's campaign pointed to the mayor's favorability ratings. "After a month of attack ads and millions from her allies, Karen Bass still can’t get ahead," the campaign said. "Today’s UC Berkeley IGS / LA Times poll shows her tied with Nithya Raman and Bass' disapproval rating rising to 65%. "To repeat: the incumbent mayor is even more unpopular in this poll than last month. And Nithya maintains a lead among Latino voters, with 43% support, compared to 40% for Bass." Bass finished with 34% of the vote in the June primary election with Raman finishing second, good enough to join the November runoff, at 29%. Pratt finished third at 25.5%. Bass was asked about the poll's favorability ratings. "It's interesting because we are in a period in our country where people are just fed up and dissatisfied and frustrated, and I understand that 100%," Bass said. "In my four years, I have made mistakes, but we have laid a very strong foundation to go into the future." The poll, the first since the two candidates met in an Oct. 13 debate hosted by NBC4 and Telemundo 52 , also asked voters about their top priorities for Los Angeles' next mayor. Reducing homeless encampments was, by far, the most important priority (43%) with ensuring public safety and building more affordable housing among other top issues (both 29%). Politics exclusive LA voters scorch state of the city, huge number seriously considering leaving California: shock poll By Jamie Paige Published Oct. 22, 2026, 5:00 a.m. PT See more of our coverage in your search results. Make California Post a Preferred Source Los Angeles voters are fed up with the city’s direction, as rampant homelessness , soaring living costs and sky-high housing prices fuel frustration, a new California Post poll found. A staggering two-thirds of those polled, 66.2%, said they were unhappy with the way the city was going, while just 16.4% believed it’s on the right track, according to the California Post-McLaughlin & Associates poll. Meanwhile, 42% said they’ve seriously considered leaving the state of California in the past four years. Overall, 74.1% named at least one pocketbook concern, along with housing affordability, inflation and government spending. The Post commissioned the survey of 400 LA general election voters, conducted by McLaughlin & Associates from Oct. 15–18, using cellphone calls, text messages and landlines. Advertisement “It seemed very high when four out of 10 residents in the city of Los Angeles wanna move out of state. They’re going to lose some of the most productive taxpayers and citizens,” pollster John McLaughlin told The Post. “I’ve not seen numbers like that. Possibly in New York, but other than that, that’s a very high number, because you’re saying seriously consider it. You know, it’s not a flippant thing,” he added. 7 Voters also returned a damning verdict on whether they want Karen Bass as their mayor after the election next month, with an overwhelming majority disapproving of the job she has done. Advertisement The survey found 71.7% of voters disapprove of her reign, while just 25.5% approve, figures that McLaughlin described as ”shocking” for a Democratic mayor in a deep blue city.” The disapproval is across all ages, races and with both sexes. It leaves LA staring down the barrel of a socialist-backed Nithya Raman sweeping to power, having surged in the ratings with younger voters. Raman, backed by the Democratic Socialists of America, leads Bass 46.7% to 38.8% in a head-to-head matchup, with 13.5% undecided. Bass is also facing a backlash from her own party, with a staggering 65.5% of registered Democrats surveyed disapproving of her job performance. Advertisement 7 Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass faces a tough reelection battle as a new California Post poll finds nearly 72% of voters surveyed disapprove of her job performance. AP Photo/Amanda Villegas 7 Bass’ numbers are particularly bad among young voters. Just 12.3% of voters ages 18 to 29 approve of her, compared with 48.4% of those older than 65. 16.6% of those polled pointed to the mayor’s job performance when asked what they disliked most about Bass, 11.5% to her personality and 8.8% to her wildfire response. Advertisement But there’s a glimmer of hope for Bass: Pollsters warned Raman’s lead could evaporate if older voters stick with the incumbent while younger voters fail to turn out. Older voters could prove critical, according to Dan Schnur, a political analyst who teaches at USC, UC Berkeley and Pepperdine. “The strength of Raman’s support comes from young voters who do not turn out as reliably as their parents and grandparents,” he said. “Bass is judged unfavorably by voters of every age group, but her strongest support comes from the oldest voters.” 7 LA mayoral challenger Nithya Raman leads incumbent Karen Bass 47% to 39% in a new California Post poll, despite significant voter concerns about her political ideology and effectiveness. ZUMAPRESS.com Advertisement 7 Just 26% of voters surveyed approve of Mayor Karen Bass’s performance, while two-thirds believe Los Angeles is headed in the wrong direction. AFP via Getty Images Despite Bass’s dismal approval ratings, Raman has yet to win over a majority of voters, with 45.4% viewing her favorably and 43.7% unfavorably. Raman’s left-wing politics drew the sharpest criticism, with 15.3% citing her socialist ties through the DSA as their biggest concern. Another 14.4% called her ineffective, 13.1% branded her policies radical and 10.3% questioned her experience. Asked which candidate was more extreme, 41% pointed to Raman, compared with just 16.4% for Bass. The remaining 42.6% declined to choose. Advertisement Veteran pollster Justin Wallin, a political strategist and fellow at USC’s Jesse M. Unruh Institute of Politics, warned Raman’s lead does not guarantee a victory. He compared the contest to a recall election, saying widespread dissatisfaction with an incumbent doesn’t automatically translate into support for a challenger. “The incumbent is not liked, this is true. But the challenger must give voters a ‘home’ that they are more comfortable with than the status quo… this is more difficult than it appears,” he said. “If anyone says they know for certain which way this race will go come Election Day, they are pulling your leg,” Wallin said. “It is simply too close to call.” The voters who backed unsuccessful independent candidate, Spencer Pratt, in the June primary, will be crucial in deciding the race, Schnur told The Post. Advertisement 7 LA mayoral challenger Nithya Raman leads incumbent Karen Bass 47% to 39% in a new California Post poll, despite significant voter concerns about her political ideology and effectiveness. ZUMAPRESS.com 7 Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass faces a tough reelection battle as a new California Post poll finds nearly 72% of voters surveyed disapprove of her job performance. London Entertainment “The Pratt vote is key. That’s why Bass talked so much about law and order and public safety in the debate, and it’s why the DSA candidate quoted Ronald Reagan in her opening statement,” he said. Raman also leads Bass on empathy, with 37.1% of voters saying she cares more about people like them, compared with 22.5% for Bass. The remaining 40.4% were undecided or declined to answer. Advertisement Meanwhile, geographically, Raman leads in the San Fernando Valley 44% to 38%. Bass dominates the combined Westside and Harbor area, 52% to 27%. But Raman is also leading in Central LA, East LA and South LA. Schnur said Bass’s only play now is to go after her opponent. “Bass isn’t gonna change the voters’ minds about her at this point,” he said. “The question is whether she can make them even more frightened of Raman.” “The path is still there, but the window’s closing very rapidly.” Election Day is on November 3. Sign Up Facebook X Print How to win the Central Valley By BLAKE JONES and MELANIE MASON 10/09/2026 09:00 AM EDT Canals carry water to Southern California in the Westlands Water District in California's Central Valley in 2009. | Russel A. Daniels/AP DIFFERENT STROKES — California Democrats’ midterm calculations hinge on two dramatically different House races in the Central Valley. National Republicans’ top incumbent target in the state, blue dog Democratic Rep. Adam Gray , is running a centrist campaign focused on issues such as water and agriculture rather than appealing to his party’s base with red meat. Meanwhile, progressive populist Randy Villegas has nationalized his race against Rep. David Valadao , calling for higher federal taxes on the rich, reining in immigration raids and passing single-payer health care in an effort to energize voters in his lower-turnout district. The divergent approaches will test Democrats’ longstanding strategy of running moderate or conservative-leaning candidates in one of California’s most fiercely contested regions. The results could matter not just for control of Congress next year, but for the future of the party in a region that has grown more important since Proposition 50 reduced the number of swing House seats in the traditionally competitive Orange and Riverside counties. “It’s almost like the fundamental question for both parties,” said Paul Mitchell , the Democratic consultant who drew each district, “whether or not the candidates that get elected from that populist wing are better because they are more motivating, or whether the candidates who are of the party but not as populist do better because they offend less people on the other side.” Both agriculture-heavy districts, Gray’s cutting through Modesto and Merced and Villegas’ encompassing rural farmland between Fresno and Bakersfield, are drawing outsize spending from national super PACs that see them as flip opportunities. Democrats in previous cycles have underperformed their double-digit voter registration advantages in each. But last year’s gerrymander marginally helped Democrats in both districts, adding Democratic voters from Fresno to Villegas’ district and from Stockton — where Gray’s opponent Kevin Lincoln was mayor — to his. Latino voters, who comprise majorities of each district’s residents, could prove to be decisive. Mike Madrid , the Lincoln Project co-founder who studies Latino voters, predicted they will swing drastically away from Republicans in both districts this year in reaction to Donald Trump ’s policies. But, he predicted, such a broad shift could obscure whether Latino voters prefer an approach more like Villegas’ or Gray’s. “What’s happening with the fundamentals of the race, and the mood of the electorate, and Latinos shifting the way that they are, there’s not going to be much to discern,” Madrid said. “Now, if something happens and Randy wins and Adam Gray loses, OK, let’s have that conversation. Do I think that happens? No. I think the chances of that are virtually nil.” House Republicans’ and Democrats’ campaign arms have been active in both races, a sign of their competitiveness. Aside from spending heavily in both, Speaker Mike Johnson recently came to the Valley to campaign for Lincoln and Valadao, while Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee Chair Suzan DelBene is in California to fundraise for candidates in both districts and stump for Gray. Gray has the advantage of incumbency — while Democrats in what are arguably the other two most competitive California House races, Villegas and Marni von Wilpert — do not. And unlike Villegas, he’s running for a district that Kamala Harris also won in 2024, even if its Democratic registration edge is smaller. “Adam Gray’s district is much more Democratic leaning in terms of not registration, but in terms of its performance, and as a result, his district is more safe even in a bad Democratic year,” said Mitchell. “Very different districts.” The campaigns are tailoring their attacks differently, too. Valadao’s district is lower income and more heavily dependent on programs including Medicaid, which helps explain why the DCCC has slammed Valadao for health care cuts. But in Lincoln’s race, it has trained its fire on the former mayor’s record in local government. Oil and gas are more instrumental to the economy in Valadao’s district, suggesting motivation for national Republicans who have spent heavily bashing Villegas over his environmental bona fides.
