Young Kim (R-Calif.) arrives for a House Republican Conference caucus meeting on Capitol Hill, on May 20, 2026. | Bill Clark/AP FIRST IN PLAYBOOK: KIM’S CASH — Young Kim raised $1.15 million last quarter and had $2 million in the bank for the final weeks of the campaign, according to her team. In all, the GOP member from Orange County has raised $10 million in her race against fellow Republican Rep. Ken Calvert in what has become an intra-party slugfest, after last year’s redistricting measure drew them into the same seat. “Raising more than $10 million from supporters who believe in her mission is a remarkable achievement for a non-targeted seat, though admittedly still less than the massive personal fortune Ken Calvert has amassed for himself after nearly four decades in Congress,” said Chris Pack , a spokesperson for Kim. LOS ANGELES LA POLLERCOASTER — Recent polls in the Los Angeles mayor’s race have pointed to a neck-and-neck race, but a new survey commissioned by a pro- Nithya Raman group says the councilmember is breaking away with a 10-point margin over incumbent Mayor Karen Bass . Raman leads 43% to 33%, with roughly a quarter of voters undecided — a significant gain for Raman since the group’s poll a month ago, which found the two candidates deadlocked. Much of the vote shift, according to the polling memo by Impact Research , was driven by a 13-point net decline in Bass’ favorability ratings. “These numbers tell a remarkable story about Nithya Raman’s rise — and Karen Bass’ failure to meet the moment. Raman entered this race as an underdog and has surged into first place because Angelenos are tired of excuses and ready for a mayor who delivers,” said Estevan J. Montemayor , chief strategist for the Estamos con Nithya for Mayor of LA 2026, which is backed by the carpenters union. FIRST IN PLAYBOOK: BLOWING SMOKE — A local ballot measure to raise money for the Pasadena Fire Department with an increased parcel tax is turning into a brawl between two statewide political heavyweights. The California Professional Firefighters and Pasadena’s local firefighters union are slamming the initiative’s opponents, particularly the California Association of Realtors, for a recent TV ad and website, which the proponents say deceptively imply that fire crews are associated with the No on Measure PFD campaign. Opponents to the parcel tax rolled out the ad this week, which begins with a brief image of emergency personnel in a fire as a narrator states, “we support Pasadena’s firefighters and paramedics.” The ad goes on to argue against the measure as adding to a series of recent tax hikes. “The California REALTORS website and ad is a slap in the face to every single firefighter in the City of Pasadena and beyond. It’s dishonest, disgraceful, and extremely misleading,” said Raffy Bitchakdjian , president of Pasadena Firefighters Association Local 809, in a statement. Darrell Roberts , president of the California Professional Firefighters, demanded the realtors group take down the ad and website. “The REALTORS want higher profits for themselves at the expense of Pasadena’s public safety, and they’re willing to trick voters to achieve that. We won’t stand for it,” Roberts said. Matt Klink , a consultant for the No campaign, said the ad would remain active. “Campaigns use images to highlight what we’re talking about,” Klink said. “We enthusiastically support firefighters. Supporting firefighters doesn’t automatically mean you have to vote for a tax increase.” Introducing: The Enforcers by POLITICO Your indispensable guide to state attorneys general, America’s most influential regulators. STATE CAPITOL HITTING BACK — Gavin Newsom used reports of a statewide federal immigration enforcement campaign to again hit the Trump administration, saying the president is “using fear and panic as a weapon — putting families at risk, undermining our economy, and terrorizing communities.”“No President is above the Constitution,” Newsom said in an X post . “No one in this country is without rights. California will stand up for our communities and hold federal agents accountable. Know your rights and exercise them safely.” — Lindsey Holden DOWN THE BALLOT Ben Allen speaks at the 2026 California Democratic Party State Convention in San Francisco on Feb. 21, 2026. | Jeff Chiu/AP FIRST IN PLAYBOOK: ALLEN’S ADS — State Sen. Ben Allen is going up with English and Spanish language ads in California’s only statewide general election race between Democrats. The digital spots for his insurance commissioner campaign against former San Francisco Supervisor Jane Kim , put together, swipe at his opponent’s plans for a state-run, universal property insurance plan, and tell voters he’d push to get costs under control. They’re set to run through Election Day with a six figure spend behind them, according to a spokesperson for Allen’s campaign. TECH TALK Waymo will offer rides to select customers at San Francisco International Airport. | Godofredo A. Vásquez/AP WAR ON WAYMOS — California’s newly recognized union for Uber and Lyft drivers is urging state utility commissioners to tighten autonomous vehicle regulations as Waymo eyes expansions in Sacramento, San Diego and beyond. “This isn’t some San Francisco problem. It’s coming to our streets right now,” Gurpreet Pannu, a ride-hailing driver and member of the SEIU-backed California Gig Workers Union, said at a Thursday rally in Sacramento. “We want a real review, real accountability, real public oversight.” The demands show how the new union is flexing its muscle against increasing competition from AVs. Rather than calling for outright bans, human drivers are seizing on safety fears to resist expansion into the Central Valley and limit driverless vehicles’ access to lucrative pickup areas like airports. They’re using high-profile incidents like last year’s power outage in San Francisco that stalled hundreds of Waymos to justify their pitch for stronger guardrails. What drivers want: Strict third-party reviews of AV training data, minimum 30-day public review before AV operators expand to new regions and new safety certifications for AV service at airports — items union officials suggested they may pursue through legislation. — Tyler Katzenberger CALIFORNIA CURRENTS BYTE ME — Concern about data centers, and the artificial intelligence they power, is hitting a fever pitch. With less than a month until Election Day, California politicians are trying to harness those fears to tear down their opponents. Read last night’s California Currents to learn how the controversial server farms are playing into campaigns across the state. Top Talkers SEEKING SAFETY — Democratic Reps. Sara Jacobs of California and Don Beyer of Virginia are working on an artificial intelligence framework that would compel the AI labs to have safety frameworks with minimum standards in place, grant the government emergency authority to shut models down if they fail testing requirements and clarify liability rules, a person with direct knowledge of the legislation told Gabby Miller . The proposal, which has not been previously reported, would also ensure a federal agency tapped to oversee the powerful technology has the resources and authority to do so effectively, the person added. Jacobs and Beyer first previewed the working framework on a panel at The Curve, an invite-only conference hosted last weekend in Berkeley, where industry luminaries, state and federal lawmakers, foreign leaders, and major donors convened to discuss major AI policy dilemmas. SPORTS POLITICS — The National Football League asked the Supreme Court to take up a case that could give states the power to regulate sports bets on prediction markets such as Kalshi and Polymarket, Gregory Svirnovskiy reports . “The NFL’s very top priority has been preserving the integrity of its games and protecting its fans as legal sports betting spread state by state,” the league wrote in an amicus brief sent to the high court Thursday. The NFL’s brief came in support of New Jersey, which asked the Supreme Court last month to decide whether state or federal officials had the power to regulate prediction markets. But President Donald Trump believes the job of regulating them should fall to the federal government alone. AROUND THE STATE — Local and federal authorities in Los Angeles arrested more than two dozen people in what they described as a sweeping crackdown on Skid Row drug trafficking. ( Los Angeles Times ) — Three San Francisco police officers allegedly beat a man so brutally last year that he nearly fell into a coma. ( Mission Local ) — Following months of stalled negotiations and a state board ruling Orange County negotiated in bad faith, hundreds of county teamsters plan to strike unless they get a new offer for raises. ( Voice of OC ) — compiled by Riley Ramirez PLAYBOOKERS FIRM MOVES — Political strategist Astine Suleimanyan is launching Capitol A Strategies , a Los Angeles-based political consulting and public affairs firm. Suleimanyan, the firm’s founder and principal consultant, is currently consulting for California State Treasurer Fiona Ma and served as manager of Ma’s lieutenant governor campaign. She is also an expert in the state’s congressional swing districts and wrote behind-the-scenes accounts of how California " bluffed its way into a redistricting war with Trump ." Melanie co-moderated the first televised debate for the race to replace former Sen. Dianne Feinstein and is a frequent moderator at other political panels around the state and beyond. She is a graduate of Georgetown University and the University of California, Berkeley Graduate School of Journalism. Melanie lives in Los Angeles, where she was born and raised and has the sports allegiances to prove it. Thank you for signing up! A new survey conducted by the Manhattan Institute examines the attitudes of California likely voters one month before Election Day. The poll surveyed 1,000 likely voters statewide and a separate sample of 449 likely voters in Los Angeles, allowing for a detailed look at both the statewide electorate and the political dynamics shaping the state’s largest city. The survey helps clarify a central question confronting California politics: Does the state’s long-running pattern of Democratic electoral success reflect an endorsement of its governing approach, or does it coexist with broader dissatisfaction about the state’s performance on its most pressing challenges? Democrats remain well positioned electorally. Xavier Becerra holds a commanding 17-point lead over Republican Steve Hilton in the race for governor. City Councilmember Nithya Raman holds a six-point advantage over incumbent Karen Bass in the Los Angeles mayoral race, narrowing to three points with leaners included. The mayoral contest is complicated by the fact that half of Spencer Pratt’s primary supporters say they plan not to vote in the race rather than back either finalist. But voters also express considerable frustration with the state’s performance. Only 32% of California voters believe that their state is headed in a better direction than other states, while 45% believe it is headed in a worse direction. More than four in five Californians (81%) and Angelenos (83%) say the state has a bigger homelessness problem than other states. A majority say California is less business-friendly than its peers, while pluralities rate the state negatively on infrastructure, public safety, and corruption. Concern about waste, fraud, and abuse in the welfare system is also widespread. Both Governor Gavin Newsom and former Vice President Kamala Harris have negative net favorability ratings among voters in their home state. Notably, nearly one in four of Harris’s own 2024 voters (24%) view her unfavorably, despite her comfortable victory in the state as the Democratic nominee for president. On a range of major policy questions, voters frequently depart from the state’s progressive reputation. Californians oppose Proposition 40, the proposed billionaire wealth tax, by a 50% to 35% margin. A majority believe that the state’s Medicaid program Medi-Cal should be limited to those with legal status. Most oppose race-conscious hiring and admissions policies, and nearly two-thirds would support limiting the power of public-sector unions if doing so would improve accountability and service delivery. On homelessness, voters overwhelmingly attribute the crisis to substance addiction and mental health issues rather than housing affordability. Taken together, the findings suggest that Democratic electoral strength in California should not necessarily be interpreted as an endorsement of the status quo. Voters continue to prefer Democratic candidates while expressing dissatisfaction with the state’s direction and performance. On issues ranging from homelessness and public-sector unions to welfare administration, infrastructure, and taxation, voters are interested in reform and more effective governance. Full Results Available: Statewide Toplines , Los Angeles Toplines , Crosstabs Methodology Between September 24 and October 1, 2026, the Manhattan Institute surveyed 1,000 likely voters in California and a separate sample of 449 likely voters in the City of Los Angeles. The sample was reached via live cell-phone interviews (300 statewide, 142 Los Angeles), SMS-to-web interviews (500 statewide, 227 Los Angeles), and online panel interviews (200 statewide, 80 Los Angeles). In addition to self-reported voting intention, voters reached through cell and SMS were drawn from a modeled universe of likely voters from the voter file, based on their previous general election participation. The statewide and Los Angeles samples were weighted separately to their own likely-voter targets based on gender, age, education, race and ethnicity, party registration, 2024 presidential vote, past general election turnout, and geographic region. Results reported for Los Angeles-specific questions are based only on respondents residing within the City of Los Angeles. The margin of error is ±3.1 percentage points for the statewide sample and ±4.6 percentage points for the separate Los Angeles sample. The Race for California Governor Democrat Xavier Becerra is the clear favorite in California’s gubernatorial race. He receives support from 55% of likely voters, compared with 38% for Republican Steve Hilton, while 7% remain undecided. ( Figure 1 ) Figure 1 Both parties appear highly consolidated behind their nominees. Becerra has the support of 93% of Democrats, while Hilton receives backing from 96% of Republicans. Among independents and other unaffiliated voters, Becerra holds a meaningful advantage, leading Hilton 48% to 39%. Becerra’s coalition is especially strong among younger voters (65% Becerra, 30% Hilton), women (59% to 33%), black voters (72% to 22%), and college-educated Californians (63% to 31%). Hilton performs best among men (43% support), non-college voters (43%), and independents and other unaffiliated voters (39%), though he still trails Becerra among each of those groups. The race is unlikely to change significantly. After the 7% of undecided respondents were pressed to make a choice, Becerra’s lead shifts modestly to 57% (+2) compared to Hilton’s 39% (+1), leaving just 3% of voters truly undecided. ( Figure 1 ) With so few voters still undecided, the electorate appears firmly settled behind the Democratic nominee. The Race for Los Angeles Mayor The Los Angeles mayoral race remains competitive, though Nithya Raman currently holds a modest advantage. Raman receives support from 38% of likely voters, compared with 32% for incumbent Mayor Karen Bass, with 30% remaining undecided. ( Figure 2 ) The topline appears to reflect the weakness of the incumbent as much as enthusiasm for the challenger. Bass is viewed favorably by just 33% of Los Angeles voters and unfavorably by 61%. Figure 2 Raman performs particularly well among younger voters (51% support among voters 18–29 and 49% among voters 30–49), college-educated voters (43%), Asian voters (42%) and women (40%). Bass’s strongest support comes from older voters (42% among those 50–64 and 36% among those 65-and-up), and black voters (48%). Despite Raman's lead, the race remains unsettled. Nearly one-third of voters reported as undecided in the initial ballot test, but after those respondents were pressed to make a choice, Raman’s advantage narrowed to 39% to 36%, while 15% of voters said they actively plan to leave the mayoral race blank, and another 10% remained truly undecided ( Figure 2 ). Much of that disengagement is concentrated among supporters of Spencer Pratt, who finished third in the June primary, leaving a sizable bloc of voters now reluctant to back either finalist. 50% of Pratt voters say that they intend to support neither Bass nor Raman, while 28% move to Bass and 10% to Raman ( Figure 3 ). Figure 3 The survey also tested whether Los Angeles voters prefer a democratic socialist or a moderate Democrat as a hypothetical mayor. Respondents were randomly divided into two groups and shown the same policy descriptions. In one group, those policies were ascribed to an unnamed moderate and democratic socialist; in the other, they were ascribed to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie. In the unnamed test, voters preferred the moderate Democrat by an eight-point margin (47% to 39%). With the names and offices included, voters preferred Mamdani by a 43% to 35% margin ( Figure 4) . The contrast suggests that candidate identity can affect responses to the same policy platforms, complicating any interpretation of a Raman victory as a mandate for democratic socialism. Figure 4 Proposition 40: A Wealth Tax on Billionaires This November, Californians will vote on Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of the state’s billionaires. Voters oppose the measure by a 50% to 35% margin, with 15% undecided ( Figure 5 ). The clearest demographic divide is generational: voters aged 18 to 29 support the measure at substantially higher rates (50%) than voters aged 50 to 64 (28%) and those 65 and older (28%). The partisan divide is equally pronounced. Republicans oppose Proposition 40 overwhelmingly (83% to 10%), while independents and other unaffiliated voters oppose it by a 51% to 34% margin. Democrats support the proposal, but far from unanimously, with 50% to 31% in favor and nearly one in five undecided. Among gubernatorial voters, Becerra supporters back the measure (52% support, 28% oppose), while Hilton supporters overwhelmingly oppose it (82% oppose, 10% support). Among Los Angeles voters, Raman supporters strongly back the measure (66% support, 17% oppose), while Bass supporters oppose it (54% oppose, 29% support). Figure 5 Favorability Ratings Two of California’s most prominent Democrats carry negative net favorability ratings with voters. Governor Gavin Newsom is viewed favorably by 46% of likely California voters and unfavorably by 52%, while Kamala Harris is viewed favorably by 47% and unfavorably by 50%. The Democratic nominee for governor, Xavier Becerra, performs somewhat better, at 47% favorable and 41% unfavorable. ( Figure 6 ) Newsom and Harris are especially unpopular among men and Asian voters. Men view Newsom unfavorably by a 57% to 41% margin and Harris unfavorably by a 56% to 40% margin. Among Asian voters, Newsom’s unfavorable and favorable ratings are 56% and 39%, respectively, while Harris’s are 58% and 36%. Independents and other unaffiliated voters also view both politicians negatively: 60% view Newsom unfavorably, compared with 37% favorably, while Harris’s ratings are 58% unfavorable and 36% favorable. Becerra’s standing is somewhat stronger, though he is also less well known. 12% of voters say they have no opinion of Becerra, compared with only 2% for Newsom and 3% for Harris. Steve Hilton is also less well known than several national figures tested. He receives a 39% favorable rating and a 47% unfavorable rating, with 14% unsure. Although his ratings are net negative, they are stronger than those of Donald Trump (32% favorable to 65% unfavorable), JD Vance (35% to 62%), and Marco Rubio (34% to 56%) ( Figure 6 ). Figure 6 [1] California’s Direction Californians are more pessimistic than optimistic about their state’s trajectory. 32% believe that California is headed in a better direction than other states, while 45% believe it is headed in a worse direction. 18% say California is headed in roughly the same direction as other states. Los Angeles voters mirror the broader statewide mood, rating California’s direction negatively by a 42% to 30% margin. ( Figure 7 ) Figure 7 Views of California’s direction differ sharply by both party and race. Among Democrats, better direction leads by a 35-point margin (52% better to 17% worse). Independents and other unaffiliated voters say worse direction by a 23-point margin (26% better to 49% worse) and Republicans by an 84-point margin (3% to 88%). [2] Black voters are the most optimistic racial group, with 35% saying California is headed in a better direction than other states and 33% saying it is headed in a worse direction. White voters are net 12 points negative, Hispanics net 7 points negative, and Asian voters net 20 points negative. Voters also express skepticism on more particular issue areas. A majority of voters (56%) say California is less business-friendly than other states, compared with just 14% who say it is more business-friendly. On several major quality-of-life measures, voters consistently rate California poorly relative to other states. More voters say California is less safe than other states (37%) than safer (23%), with 36% saying it is as safe as other states. 81% say California has a bigger homelessness problem than other states. More voters describe the state’s infrastructure as worse than that of other states (43%) than better (16%). A 42% plurality believe that California has a larger corruption problem than its peers. ( Figure 8) Taken together, these results paint a picture of an electorate that is broadly dissatisfied with the condition and trajectory of the state. Figure 8 [3] What Matters Most to California Voters For California voters, the dominant issue is the cost of living. Nearly half (47%) identify cost of living, taxes, and jobs as the most important issue facing the state, far outpacing government waste and corruption (17%), healthcare costs and access (7%), homelessness (6%), immigration (6%), and crime and public safety (4%). ( Figure 9 ) Across virtually every major demographic and political group, pocketbook concerns rank first. Figure 9 Government waste and corruption ranks as the second-most important issue, selected by 17% of voters overall, 22% of independents, and 29% of Republicans. Concern spans generations: 20% of voters aged 18–29 and 18% of those 65 and older identify it as their most important issue. Healthcare costs and access—selected as most important by only 7% of voters—is particularly salient among Democrats (11%), black voters (11%), and seniors (9%). Immigration is a higher priority among Hispanic (8%) and Asian (8%) voters than white (4%) or black (1%) voters. Crime and public safety attract greater attention among Asian voters (7%). Homelessness Homelessness remains one of the state’s defining challenges for California voters. More than four in five Californians (81%) believe that homelessness is a bigger problem in their state than elsewhere, a figure that rises to 83% in Los Angeles. Voters overwhelmingly reject the view that housing costs is a primary driver of homelessness. By a 60% to 29% margin statewide, Californians say homelessness is mainly driven by substance addiction and mental health issues, rather than housing affordability. ( Figure 10 ) Figure 10 Los Angeles voters reach the same conclusion. Angelenos attribute homelessness to substance addiction and mental health issues, rather than affordability, by a 61% to 30% margin. Even among Raman supporters, a majority (53%) identify addiction and mental illness as primary causes, compared with 40% who point to housing affordability. Among voters backing neither Bass nor Raman, fully 77% identify substance addiction and mental health issues as the chief drivers of homelessness. Californians are also united on what constitutes a compassionate response to homelessness. By a 62% to 20% margin, voters agree that providing treatment to homeless individuals suffering from substance addiction—even without their consent—is more compassionate than leaving them on the streets. That position receives majority support across virtually every demographic and political group, including Democrats (56%), younger voters (59%), black voters (53%), Becerra supporters (53%), and Raman supporters (60%) ( Figure 11 ). Figure 11 Support for treatment without consent is similarly strong in Los Angeles, where 66% say it is the more compassionate option. Homelessness also ranks higher among Angelenos’ priorities: 14% identify it as the state’s most important issue, compared with 6% of Californians overall. These findings suggest broad support for a response to homelessness that places greater emphasis on addiction, mental illness, and treatment. Organized Labor and Public Sector Unions Californians hold generally favorable views of unions in the abstract. Nearly half (46%) say unions benefit workers in both the private and public sectors, while only 22% believe that unions generally do more harm than good. Democrats are particularly supportive, with roughly two-thirds expressing a broadly positive view of unions. Voters are less favorable when asked specifically about public-sector unions and their role in government. Nearly half of Californians (48%) believe that public-sector unions have too much influence over elections and government decision-making, compared with just 14% who say they have too little influence. Nearly two-thirds of Californians (63%) also support limiting the power of public-sector unions if doing so would make it easier to reward high-performing employees, discipline poor performers, and deliver better public services at a lower cost. Notably, majorities of independents (62%), Democrats (53%), Raman supporters (59%), and Bass supporters (52%) are in favor of reforms aimed at limiting public-sector union power and improving accountability and service delivery ( Figure 12 ). Support for organized labor therefore coexists with skepticism about public-sector unions and openness to limits tied to better government performance. Figure 12 Welfare Fraud, Government Waste, and Corruption Concern about waste, fraud, and abuse in California’s welfare system is widespread. More than seven in ten voters (71%) say they are concerned, including majorities of Democrats (54%) and Becerra supporters (52%). As a result, California voters are more likely to support fraud enforcement than expansion of welfare programs. A majority of Californians (53%) believe the state should crack down on waste, fraud, and abuse, while only 32% say it should be easier for eligible people to obtain benefits. 9% favor keeping the system largely as it is today. Concerns about corruption extend beyond the welfare system. A 42% plurality of Californians believe that their state has a bigger corruption problem than other states, compared with 18% who believe it has a smaller one. Angelenos are somewhat less negative, though 38% still say corruption is a larger problem in California. Among voters planning to support neither Bass nor Raman, that figure rises to 78%, indicating that concerns about corruption are especially prevalent among swing voters. High-Speed Rail and Public Infrastructure Californians are broadly dissatisfied with the condition of the state’s infrastructure. Asked to compare California’s roads, bridges, and other public infrastructure to those in other states, more voters (43%) than say they are in worse condition, while only 16% say better condition and 34% say about the same. Voters are even more critical of the state’s management of major infrastructure projects. Only 25% believe that the state should continue investing in projects such as California High-Speed Rail despite cost overruns and delays. By contrast, 42% say the state should stop wasting resources on such projects altogether, while another 27% believe major infrastructure investments are needed but do not trust California’s current leadership to manage them effectively. Taken together, roughly seven in ten voters express either opposition to continued spending on projects like High-Speed Rail or skepticism about the state’s ability to deliver them successfully ( Figure 13 ). Figure 13 Medi-Cal Eligibility California voters lean toward restricting Medi-Cal eligibility based on legal status. A majority (51%) say that the program should only be available to those with legal status, while 31% believe it should be available regardless of immigration status. Another 11% favor allowing current beneficiaries without legal status to retain coverage while ending new enrollment, and 7% are unsure ( Figure 14 ). Figure 14 The partisan divide is particularly striking. Independents favor restricting eligibility by a 55% to 24% margin, while Republicans do so overwhelmingly (87% to 4%). Democrats are the only major partisan group in which a majority (52%) support making Medi-Cal available regardless of legal status. Los Angeles voters are more supportive of making Medi-Cal available regardless of legal status than Californians overall. A plurality (40%) support no eligibility restriction, compared with 36% who favor limiting the program to those with legal status. Raman supporters back eligibility regardless of legal status by a 58% to 15% margin, while Bass supporters are more divided (42% to 36%). Race and Merit California voters are opposed to race-conscious hiring and admissions policies. A majority (53%) agree that using race to make hiring or admissions decisions is discriminatory no matter who it helps or hurts, while 37% say that America’s history of discrimination creates an obligation to take race into account today. 10% are unsure ( Figure 15 ). Figure 15 Views on race-conscious hiring and admissions vary across demographic groups. Men believe that using race is discriminatory by a 57% to 33% margin, while women are more divided (50% to 42%). Younger voters are more receptive to race-conscious policies, but that view is still rejected by voters aged 18–29 (47% oppose to 42% support). Among those aged 50–64, a majority oppose race-conscious policies (58%), with only 33% in favor. Racial divisions are similarly pronounced. Black voters strongly support affirmative action, backing race-conscious hiring and admissions policies by a 64% to 24% margin. Asian voters, meanwhile, are among the strongest critics, opposing race-conscious hiring and admissions policies by a 56% to 31% margin. White voters are similarly opposed (56% to 35%), while Hispanic voters oppose affirmative action by a narrower 50% to 41% margin. College-educated voters are evenly divided, with 45% on each side of the question, whereas voters without a four-year degree oppose affirmative action by a 59% to 32% margin. On affirmative action, Los Angeles stands apart from the statewide electorate. Los Angeles voters support it by an eight-point margin (48% to 40%), while California voters overall oppose it by a 16-point margin. [1] Net favorability calculated from unrounded figures; numbers may not appear to sum due to rounding. [2] Net value calculated from unrounded figures; numbers may not appear to sum due to rounding. [3] Net value calculated from unrounded figures; numbers may not appear to sum due to rounding. Most voters who cast ballots for Spencer Pratt in the primary haven’t chosen a runoff candidate, leading to an unusually high number of undecided voters so close to an election. p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> Los Angeles Councilmember Nithya Raman has taken a wide lead over incumbent Karen Bass in the L.A. mayor’s race, according to a new poll released Wednesday, although a high percentage of voters remain undecided less than two weeks before mail-in ballots are sent out for the Nov. 3 election. Raman is favored by 39% of likely L.A. voters, compared with 28% for Bass, according to the poll by the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies, which was co-sponsored by The Times. The poll found that 33% of voters were undecided. “Raman clearly has the advantage. Her task is a little less onerous than Bass’,” said Mark DiCamillo, the director of the Berkeley IGS Poll . Adding to Bass’ low poll numbers are high unfavorability ratings. The mayor had 63% unfavorable ratings, the poll found, with 28% favorable and 9% having no opinion. By comparison, 40% had a favorable view of Raman, according to the poll, while 39% said they had an unfavorable view of her and 21% had no opinion. The survey released Wednesday was conducted online with a sample of 2,150 likely city voters between Sept. 15 and Sept. 20. It has a margin of error of about 3 percentage points. Advertisement The poll represented the strongest showing yet for Raman, who trailed Bass in almost every poll during the primary campaign and who came in second to Bass in the primary election, with 29% of the vote compared with Bass’ 34%. Mayoral candidate and Councilmember Nithya Raman, center, enjoys a light moment with Alliance of Californians for Community Empowerment (ACCE) Action members at La Cita Bar in downtown Los Angeles. (Genaro Molina / Los Angeles Times) Even so, DiCamillo said the large number of undecided voters means the race is far from over. Advertisement “It’s extraordinarily unusual to see this many undecided voters at this point in the race,” he said. Mail-in ballots will be sent out beginning Oct. 1, local elections officials say. The large number of undecided voters can be linked to the elimination of mayoral candidate Spencer Pratt in the June 2 primary, according to DiCamillo. The former reality TV star received 26% of the vote in the primary, and most of the voters who cast ballots for him — 63% — say they haven’t decided whom to vote for in the runoff, the poll found. Among those Pratt voters who have decided, 22% favored Bass compared with 16% for Raman. One of the most significant findings in the poll was a massive “generational divide” among L.A. voters, DiCamillo said. Raman, 45, dominated the 72-year-old Bass among younger voters, with 66% of likely voters ages 18 to 29 choosing the council member while just 4% chose Bass, according to the poll. Raman also had 64% of likely voters ages 30 to 39 compared with Bass’ 12%, and the council member had 50% of likely voters ages 40 to 49 compared with Bass’ 18%. Raman also was leading among voters 50 to 64 years old by a slim margin of 35% to 33%. Advertisement Bass, meanwhile, led among the oldest set of voters — those 65 and up — but not by the same margins. Bass had 41% of likely voters in that group compared with Raman’s 21%. The mayor has had negative favorability ratings since the 2025 Palisades fire. According to the poll, 56% of likely voters thought Bass did a poor or very poor job responding to the disaster, which killed 12 people and destroyed more than 4,000 homes, including Pratt’s. Fourteen percent of the likely voters thought Bass had done either an excellent or a good job and 17% thought she had done a fair job. Mayor Karen Bass campaigns at Ernest E. Debs Regional Park on Sunday. (Kayla Bartkowski / Los Angeles Times) The most important issues to likely voters were fixing city infrastructure, moving homeless people indoors, crime and public safety, and building more affordable housing, the poll found. The poll shows Raman leading in nearly every geographic area of the city. Bass was leading in South Los Angeles and the Harbor region, 37% to 34%, but central Los Angeles as well as northeast and the east side of Los Angeles broke strongly for Raman. The San Fernando Valley went 34% to Raman and 26% to Bass with 40% still undecided. The Westside favored Raman by a single percentage point, at 35% to 34%. Advertisement Raman has led in other polls recently, though none by as wide a margin as in the Berkeley IGS/L.A. Times poll. Shortly before the primary, a separate Berkeley IGS/L.A. Times poll showed Raman leading Bass in a potential head-to-head matchup by just four percentage points, with 32% support compared with the mayor’s 28%. But the gap between the two has widened since then, the latest poll found, as Bass weathered a difficult news cycle , including rising homelessness numbers citywide as well as the fallout from the Lineage warehouse fire in Boyle Heights that burned for nearly a week, leaving rotting food and a rancid stench in the neighborhood for more than a month. Raman, meanwhile, picked up largely positive headlines this summer. She gained key endorsements from the carpenters’ union and Unite Here Local 11, the union representing hospitality workers at hotels and the airport, as well as an endorsement from the Democratic Socialists of America . Street homelessness also dropped in her district, which she said was due to her office’s strong outreach, though the Bass campaign credited the mayor’s Inside Safe program for the reduction in Raman’s district. On the negative side, Raman was booted from her position in the council as chair of the Housing and Homelessness Committee, a move she said was politically motivated. In an internal Raman campaign poll from early September , the council member was ahead, 44% to 39%, with 17% undecided. She was also leading, 38% to 32%, in a poll commissioned by the group Streets for All , which is backing Raman. In an early August poll commissioned by an independent expenditure group supporting Bass, the mayor had the edge, 41% to 35%, with 24% undecided. (Los Angeles Times) By David Zahniser and Noah Goldberg Sept. 19, 2026 8 AM PT 12 Share via Close extra sharing options Email Facebook X LinkedIn Threads Reddit WhatsApp Copy Link URL Copied! Print See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> The advertising blitzkrieg of L.A.’s mayoral campaign is here. Mayor Karen Bass and her opponent, City Councilmember Nithya Raman , dropped new campaign commercials over the last week, buying time on television, streaming channels and other platforms. Supporters of both candidates released ads as well. The two candidates relied heavily on free media for most of the summer, putting videos on Instagram and inviting the news media to cover their appearances. The dam effectively burst on Monday, with Raman touting her new Hollywood-themed ad “For Your Consideration,” timed to coincide with the Emmy Awards . Advertisement You’re reading the L.A. on the Record newsletter Sign up to make sense of the often unexplained world of L.A. politics. By continuing, you agree to our Terms of Service , which include arbitration and a class action waiver. You agree that we and our third-party vendors may collect and use your information, including through cookies, pixels and similar technologies, for the purposes set forth in our Privacy Policy such as personalizing your experience and ads. Login or register with email Agree & Continue The 30-second spot starts with Raman stepping out on the town, then shifts to some standard L.A. imagery: freeways, palm trees, Echo Park Lake and, of course, the Hollywood sign. “L.A. shows the world what it means to be a star,” declares the ad’s narrator, actor and screenwriter Bob Odenkirk . “And every Angeleno deserves the chance to reach for their own.” After Raman has stopped off at a taco stand and hugged a dog, Odenkirk delivers the ad’s final message: “Change. Affordability. An L.A. that loves you back.” Advertisement That ad ran on television a few times before being cycled onto social media, per the Raman campaign. Three days later, Bass went up with a 30-second spot — on digital platforms for now — centered on President Trump’s immigration raids. The ad offers footage from the day in July 2025 when Bass confronted federal immigration agents in MacArthur Park. The video features images of gun-toting federal agents in military uniforms and Bass hopping out of a car in an aquamarine pantsuit to face them. “When someone comes after your family, you don’t hesitate,” Bass says. “You stand up. You fight.” One of Bass’ most formidable allies — the Los Angeles Police Protective League — went hard negative with its first ad of the runoff campaign, offering the message that Raman “Doesn’t Get It.” The commercial, released Friday, follows a young girl as she walks past a homeless encampment, juxtaposed against video of Raman talking about her opposition to a law that prohibits encampments near schools. Advertisement “I don’t think a kid’s gonna be safer because a tent is 500 feet away from a school,” Raman said in the clip, which was taken from a 2024 candidate forum in Sherman Oaks. The backpack-wearing child speaks to the camera and says: “Walking to school shouldn’t be scary.” “I’m just a kid,” she says. “But even I know I’d be safer if this was 500 feet away.” The police union says the ad will start running on television this weekend and already is on social media platforms. Meanwhile, Raman’s backers have an assortment of attack ads running on Facebook and Instagram. Streets For All, a group that wants to expand the city’s bus and bike lane network, pulled video footage from a different Sherman Oaks candidate forum — this one featuring Bass and Raman last month. At that event, Bass told the audience that Raman is unresponsive to her constituents, forcing many in Sherman Oaks to contact the mayor’s office directly. Advertisement “Many of you have my cellphone, you have called me,” Bass says in the ad. “You called on me specifically for help.” Streets For All contends those remarks show that Bass gives wealthy homeowners her number while “regular Angelenos get ignored.” “L.A. deserves a mayor who doesn’t just listen to the rich and powerful,” the ad says. By Friday, Streets For All had nearly two dozen different video spots opposing Bass over such issues as homelessness, transparency and the Palisades fire, according to Ethics Commission filings. The biggest backer of the group’s political action committee is hedge fund manager Aaron Sosnick . Of the $1.2 million that the group plans to spend in the mayor’s race, Sosnick has provided $1 million, said Michael Schneider , who heads the group. Schneider said the committee also has financial support from retired real estate developer Yuval Bar-Zemer — known for his work in the Arts District — and Todd Wexman , chief principal of 4SITE Real Estate, a real estate development company. Raman pollster says she’s in the lead The Raman campaign shared the results of a new internal poll that showed their candidate with a five-point lead over Bass. Advertisement Of the 600 likely voters who were surveyed, 44% supported Raman and 39% backed Bass, with 17% undecided, according to a memo provided to the campaign and viewed by The Times. The survey, conducted by Hart Research Associates in early September, had a margin of error of 4 percentage points. “In the initial trial heat for Los Angeles mayor, Councilmember Nithya Raman is in the rare position for a challenger of already LEADING the incumbent,” the polling firm wrote. Another poll, commissioned by an independent expenditure group supporting Raman, portrayed the race as a statistical tie, at least initially. Estamos con Nithya for Mayor of LA 2026, sponsored by the Western States Regional Council of Carpenters, said its poll showed Bass with 38% and Raman at 37%. However, when voters received more information on the candidates, Raman took a 7-percentage-point lead, with 41% supporting her and 34% supporting Bass, according to a memo prepared by the group’s pollster. The margin of error was 3.7 percentage points. The Bass campaign declined to share its internal polling when contacted by The Times. However, Neighborhoods for a Better L.A., an independent expenditure group supporting the mayor, said a survey it commissioned in early August showed the mayor with an edge over Raman of 41% to 35%, with 24% of the electorate undecided. That poll, conducted by Tulchin Research, surveyed 1,200 likely Los Angeles voters and has a 2.8-percentage-point margin of error, the group said. Advertisement The poll also found that when given “balanced biographies” about both candidates, Bass’ support grew to 45% while Raman went down to 33%. “Communications focused on Raman’s record can both reduce her support and consolidate voters behind Bass,” the pollsters wrote. Giving back El Grito cash Los Angeles City Councilmember Imelda Padilla locked down sponsorships for the city’s celebration of El Grito, which marks Mexico’s independence. Tuesday’s event, which featured an evening of musical performances, was sponsored by an assortment of city contractors and government agencies, including waste hauler Athens Services and the Department of Water and Power. Still, Padilla decided she didn’t want to partner with one particular business, announcing at the last minute that organizers no longer would accept a $5,000 sponsorship from Home Depot. On the day of the celebration, Padilla issued an apology on Instagram, saying she had heard from community members upset over the event’s affiliation with Home Depot, whose parking lots have been the site of many federal immigration raids. Advertisement “We have rescinded their partnership for this event,” Padilla said in her post. “The spirit of El Grito is rooted in celebrating our Latino heritage and creating a space where our families feel welcomed, safe, and celebrated.” In an email, a Home Depot spokesperson said the company is not involved in immigration enforcement activities and doesn’t coordinate with Immigration and Customs Enforcement or U.S. Border Patrol. The company also doesn’t receive advance warning about enforcement actions, the representative said. “We cannot legally interfere with federal enforcement agencies, including preventing them from coming into our stores and parking lots,” Home Depot spokesperson Evelyn Fornes said. State of play — COZY WITH CARUSO: Billionaire developer Rick Caruso, who was defeated by Bass in 2022, appeared alongside the mayor at a groundbreaking for the Palisades Recreation Center. Caruso praised her for her work on the project but stopped short of endorsing, saying he intends to meet with Raman in the coming weeks. — LIFE AFTER PRATT: The voters who picked reality TV personality Spencer Pratt in the June 2 primary election are now up for grabs . But will they stay home instead of picking a mayoral candidate? — BASS BAILS: The mayor skipped a congressional hearing on waste and fraud in homeless spending this week, calling the session politically motivated. Rep. Tim Burchett , the Republican who chaired the subcommittee meeting, accused her of dodging accountability. Advertisement — FINDING FRAUD: Federal authorities arrested three people who were working in Los Angeles-area homeless nonprofits this week, accusing one of them of misappropriating more than $7.5 million in taxpayer funds. Scott Turner , secretary of the Department of Housing and Urban Development, said the Los Angeles Homeless Services Authority, which provided the funding, had allowed fraud to “run rampant.” — WE’RE IN THE MONEY: The 2028 Summer Olympic Games in Los Angeles will generate up to $40.6 billion in increased economic output and add as many as 224,000 jobs, according to an upbeat economic forecast released this week. Another, more tempered estimate put the increase at $20.5 billion to $25.4 billion. — SEETHING OVER SKID ROW: Some activists want dogs taken away from homeless residents living in Skid Row, saying those animals are living in an unsafe environment . A Bass aide responded by cautioning that it is “neither humane nor legal to remove animals from their human companions without appropriate cause.” QUICK HITS Where is Inside Safe? The mayor’s signature program to combat homelessness went to Avalon Boulevard and 64th Street in South L.A., an area represented by Councilmember Curren Price . On the docket next week: The council’s Public Works Committee meets Tuesday to discuss ways of cleaning, safeguarding or demolishing nuisance properties. Stay in touch That’s it for this week! Set us as preferred The phony poll by a company called Median Strategies showed Bass leading Raman by a wide margin, but the company acknowledged Monday that it was fake. Median said the “poll” was instead a “short term social experiment” to see how polling information could be distributed without verification. p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> A poll claiming Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass was leading Councilmember Nithya Raman by a wide margin — and picking up support from most voters who backed Spencer Pratt in the mayoral primary — was bogus, the company behind the poll acknowledged Monday. The fake poll by Median Strategies showed Bass leading Raman by nearly 12 percentage points ahead of the Nov. 3 mayoral runoff, and said the results were based on a survey of 560 Los Angeles voters between July 30 and Aug. 5. It said it had a 4.1% margin of error. But Monday, in response to repeated inquiries from The Times, the company said the purported “poll” was nothing of the kind. Advertisement “Median Strategies was created as a short term social experiment to examine how purported polling information could enter and spread through the political information ecosystem without independent verification,” the company said in an email to The Times. “We are not seeking publicity or attribution for the individuals involved and are declining interviews.” The phony poll also claimed that 16% of its respondents said they had voted for Pratt, and that of those voters, about 85% were planning to vote for Bass in the general, while about 7% would support Raman. Login or register with email Agree & Continue Advertisement “Faced with a choice between the incumbent and a Democratic Socialists of America-aligned challenger, most Pratt voters appear to be treating Bass as the more familiar, more moderate option rather than sitting out the race,” Median wrote in its analysis. That angle led to a headline in the California Post, which declared that “Spencer Pratt’s voters could be deciding factor in LA mayor showdown according to latest poll.” The Post didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment. Bass cheered the results after the fake survey was released last week. “Doing the work, showing up, and gaining momentum. Let’s do this, LA!” Bass posted on X from her campaign account, citing Median Strategies as the source. The post has since been deleted. “This poll was reported on by a news outlet,” a Bass campaign spokesperson said. “Any bad faith attempts to influence elections should be investigated and prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.” Controller Kenneth Mejia, who endorsed Raman in the race, also took note of the poll last week — but in a post on X noted that polls had shown him losing, only to be proven wrong when he won his election by a wide margin. Median, which declined an interview, began posting on social media on Aug. 9 and had about 20 followers. Advertisement “Polling has a credibility problem. Ours is the fix: no partisan clients, no campaign or party money, numbers that go wherever the data takes them even when it’s inconvenient. Trustworthy polling, rebuilt,” it wrote in its first post. Median then released a poll on the Wisconsin gubernatorial race showing Democratic socialist Francesca Hong up by more than 20 percentage points. Hong ended up losing. “We got Wisconsin wrong- and by quite a margin too,” the firm posted on Aug 12. The next day it released its L.A. mayor’s race poll. Set us as preferred The phony poll by a company called Median Strategies showed Bass leading Raman by a wide margin, but the company acknowledged Monday that it was fake. Median said the “poll” was instead a “short term social experiment” to see how polling information could be distributed without verification. p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> A poll claiming Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass was leading Councilmember Nithya Raman by a wide margin — and picking up support from most voters who supported Spencer Pratt in the mayoral primary — was bogus, the company behind the poll acknowledged Monday. The fake poll by Median Strategies showed Bass leading Raman by nearly 12 percentage points ahead of the Nov. 3 mayoral runoff, and said the results were based on a survey of 560 Los Angeles voters between July 30 and Aug. 5. It said it had a 4.1% margin of error. But Monday, in response to repeated inquiries from The Times, the company said the purported “poll” was nothing of the kind. Advertisement “Median Strategies was created as a short term social experiment to examine how purported polling information could enter and spread through the political information ecosystem without independent verification,” the company said in an email to The Times. “We are not seeking publicity or attribution for the individuals involved and are declining interviews.” The phony poll also claimed that 16% of its respondents said they had voted for Pratt, and that of those voters, about 85% were planning to vote for Bass in the general, while about 7% would support Raman. “Faced with a choice between the incumbent and a Democratic Socialists of America-aligned challenger, most Pratt voters appear to be treating Bass as the more familiar, more moderate option rather than sitting out the race,” Median wrote in its analysis. Advertisement That angle led to a headline in the California Post, which declared that “Spencer Pratt’s voters could be deciding factor in LA mayor showdown according to latest poll.” The Post didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment. Bass cheered the results after the fake survey was released last week. “Doing the work, showing up, and gaining momentum. Let’s do this, LA!” Bass posted on X from her campaign account, citing Median Strategies as the source. The post has since been deleted. “This poll was reported on by a news outlet,” a Bass campaign spokesperson said. “Any bad faith attempts to influence elections should be investigated and prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.” Controller Kenneth Mejia, who endorsed Raman in the race, also took note of the poll last week — but in a post on X noted that polls had shown him losing, only to be proven wrong when he won his election by a wide margin. Median, which declined an interview, began posting on social media on Aug. 9 and had about 20 followers. “Polling has a credibility problem. Ours is the fix: no partisan clients, no campaign or party money, numbers that go wherever the data takes them even when it’s inconvenient. Trustworthy polling, rebuilt,” it wrote in its first post. Advertisement Median then released a poll on the Wisconsin gubernatorial race showing Democratic socialist Francesca Hong up by more than 20 percentage points. Hong ended up losing. “We got Wisconsin wrong- and by quite a margin too,” the firm posted on Aug 12. The next day it released its L.A. mayor’s race poll. title: Fake Poll Scandal Has All the Earmarks of a Pump-and-Dump Scheme - The American Prospect
desc: If you wanted to rig political prediction markets, this is exactly how you would do it.
body: Fake Poll Scandal Has All the Earmarks of a Pump-and-Dump Scheme - The American Prospect Close Subscribe Donate Newsletters Sign In Search for: Search Election 2026 AI & Data Centers War in Iran ICE In the Magazine The American Prospect About Us Meet the Staff Donate Subscribe to Our Magazine Newsletter Sign-Up Why We’re Removing Our Programmatic Ads Careers Frequently Asked Questions Close The American Prospect About Us Meet the Staff Donate Subscribe to Our Magazine Newsletter Sign-Up Why We’re Removing Our Programmatic Ads Careers Frequently Asked Questions Skip to content Menu The American Prospect Ideas, Politics & Power Subscribe Donate Newsletters Sign In Open Search Search for: Search Donate Menu Sign In Election 2026 AI & Data Centers War in Iran ICE In the Magazine Home / Politics / Fake Poll Scandal Has All the Earmarks of a Pump-and-Dump Scheme Posted in Politics Fake Poll Scandal Has All the Earmarks of a Pump-and-Dump Scheme If you wanted to rig political prediction markets, this is exactly how you would do it. by David Dayen August 19, 2026 August 19, 2026 Share: Share on Make us preferred on Google (Opens in new window) Make us preferred on Google Share on Bluesky (Opens in new window) Bluesky Share on X (Opens in new window) X More Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on Reddit (Opens in new window) Reddit Share on Threads (Opens in new window) Threads Share on WhatsApp (Opens in new window) WhatsApp Share on Mastodon (Opens in new window) Mastodon Share on LinkedIn (Opens in new window) LinkedIn Email a link to a friend (Opens in new window) Email Print (Opens in new window) Print Nithya Raman speaks at an election night party in June 2022. Credit: John McCoy/AP Photo Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass spent last week touting a poll released on Thursday from an unknown company called Median Strategies showing her leading challenger Nithya Raman in her re-election campaign by double digits and winning 85 percent of third-place finisher Spencer Pratt’s voters. The poll was a rare bit of good news for Bass after a tough summer that featured a statistical rise in homelessness and an adviser going to work for a reviled logistics firm responsible for a disastrous warehouse fire in Boyle Heights. The only problem with the poll is that it was fake. More from David Dayen Persistent Los Angeles Times reporter Noah Goldberg got Median Strategies to admit that the Bass-Raman poll was bogus and “should not be treated as genuine polling data.” Indeed, all three Median Strategies polls, including one showing Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong up in her primary by 23 points (she lost) and another showing Nevada Gov. Joe Lombardo up in his general-election campaign by five, were not backed up by any numbers. On its website , Median Strategies would only say that it was engaged in a “short-term social experiment” to see how polling data could “spread through the political information ecosystem.” But the financial disclosure that Median added was much more interesting. It insisted that nobody involved with the project received any “financial benefit” from the scheme, and it explicitly cited prediction markets. “No individual involved held or traded any position in an election prediction market, betting market, or other financial instrument tied to the races covered by Median Strategies. The project was not undertaken for financial gain or to influence the value of any financial or prediction-market position,” the note reads. Median Strategies could not be reached for comment. Read: The CFTC’s word games legalizing gambling Of course, there’s no reason to believe an entity whose only public action involves lying. Because there is literally no other motivation to introduce fake polling into the political bloodstream other than to game a prediction market. And while this one may not have made any money, the point may simply have been to offer a road map to any political actor using invented information to make money from elections. In fact, the strategy was not even particularly innovative. It has been used for decades, primarily in thinly traded “penny stock” markets, where information of any kind is highly sought. The term of art is a “pump-and-dump” scheme. Here’s the short version: A promoter touts some inside information about the stock, either by directly cold-calling prospective investors, sending voluminous email spam, dropping it into internet forums or social media, or publishing a fake press release or misleading “investment research.” The information isn’t true, but if it works it generates enough interest to get movement on the stock, which the promoter has already purchased. Having bought low, the promoter sells high and makes off with the profits, and as the scheme collapses when the truth is revealed, all the investors who piled in lose their shirts. An election prediction market has the same character as a stock. The markets are too new and too numerous to be heavily traded, and in head-to-head matchups, new developments can cause the market to tilt in favor of one candidate. The poll takes the place of the inside information, though you could imagine other things, like fake news about fundraising data or outside spending, erroneous reports about a misstep on the campaign trail, or whatever, can move numbers. The Bass poll worked perfectly for this purpose. The California Post , Rupert Murdoch’s attempt to penetrate the Golden State with right-leaning news, enthusiastically ran with the poll because of the inference that Pratt voters were kingmakers. (That web URL is still live on the California Post website, but it’s been gutted and replaced with a story about Bass demanding legal action.) In a classic pump-and-dump, one story like that is all it takes for a market to move. The perpetrators already have their investment and can sit back, watch it rise, and sell when they want. There are resemblances between that and what happened in L.A. mayoral markets around the time of the poll release. The Post story was published on August 13 at 10:53 p.m. Eastern time. On prediction market Kalshi, a contract on Bass to win the mayor’s race was trading at 64.3 cents on the dollar before the poll drop and 65.9 cents shortly thereafter, peaking at 67.2 cents before falling once the polling fiasco was revealed. The equivalent contract on Polymarket, a Kalshi competitor, was even more pronounced. The market was hovering at 61 cents the day before the poll release. You can see some action around that time, including one $6,000 bet on Bass . The market for Bass peaked on August 17 at 5:30 a.m., before the L.A. Times exposure, at 70 cents. The Associated Press cited 20 separate Bass trades on Polymarket within 15 minutes of Median Strategies releasing their fake poll. These can be viewed at the market site . The Last Big Primary Night of the Year A smoking gun of a whale trade on Bass followed by a sell-off is hard to discern, but on prediction markets, where everything is anonymous and unlimited new traders can be conjured up, that can be hard to uncover. If nothing else, Median Strategies proved the concept that a pump-and-dump scheme is easily transferrable to election prediction markets, which have the same mix of thin trading, high emotion, and easily led traders as penny stocks. That’s valuable information for would-be scam artists. “I think this falls into the category of hard to prove but very hard to think it’s anything else,” said Corey Frayer, a former financial regulatory staffer in Congress now with the Consumer Federation of America. Pump-and-dump schemes, incidentally, are securities fraud, and those caught setting them up can get prison time . Jordan Belfort, the famed Wolf of Wall Street, was convicted for running pump-and-dump schemes. But those cases, rooted in investor protection, are typically enforced out of the Securities and Exchange Commission . Prediction markets have been adopted by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which has a market integrity mandate . Certainly, manipulating markets represents a threat to market integrity. But that slight change in focus, the generally outgunned nature of the CFTC, and its current role as an evangelist and indeed the rescuer of prediction markets from state regulation put it in a bad position to uncover and refer fraud of this nature for prosecution. Nearly all the prediction market manipulation we have heard about is a result of self-regulation from the companies, which could be selective. What the Median Strategies saga reveals is the ease with which pump-and-dump schemes can be carried out in election markets. That is supposed to be an acceptable price to pay for learning the future. But it’s becoming very clear that, as applied to elections, prediction markets don’t know a damn thing and are of no utility. Last night’s Florida Senate race is a good example; Democrat Angie Nixon never rose above 11 cents on Kalshi until she won and paid out $1. One reason? There weren’t any polls. Photograph: Kayla Wolf/AP US midterm elections 2026 This article is more than 2 months old Website behind widely shared fake election polls run by 21-year-old This article is more than 2 months old Exclusive: Rahil Prakash tells the Guardian: ‘I wanted to see if fake polls could penetrate the ecosystem that easily’ Sophie Sullivan , Anna Betts and Sam Levine Thu 20 Aug 2026 17.33 EDT Last modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 18.15 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A 21-year-old recent college graduate was behind an anonymous website that put out widely shared fake election polling in Wisconsin, Nevada and California , the Guardian can reveal. The website, Median Strategies, abruptly shut down and withdrew its polling earlier this week following questions from a reporter from the Los Angeles Times . In an unsigned statement , it described a “short-term social experiment” to examine how fake polling “could enter and spread through the political information ecosystem without independent verification”. “I wanted to see if fake polls could really penetrate the ecosystem that easily,” Rahil Prakash told the Guardian on Thursday when reached by phone. “And as it turned out, it could.” Karen Bass, the mayor of Los Angeles, touted Median polling data after it appeared to put her ahead of her election challenger by more than 10 percentage points. The poll was also cited by the California Post . A widely followed polling aggregator on X also shared the group’s Nevada poll , although several credible polling organizations did not aggregate Median polling because they could not verify its methodology. “Did I expect it to perhaps expedite in the way it did? Most definitely not,” said Prakash. “I did not expect the California political press to pick it up on their own.” He added: “I’ll apologize straight out to the campaigns of Karen Bass, Nithya Raman and Francesca Hong for this.” Raman is running against Bass in November’s LA mayoral election. Hong lost the Democratic primary for Wisconsin governor earlier this month, after Median suggested she had led the race by more than 20 percentage points. It also released a fake poll showing the Nevada governor, Joe Lombardo, up by five points before November’s general election. In an interview, Prakash said he was motivated to start the fake polling project after a significant polling miss in the Michigan Senate primary, where polls had showed Abdul El-Sayed with a heavy lead over his opponent Haley Stevens before election day. In the event, El-Sayed wound up winning by a much smaller margin than polls had suggested. “This is what inspired me to test my theory,” said Prakash. “I was a bit shocked, perhaps at how fast this sort of information can spread.” As of Thursday morning, Median had about 20 followers on its X account. According to the Los Angeles Times, the account began posting on 9 August. “I think my overall takeaway was that if you just make it look a bit pretty, it’s rather easy for it to spread,” Prakash said. “And I hope it gives a really good lesson going forward in that we need to be very serious about these things and very serious in how, if one person can do this, what can a serious operation do in the future – a real, you know, operation for an organization, country, whatever.” Prakash, who said that he made the website using artificial intelligence, said he alone created Median. The Guardian identified Prakash using domain registration data tied to the Median Strategies website. By reverse-searching two domain nameservers tied to the site, the Guardian obtained lists of several thousand other domains also using those nameservers. About 115 domains used the same two nameservers, but only one used the same two nameservers and used the same domain name registrar as Median Strategies. Only a GitHub 404 message appears on that matching website now. But additional web records tied it to a GitHub profile, which included a file with Prakash’s name. The lengthy anonymous statement on Monday posted to Median’s website also stressed that “no individual involved with Median Strategies received compensation or financial benefit from the project”, which it claimed had not been “funded, commissioned or directed” by any campaign, party, media outlet or other “outside entity”. When asked on Thursday whether he had traded on any prediction markets after publishing the sham data, Prakash said: “No, not at all.” On Wednesday, before the Guardian contacted Prakash, the American Association of Political Consultants condemned the effort . “Publishing fabricated survey data as independent research is not a social experiment,” it said, describing the project as “a deception directed at voters, at the press, and at the campaigns that rely on public data to make decisions”. The two candidates vying for the job of Los Angeles mayor — incumbent Karen Bass and challenger Nithya Raman — will face off Wednesday night in their first debate ahead of the general election in November. The backstory Bass finished ahead of Raman in the June primary with 34% of the vote to Raman's 29%. With no one in the crowded field topping 50% the two women moved to a runoff. While Bass was ahead of Raman. she's considered a vulnerable incumbent. Rising street homelessness, skyrocketing housing costs and a shortage of basic city services like pothole repair have left some voters disenchanted with Bass, whose unfavorable ratings top 50%. She’s also been criticized for her handling of the Palisades Fire. Here's a look at the candidate's standard positions so far in this election cycle: Bass The incumbent has said she understands that people are frustrated, but she’s “not done” doing the job of mayor. Sponsored message “You want to hear frustrated?” Bass said at a recent campaign event. “I’m frustrated too. But I’ll tell you what frustration does to me. Frustration makes me fight even harder.” She says there’s been progress: fewer homeless encampments in many neighborhoods, more permits issued to build affordable housing and a drop in crime. Much of the establishment is backing Bass, including the L.A. County Democratic Party, L.A. County Federation of Labor and Chamber of Commerce. Raman A city council member since 2020, two years before Bass became mayor, Raman remains relatively unknown to many voters. She says she's running against “the political machine.” Raman has touted a 49% drop in unsheltered homelessness in her council district, District 4, which runs from Silver Lake to Sherman Oaks, and she says she has a plan to cut street homelessness in half citywide by the Olympics and eliminate it entirely by the end of four years. Her supporters include City Controller Kenneth Mejia, various local Democratic clubs and the Western States Carpenters Association.
