Los Angeles, with its extraordinary diversity, is a national case study in coalition politics — the cobbling together of constituencies to create a political and governing majority.

This election for mayor, which pits incumbent Karen Bass against Councilmember Nithya Raman, offers a new opportunity to consider the city’s shifting voting blocs and the ways that growth replaces previous models.

Some of what drives politics in Los Angeles is time-tested: Mayor Tom Bradley, the city’s longest-serving and first Black chief executive, was famously able to unite the city’s Black voters with liberals, then concentrated on the Westside, into a coalition powerful enough to elect him in 1973, and durable enough for four more mayoral victories.

Richard Riordan, a moderate Republican and a Catholic who followed Bradley, upended that fusion by bringing together the San Fernando Valley, central city moderates and Latino voters in 1993. That coalition easily swept him to re-election, but has eluded every Republican who has tried to replicate it since, mainly because Republican numbers have dwindled (less than 15% of city voters are registered Republicans).

The mayors who have followed have been able to either marshal the city’s voting blocs or been punished by them. James Hahn brought together the Valley and Black voters, but lost both after opposing Valley secession and refusing to re-up Police Chief Bernard C. Parks; he was defeated in his bid for re-election. 

Antonio Villaraigosa energized Latinos and liberals and served two terms. Eric Garcetti extended that political coalition through the COVID era.

Bass’s tenure represents a new iteration of coalition politics, though with a distinctly difficult twist. Her 2022 victory was in some ways a throwback to Bradley. She started with core support from the city’s Black community and extended her base to progressives with the help of organized labor. That effort was enough to trounce Rick Caruso, a onetime Republican running as a Democrat and funded by more than $100 million of his own money.

For Bass, the twist is that the coalition she built to fend off a former Republican now is being tested against a very different political challenge. Raman also is a woman of color, one who is younger and even more progressive than Bass. No modern mayor has ever won with one coalition and then had to turn it to run in the opposite direction. That’s a tough pivot, and it has both campaigns looking to reassemble the coalition matrix that is L.A. 

Initial results from the election earlier this month showed Bass was strongest in the city center, home to many Black and Latino voters. Raman was the winner in the hipper, younger environs of Silver Lake, Echo Park and southeast Valley. Those results are, by themselves, not terribly surprising.

But a closer look at the city’s demography suggests other opportunities. Start with the areas won by Spencer Pratt in June. Despite his utter lack of a serious message or job qualifications, Pratt rolled up precinct victories on the Westside and the western reaches of the Valley. What’s notable about those returns, however, is that while Pratt won those precincts, Bass finished second place in most of them — surprising, given that Pratt’s campaign was built on anger at City Hall, and Bass in particular.

In a runoff where Bass represents the more conservative politician, those results may limit Raman, forcing her to look elsewhere for the votes she needs to grow her total from 28.5% to more than 50%.

One promising pool of voters is new residents. Those who have lived in Los Angeles for a relatively short time bring a distinctly different set of priorities than longtime Angelenos, a phenomenon observed last week by one of the city’s shrewder political minds, Council President Marqueece Harris-Dawson.

At a recent event hosted by UCLA’s Blueprint magazine (and co-sponsored by CalMatters), Harris-Dawson asserted that L.A. newcomers often see the city differently. He noted, for instance, that many newcomers passionately favor increasing the density of Los Angeles housing, which might help reduce housing costs and even alleviate homelessness.

Those are laudable aims, but they overlook some of what has made Los Angeles appealing to generations of migrants. Harris-Dawson observed that his own family, like many of the city’s Black residents, came to Los Angeles from the South and settled here because it was the rare city that offered them the opportunity to buy a home, to have a yard, to enjoy space. For those families, single-family residences — and a city that values them — represent not wasted land but new opportunity. It is liberty itself.

Similarly, new residents may view crime differently from those who have been here a while. Pratt’s supporters, many of whom chimed in through social media without ever having lived or worked in L.A., deplored Los Angeles as a city descending into the abyss. For those relatively new to the area, or those who grew up in its most sheltered neighborhoods, that may feel accurate. It is a big city with plenty of serious crime: Last year, 230 people were murdered here.

For longtime residents, however, those same numbers feel more like relief than dystopia. Two-hundred murders a year is more than any community should tolerate, but the city once was home to more than 1,000 annually. That’s not to mention the flashpoint of a race riot in 1992 that erupted upon the acquittals of LAPD officers for beating a Black man, part of the long legacy of police abuse that once haunted residents of Los Angeles.

Do 250 murders a year represent a shocking level of violence? Yes. Do they represent progress? Also yes. It depends on whether you compare 250 to zero or 1,000. 

Newcomers bring energy and excitement to a city, and their demands for improvement are politically relevant. They are less likely to draw upon nostalgia or to accept bygone habits. As such, they represent an important voting bloc in city politics, one that transcends geography or race. 

But they also may draw resentment from longstanding residents, who view their complaints as naive and lacking historical perspective.

In this election, Bass is likely to run strongest with voters who have been here longest, while Raman is the more natural candidate for newcomers. A city whose politics have long been built up by blocs has a new one to consider.

title: Opinion | LA's homelessness increase helps Raman target Bass
desc: The mayoral hopeful criticized incumbent Karen Bass on the homelessness count. Disentangling their records on this issue is not so simple.

Learn more here . On Monday, Aug. 10, multiple news outlets reported that L.A. City Councilwoman Nithya Raman was going to lose her role as chair of the city’s housing and homelessness committee, a move several observers (and Raman) believe was politically motivated. After two consecutive years of declines in the number of people sleeping on the streets of Los Angeles, the progress appears to have been nearly wiped out. That’s discouraging news for a city exhausted by the issue, and it throws a strange curve into the race for mayor. The latest annual count , released last week, registered 45,194 unhoused people in the city of Los Angeles this year, up from 43,695 the year prior. That’s still below the level recorded during Mayor Karen Bass’ first year in office, but it follows back-to-back declines, suggesting that any momentum under Bass is tentative at best. This is hardly what city residents and voters wanted after years of concentrated effort and the investment of hundreds of millions of dollars. Bass is up for reelection in November, and her opponent, Councilmember Nithya Raman , highlighted the latest report as evidence of Bass’ inability to tackle the city’s most pressing crisis. “This,” Raman said, “is a moral outrage. And it is a failure.” On Monday, an energized Raman toured a training facility in Sylmar, where apprentice carpenters are learning their craft and pining for the chance to participate in a Los Angeles building boom. The council member picked up the endorsement of the Western State Carpenters union, while pledging to usher in a wave of new construction. READ NEXT Commentary LA’s political coalitions have been shifting. Nithya Raman will shuffle them even more by Jim Newton “You are the people who build Los Angeles,” she told a cheering crowd of workers, nimbly moving back and forth between English and Spanish. “And together, we are going to build its future.” Raman beamed. It’s hard not to be buoyed when dozens of working men and women are chanting your name. There’s something topsy-turvy in all of this politically. Raman is a democratic socialist, but her message to the carpenters was heavy on the importance of reducing government regulation and letting private industry build new homes, schools and roads. “Mayors don’t build housing,” she acknowledged ruefully. At the same time, the endorsement is particularly helpful to Raman, as the carpenters backed Bass four years ago and helped her handily defeat businessman Rick Caruso. Meanwhile, Bass, who would be the liberal in almost any other run-off election in America, is campaigning in this race as the candidate of order — the leader willing to emphasize police in enforcing public safety and willing to disrupt encampments in order to reduce homelessness. As such, the campaign scrambles many of the assumptions of Los Angeles and municipal politics — that the path to victory is through command of the political center, that homeowners are the core of the electorate, that unions favor incumbents, and that older and more established voters form a more reliable base than young people and newcomers. Those things have long been true in politics, but they may not be true anymore. Los Angeles is a very liberal place , one where renters dominate the electorate and where Raman’s blend of democratic socialism, personal appeal and practical compromise may be closer to most voters than Bass’ more traditional liberalism. The upward tick in the city’s unhoused population is especially notable in political terms because it was accompanied by sharp reductions in Raman’s council district, which covers mostly affluent areas from Silver Lake and Los Feliz in the East, to Encino and Sherman Oaks on the other side of the Hollywood Hills. But the district envelopes working-class communities along the way, and struggles — as does all of Los Angeles — with street homelessness and its attendant community concerns, such as blight and petty crime. While street homelessness was on the rise citywide, it dropped by nearly 50% in District 4, which Raman represents. Nithya Raman, a candidate in the Los Angeles mayoral race, talks to reporters after a campaign event in Los Angeles, on June 1, 2026. Photo by Jae C. Hong, AP Photo Of course, there’s a wrinkle in all of that. Raman is not just the council member for her own district. She also chairs the council’s Housing and Homelessness Committee, so she, too, has citywide responsibilities. Bass says her signature program, called Inside Safe , has helped Raman’s district — that Raman is effectively benefiting from the mayor’s initiative while simultaneously criticizing it. Raman’s role as a committee chair blurs the edges of her accountability. It is just one example of the difficulty in disentangling the records of these two mayoral candidates. If elected, Raman has pledged to reduce street homelessness by 50% citywide in time for the Olympics in 2028, but Bass obviously has struggled to meet similar targets. Pressed for why the current efforts are falling short of expectations, Raman forcefully responded. “Mayor Bass’ Inside Safe program is an emergency response that is only the first step of systemic changes that need to happen to get people indoors and off the streets,” she said on Monday, speaking loudly over the clatter of hammers and electric saws. Raman believes her plan would go beyond shelter and get those who are unhoused “the mental health (treatment) and the services that they need to stay housed and to actually move … to that next step — whether it is reunification with their families, whether it is moving into mental health housing, whether it is getting a job and actually becoming self-sufficient. “All of that is possible. None of that is being done at the city right now.” Why not, I asked her. Why is the city — one that she serves in an important council position, and that Bass serves as mayor — not taking those steps now? “That is not a question for me to answer,” she said sharply. “That is a question for this mayor to answer.” None of this is easy. Homelessness is a stubborn pathology, a tragic confluence of failed public policies and eternal social conditions. There is nothing new about poverty, nor nothing novel about addiction. These problems are not easily wished away. If there was a simple fix to helping tens of thousands of people sleeping in tents and on the street, policymakers would fix it. Instead, it requires a blend of responses, a willingness to try things and then abandon them if they don’t work. And it demands public patience, a quality in short supply these days. So Raman and Bass slug it out, raising money (there Bass is showing strength ), holding events, circling each other with policy ideas and preparing to dash to the finish from Labor Day to Election Day. On Monday, Raman took in the carpenter training facility with interest and enthusiasm. She asked questions of her guide as she moved through a simulated construction site. At one point, Raman stepped on a large nail. Without pausing, she slipped off her loafer, yanked out the nail and kept going. That’s a mayor’s race in a nutshell. LA’s homelessness uptick lets Raman target Bass. If only accountability was that simple

By Jim Newton, CalMatters

This commentary was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

On Monday, Aug. 10, multiple news outlets reported that L.A. City Councilwoman Nithya Raman was going to lose her role as chair of the city's housing and homelessness committee, a move several observers (and Raman) believe was politically motivated.

After two consecutive years of declines in the number of people sleeping on the streets of Los Angeles, the progress appears to have been nearly wiped out. That’s discouraging news for a city exhausted by the issue, and it throws a strange curve into the race for mayor.

The latest annual count, released last week, registered 45,194 unhoused people in the city of Los Angeles this year, up from 43,695 the year prior. That’s still below the level recorded during Mayor Karen Bass’ first year in office, but it follows back-to-back declines, suggesting that any momentum under Bass is tentative at best. 

This is hardly what city residents and voters wanted after years of concentrated effort and the investment of hundreds of millions of dollars. Bass is up for reelection in November, and her opponent, Councilmember Nithya Raman, highlighted the latest report as evidence of Bass’ inability to tackle the city’s most pressing crisis.

“This,” Raman said, “is a moral outrage. And it is a failure.”

On Monday, an energized Raman toured a training facility in Sylmar, where apprentice carpenters are learning their craft and pining for the chance to participate in a Los Angeles building boom. The council member picked up the endorsement of the Western State Carpenters union, while pledging to usher in a wave of new construction.

“You are the people who build Los Angeles,” she told a cheering crowd of workers, nimbly moving back and forth between English and Spanish. “And together, we are going to build its future.”

Raman beamed. It’s hard not to be buoyed when dozens of working men and women are chanting your name.

There’s something topsy-turvy in all of this politically. Raman is a democratic socialist, but her message to the carpenters was heavy on the importance of reducing government regulation and letting private industry build new homes, schools and roads. 

“Mayors don’t build housing,” she acknowledged ruefully. At the same time, the endorsement is particularly helpful to Raman, as the carpenters backed Bass four years ago and helped her handily defeat businessman Rick Caruso.

Meanwhile, Bass, who would be the liberal in almost any other run-off election in America, is campaigning in this race as the candidate of order — the leader willing to emphasize police in enforcing public safety and willing to disrupt encampments in order to reduce homelessness.

As such, the campaign scrambles many of the assumptions of Los Angeles and municipal politics — that the path to victory is through command of the political center, that homeowners are the core of the electorate, that unions favor incumbents, and that older and more established voters form a more reliable base than young people and newcomers. 

Those things have long been true in politics, but they may not be true anymore. Los Angeles is a very liberal place, one where renters dominate the electorate and where Raman’s blend of democratic socialism, personal appeal and practical compromise may be closer to most voters than Bass’ more traditional liberalism.

The upward tick in the city’s unhoused population is especially notable in political terms because it was accompanied by sharp reductions in Raman’s council district, which covers mostly affluent areas from Silver Lake and Los Feliz in the East, to Encino and Sherman Oaks on the other side of the Hollywood Hills. But the district envelopes working-class communities along the way, and struggles — as does all of Los Angeles — with street homelessness and its attendant community concerns, such as blight and petty crime. 

While street homelessness was on the rise citywide, it dropped by nearly 50% in District 4, which Raman represents.

Of course, there’s a wrinkle in all of that. Raman is not just the council member for her own district. She also chairs the council’s Housing and Homelessness Committee, so she, too, has citywide responsibilities. Bass says her signature program, called Inside Safe, has helped Raman’s district — that Raman is effectively benefiting from the mayor’s initiative while simultaneously criticizing it.

Raman’s role as a committee chair blurs the edges of her accountability. It is just one example of the difficulty in disentangling the records of these two mayoral candidates. 

If elected, Raman has pledged to reduce street homelessness by 50% citywide in time for the Olympics in 2028, but Bass obviously has struggled to meet similar targets. Pressed for why the current efforts are falling short of expectations, Raman forcefully responded.

“Mayor Bass’ Inside Safe program is an emergency response that is only the first step of systemic changes that need to happen to get people indoors and off the streets,” she said on Monday, speaking loudly over the clatter of hammers and electric saws.

Raman believes her plan would go beyond shelter and get those who are unhoused “the mental health (treatment) and the services that they need to stay housed and to actually move … to that next step — whether it is reunification with their families, whether it is moving into mental health housing, whether it is getting a job and actually becoming self-sufficient.

"All of that is possible. None of that is being done at the city right now.”

Why not, I asked her. Why is the city — one that she serves in an important council position, and that Bass serves as mayor — not taking those steps now?

“That is not a question for me to answer,” she said sharply. “That is a question for this mayor to answer.”

None of this is easy. Homelessness is a stubborn pathology, a tragic confluence of failed public policies and eternal social conditions. There is nothing new about poverty, nor nothing novel about addiction. These problems are not easily wished away. If there was a simple fix to helping tens of thousands of people sleeping in tents and on the street, policymakers would fix it. Instead, it requires a blend of responses, a willingness to try things and then abandon them if they don’t work. And it demands public patience, a quality in short supply these days.

So Raman and Bass slug it out, raising money (there Bass is showing strength), holding events, circling each other with policy ideas and preparing to dash to the finish from Labor Day to Election Day. 

On Monday, Raman took in the carpenter training facility with interest and enthusiasm. She asked questions of her guide as she moved through a simulated construction site. At one point, Raman stepped on a large nail. Without pausing, she slipped off her loafer, yanked out the nail and kept going. 

That’s a mayor’s race in a nutshell.

title: Opinion | LA mayoral rivals clash over police, but miss key issues
desc: Mayor Karen Bass’ challenger, Councilmember Nithya Raman, says LA has lost confidence in Chief Jim McDonnell. That prompted Bass to back him, even as police protect ICE agents and draw the public's anger.
body:
Opinion | LA mayoral rivals clash over police, but miss key issues Nonprofit & Nonpartisan News About Us Newsletters Donate About Newsletters Search Politics Justice Environment Economy Health Housing Education Inequality Digital Democracy Technology Commentary Daily Newsletter Explainers Data & Trackers Programs California Divide CalMatters for Learning Knowledge Hub College Journalism Network Mental Health Reporting Initiative Events Donate Manage your donation Newsletters About Us Impact News and Awards How We’re Funded Republish Our Stories Policies Our Team Jobs Advertise Contact Us Inside the Newsroom CalMatters en Español Videos CalMatters is your nonprofit and nonpartisan newsroom dedicated to explaining how state government impacts our lives. Bluesky Instagram Facebook X TikTok LinkedIn YouTube Election Results Politics Housing Education Economy Immigration Environment California Voices Investigations Impact Ideas Festival Posted in Commentary LA mayoral rivals clash over public safety and the police chief but miss key issues by Jim Newton September 17, 2026 September 16, 2026 Republish Share this: Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on WhatsApp (Opens in new window) WhatsApp LA Mayor Karen Bass arrives as federal agents descend on MacArthur Park in Los Angeles on July 7, 2025. Photo by J.W. Hendricks for CalMatters Welcome to CalMatters, the only nonprofit newsroom devoted solely to covering statewide issues that affect all Californians. Sign up for WeeklyMatters for a Saturday morning digest of the latest news and commentary from the Golden State. This story is part of California Voices, a commentary forum aiming to broaden our understanding of the state and spotlight Californians directly impacted by policy or its absence. Learn more here . As Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass and Councilmember Nithya Raman vie to become the next mayor of California’s largest city, they are sparring over the wrong issues regarding public safety, discussing it in terms that fail to illuminate the most important questions about the direction of the Los Angeles Police Department. Start with the department’s top cop, Chief Jim McDonnell. Raman says McDonnell has “ lost the confidence ” of the city, an assertion for which she offers no real evidence. She says there‘s a perception that the LAPD is doing too much to cooperate with federal immigration authorities. Both observations are, at best, debatable and, at worst, wrong. Bass, meanwhile, is responsible for McDonnell and has supported his efforts to stem attrition and rebuild the department’s ranks. She appointed him to a five-year term in 2024, with Raman joining 10 other council members who voted in support. Shortly after that, the first wave of President Donald Trump’s strategy to militarize immigration enforcement blasted into Los Angeles , ratcheting up the level of violence in other Democratic cities. That placed McDonnell and the LAPD in a delicate position: Department policy has long prohibited police officers from making stops based on suspicion of immigration status, a measure adopted in 1979 to protect all residents by encouraging witnesses and victims to come forward. Los Angeles City Council Member Nithya Raman speaks during the Karen Bass election night party at the W Hotel in Hollywood on June 7, 2022. Photo by John McCoy, AP Photo But the LAPD also has an historic obligation to “protect and serve” all those who are in the city, regardless of race, orientation, immigration status — or even professional position. That means LAPD officers have sometimes found themselves protecting ICE officers from angry residents, a situation Raman and others have complained creates “bad optics” of local police seeming to side with ICE over immigrants. That’s nonsense. ICE officers are doing dumb and counterproductive work in Los Angeles, and the mayor, council and chief have every responsibility to resist that work at the policy level. That does not mean allowing ICE officers to be assaulted, though. LAPD’s obligation to protect and serve extends to the hapless ICE agent who is here only because Trump’s ego requires a show of force. Moreover, federal immigration authorities have the right to deport those who are in the country illegally. That does not mean the LAPD should lend a hand — it should not — but police officers cannot impede federal law. Marijuana enforcement provides a good analogy: Police officers in Los Angeles may not stop a Drug Enforcement Administration agent from enforcing federal drug laws, but that doesn’t mean the police are required to cuff every kid smoking a joint. Whatever the merits of McDonnell’s leadership of the LAPD, his continued service should not rest on a false assumption that the LAPD should withhold protection from ICE agents to assure residents the department is not an agent of federal authority. ICE’s work is deplorable; leaving its agents at risk of harm is not the right response. As to the claim that McDonnell does not deserve to continue in his job, that warrants a larger analysis than a campaign soundbite. The critical criteria for evaluating a chief of police are crime, the behavior of officers and the department’s response to allegations of misconduct. Are LAPD officers respecting the constitutional protections of those they arrest or otherwise encounter? And are those officers doing their work in ways that serve the public? READ NEXT Commentary Los Angeles police chief takes over in a period of uncertainty and mixed signals by Jim Newton In other words, are police obeying and enforcing the law, and doing so in ways that make the city safer? McDonnell has some significant points in his favor. Violent crime in Los Angeles is at historic lows: The city had 230 homicides in 2025, down 54 from the year before and the fewest of any year since 1966. Overall, violent crimes and property crimes were down. That is evidence of a city getting safer. Meanwhile, however, LAPD officers increased their uses of force — firing their guns more than 45 times in 2025, a 70% increase, and leaving 14 people dead. Responding to Bass’ concern about the uptick in officer-involved shootings, McDonnell warned that every shooting would be “rigorously investigated , both internally as well as externally, through independent oversight bodies.” McDonnell’s statement is to be commended, and city leaders should hold him and his subordinates responsible for any violence committed by police, with the obvious understanding that some violence is inevitable and may be justifiable. Former Chief Bernard C. Parks used to say that the LAPD disciplines too many officers and fires too few. Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass introduces newly appointed police chief Jim McDonnell during a news conference in Los Angeles on Oct. 4, 2024. Photo by Jae C. Hong, AP Photo His point about leniency still stands: A chief cannot prevent every unwarranted use of force or inappropriate contact with the public, but the chief can — and must — set firm standards and hold officers to them. The other issue that creeps into the discussion of policing is money, and there the mayoral campaign has tended to distort rather than clarify. Bass has called for more funding for the LAPD while Raman has objected — seeming to place the mayor in defense of the department and Raman as its critic. To put it simply, the right political response to criticism of the LAPD is not to cut the department’s budget. Throwing money at the LAPD also won’t solve its problems, but sometimes more officers are needed to do better work, and cutting budgets can result in more violence and misunderstanding, not less. Budgets should not be used to punish or reward the LAPD. They should be tailored to fighting crime and holding police accountable for doing their important work within the strictures of the law and constitution. LA mayoral rivals clash over public safety and the police chief but miss key issues

By Jim Newton, CalMatters

This commentary was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

As Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass and Councilmember Nithya Raman vie to become the next mayor of California’s largest city, they are sparring over the wrong issues regarding public safety, discussing it in terms that fail to illuminate the most important questions about the direction of the Los Angeles Police Department.

Start with the department’s top cop, Chief Jim McDonnell. 

Raman says McDonnell has “lost the confidence” of the city, an assertion for which she offers no real evidence. She says there‘s a perception that the LAPD is doing too much to cooperate with federal immigration authorities. Both observations are, at best, debatable and, at worst, wrong. 

Bass, meanwhile, is responsible for McDonnell and has supported his efforts to stem attrition and rebuild the department’s ranks. 

She appointed him to a five-year term in 2024, with Raman joining 10 other council members who voted in support. Shortly after that, the first wave of President Donald Trump’s strategy to militarize immigration enforcement blasted into Los Angeles, ratcheting up the level of violence in other Democratic cities. 

That placed McDonnell and the LAPD in a delicate position: Department policy has long prohibited police officers from making stops based on suspicion of immigration status, a measure adopted in 1979 to protect all residents by encouraging witnesses and victims to come forward. 

But the LAPD also has an historic obligation to “protect and serve” all those who are in the city, regardless of race, orientation, immigration status — or even professional position. That means LAPD officers have sometimes found themselves protecting ICE officers from angry residents, a situation Raman and others have complained creates “bad optics” of local police seeming to side with ICE over immigrants.

That’s nonsense. ICE officers are doing dumb and counterproductive work in Los Angeles, and the mayor, council and chief have every responsibility to resist that work at the policy level. 

That does not mean allowing ICE officers to be assaulted, though. LAPD’s obligation to protect and serve extends to the hapless ICE agent who is here only because Trump’s ego requires a show of force.

Moreover, federal immigration authorities have the right to deport those who are in the country illegally. That does not mean the LAPD should lend a hand — it should not — but police officers cannot impede federal law. 

Marijuana enforcement provides a good analogy: Police officers in Los Angeles may not stop a Drug Enforcement Administration agent from enforcing federal drug laws, but that doesn’t mean the police are required to cuff every kid smoking a joint.

Whatever the merits of McDonnell’s leadership of the LAPD, his continued service should not rest on a false assumption that the LAPD should withhold protection from ICE agents to assure residents the department is not an agent of federal authority. ICE’s work is deplorable; leaving its agents at risk of harm is not the right response.

As to the claim that McDonnell does not deserve to continue in his job, that warrants a larger analysis than a campaign soundbite. 

The critical criteria for evaluating a chief of police are crime, the behavior of officers and the department’s response to allegations of misconduct. Are LAPD officers respecting the constitutional protections of those they arrest or otherwise encounter? And are those officers doing their work in ways that serve the public? 

In other words, are police obeying and enforcing the law, and doing so in ways that make the city safer? 

McDonnell has some significant points in his favor. Violent crime in Los Angeles is at historic lows: The city had 230 homicides in 2025, down 54 from the year before and the fewest of any year since 1966. 

Overall, violent crimes and property crimes were down. That is evidence of a city getting safer.

Meanwhile, however, LAPD officers increased their uses of force — firing their guns more than 45 times in 2025, a 70% increase, and leaving 14 people dead. 

Responding to Bass’ concern about the uptick in officer-involved shootings, McDonnell warned that every shooting would be “rigorously investigated, both internally as well as externally, through independent oversight bodies.” 

McDonnell’s statement is to be commended, and city leaders should hold him and his subordinates responsible for any violence committed by police, with the obvious understanding that some violence is inevitable and may be justifiable. 

Former Chief Bernard C. Parks used to say that the LAPD disciplines too many officers and fires too few. 

His point about leniency still stands: A chief cannot prevent every unwarranted use of force or inappropriate contact with the public, but the chief can — and must — set firm standards and hold officers to them.

The other issue that creeps into the discussion of policing is money, and there the mayoral campaign has tended to distort rather than clarify. Bass has called for more funding for the LAPD while Raman has objected — seeming to place the mayor in defense of the department and Raman as its critic. 

To put it simply, the right political response to criticism of the LAPD is not to cut the department’s budget. Throwing money at the LAPD also won’t solve its problems, but sometimes more officers are needed to do better work, and cutting budgets can result in more violence and misunderstanding, not less.

Budgets should not be used to punish or reward the LAPD. They should be tailored to fighting crime and holding police accountable for doing their important work within the strictures of the law and constitution.

To be clear, the right debate over public safety is not about whether Jim McDonnell should be fired or whether he or the LAPD has “lost the confidence” of the city.

The real conversation starts with both mayoral candidates articulating a vision for the police department’s responsibilities. 

Then it moves to the work of civilian authorities to solidify that vision into a set of directions for the department. Once it has those directions, the LAPD and its chief should be held responsible for carrying them out — lawfully and effectively. 

A chief who carries out that mandate, who brings down crime and holds his (or her) officers accountable for genuinely protecting and serving the community should be rewarded. One who does not should be replaced.

Friends who’ve fallen out feud during gritty, final LA mayoral debate

By Jim Newton, CalMatters

This commentary was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

Voters have been good to Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass. For the past two decades, she has won elections to the California Assembly, to Congress and to the mayoralty she now holds. She has never lost an election.

But her grip on her current job is tenuous.

That was evident Tuesday night during a close, sometimes gritty debate with her rival, City Councilmember Nithya Raman. Bass was measured and unflappable but also biting. Polls show her trailing in her bid for re-election, but she made it clear Tuesday she has no intention of leaving quietly.

Separated from each other by a panel of questioners, the two candidates were warned at the outset to refrain from personal attacks. Both ignored that admonishment.

In the final televised debate of a close campaign, Bass was particularly assertive, several times accusing Raman of lying and misrepresenting the mayor’s record, as well as suggesting Raman would plunge the Los Angeles Police Department into “disarray” on the eve of the Olympic games and maintaining that the mayor’s office was forced to handle constituent services in Raman’s district when residents became frustrated with the council member and her staff. 

Raman shook her head in annoyance as the mayor’s accusations piled up.

Portraying Raman as naïve and slippery, Bass concluded: “Now is not the time to turn the city over to Nithya Raman.”

Those are tough words, especially for an official the mayor once favored. Raman and Bass have supported each other in prior campaigns, and Raman backed Bass in this one before jumping in herself. 

That has left Bass feeling betrayed, and some of that bitterness Raman reflected back during the debate. Raman charged the mayor with paying “lip service” to reducing red tape that bottles up housing construction and with overseeing a listless, lost administration. The Bass mayoral record, Raman insisted, was “four years of decline, of mismanagement, of excuses.”

There are no enemies in politics quite like friends who have fallen out, and that’s what this race has become. 

Substantively, their debate covered familiar ground: Raman accused the mayor of being “MIA” during and after the fire that destroyed thousands of homes in the Pacific Palisades and more broadly MIA as a manager of city services. Under Bass, the councilwoman argued, city departments have become dysfunctional, paralyzed when faced with complaints and unable to make changes that might bring down the cost of new housing.

In fact, although the two agree on the crying need for new housing construction, they managed to fight over that, too, with Bass touting the construction of 10,000 new affordable housing units during her tenure and Raman pointing out that overall apartment construction in the city is falling. Both are right.

As the two make the final turn toward Election Day, their similarities are as striking as their differences. 

Both champion affordability. Raman focuses on housing, by far the biggest expense for most L.A. residents, and Bass agrees, while also suggesting that the city should expand childcare services to provide some relief there. 

Both also support tax credits and services to the film industry as part of their effort to keep jobs in Los Angeles. But they differ over who cares more about that issue or who has done more about it so far.

And both compete for the title of being the leader who most dislikes President Donald Trump. 

Bass highlights her visible role in standing against the ICE raids last summer. Raman argues the city needs to be even more forceful in refusing cooperation with federal authorities bent on turning the city into a showcase for the militarized rousting of undocumented migrants or anyone who looks like them. 

Trump and ICE are among the most hated figures and institutions in Los Angeles, so it’s hardly a surprise the top contenders for mayor would find common ground there.

In the debate, however, were glimmers of ways these candidates are different, substantively and temperamentally. 

Bass places greater confidence in police and in the current leadership of the LAPD. Raman starts from a place of greater skepticism about the department and Police Chief Jim McDonnell, who was appointed in 2024 and has a five-year term.

But Raman seems torn by the issue. During the debate, she said she would seek to remove McDonnell, but she shuffled over the questions of how and when she would do that. 

McDonnell, Raman said, had “lost the trust” of the city’s immigrant community by defending ICE against protesters and, she maintained, by sharing data with the federal government. 

Yet, when pressed on what action she would take, Raman — as she has before — equivocated, saying the chief’s removal required the agreement of the Police Commission and the involvement of City Council. 

That’s sort of true, but mostly not. The mayor appoints the Police Commission, so the mayor has no real impediment to firing a chief. And yes, an ousted chief could appeal to the council for reinstatement, but that’s never happened. It’s also hard to imagine a chief being fired, then winning reinstatement and going back to work for the mayor who fired him.

When NBC’s Conan Nolan pushed harder, asking whether Raman would get rid of McDonnell before the 2028 Olympics, she retreated further. “It will depend on these other factors.”

Bass was more sure-footed while talking about public safety, but she has her own struggles — starting with any proposal she now brings to the table. Improved childcare in city parks? Better data and transparency on police shootings? Expanded use of cameras to monitor traffic violations? 

All have merit, but why is a mayor who’s been in office for nearly four years suddenly pulling out new ideas for the future? 

It’s an exposed flank for an incumbent who both wants credit for progress and at the same time resists being accused of letting the city down. And it feeds Raman’s argument that Bass looks for excuses and only produces policies in response to the challenge she’s facing to win re-election.

Ballots are in the hands of voters, and polling in the race is frustratingly ambiguous. 

All the credible surveys suggest many voters are tired of Bass.But the mayor does better among older and most established residents, who happen to be the most likely to vote. She also has the support of most unions, and they are famous for turning out their members.

Bass’s challenge is unlike any she’s faced before. She needs to stage a comeback, to persuade voters that Raman is too extreme, too untested, “not ready for prime time,” as the mayor offered on Tuesday. 

But that’s a hard sell against the reality of Raman, who comes off as educated and careful, more nerdy than dangerous. Her eyes light up when she talks about data.

This week’s debate did not seal the deal for either candidate, but it offered a glimpse of what lies ahead: Tough disagreements between former friends who have become wary rivals, a choice of personalities and ideas, with the future of the city very much at stake.

Neither LA mayoral candidate has a compelling answer to the affordability crisis

By Jim Newton, CalMatters

This commentary was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

In Los Angeles, Karen Bass and Nithya Raman have both vowed that they would stress affordability if elected to serve as the city’s next mayor. Given their agreement, Los Angeles surely will be less expensive soon, no matter who wins, right?

Probably not. Neither candidate has produced a plan that would reduce the price of anything, at least anytime soon. That’s not because they don’t care. Both Bass, the incumbent mayor, and Raman, a city council member, have records of attempting to hold down increases in the price of housing. Each has ideas about how to do so over the next four years.

Beyond that, they have very little to offer that would quickly or significantly decrease the cost of living in America’s second-largest city.

L.A. is a very expensive place to live. The average apartment goes for about $2,600 a month. Average utility costs add another $500 or so to a household’s expenses. Throw in car payments, parking, insurance and gas (since most Angelenos drive cars), along with groceries (since all of them eat), and the basic cost of living inside the city quickly soars to roughly $6,000 a month. That’s before anything discretionary or fun — and if you don’t have children.

It’s no wonder that Los Angeles voters rank the cost of living at or near the top of their list of concerns.

In a mayoral forum this week, Raman and Bass each acknowledged the importance of affordability to Angelenos. Raman called it the “single driving (force) that is reshaping Los Angeles” by pushing out working people. Bass recalled growing up in L.A. when it was a place that working people could afford, and she lamented the city’s transformation into one of the nation’s most expensive places to live.

But when it came to fixing that problem, what was most obvious were the limits of the mayoralty — or of the imagination of the candidates. Raman promised to create an office devoted to expediting housing. Bass said she’s already cut red tape and would do even more in the second term. Both said they would reduce regulations that interfere with market-rate and affordable housing construction.

To be fair, affordability is not a natural topic for mayors, but it’s an inescapable issue in this election cycle, which includes a closely contested race for mayor along with a cakewalk in the governor’s race and a potential referendum on President Donald Trump.

Candidates like to address what’s bothering people, and prices are on the nation’s mind. Costs keep rising, and the issue of affordability is driving much of the energy in the midterms. That makes perfect sense, since national policies are behind much of the inflation that’s hurting consumers. 

President Trump’s impetuous war in Iran has roiled global oil markets and resulted in skyrocketing prices for gasoline and diesel, with cascading effects: Groceries are more expensive as the cost of fertilizer increases; prices for all kinds of goods go up when the cost of moving them from producers to consumers increases.

Some candidates, even for major local offices, have tackled affordability head on and to winning effect. In New York City, most notably, Mayor Zohran Mamdani won by proposing a host of measures intended to curb the cost of living. Since taking office, Mamdani has frozen rents, recommended making buses free and moved forward with plans for creating five city-run grocery stores, among other affordability measures. 

They may not all come to fruition, but he is visibly responding to his electorate.

What they offer won't bring relief soon

None of that is in the works for residents of Los Angeles, regardless of who prevails in November. Here, the two candidates for mayor echo the importance of affordability, but they have settled for far less ambitious solutions. Asked about affordability during their forum Tuesday, neither Bass nor Raman even floated making buses free, opening city-run grocery stores or using the mayor’s authority over the utilities department to, for example, shake up the board or expand savings programs. 

The intertwining of the Raman and Bass records also complicates matters. Raman, a democratic socialist in the mold of Mamdani, is rightly recognized for pioneering the city’s overhaul of its rent control structure, but Bass signed that bill into law, so she claims some credit, too. Under that rent stabilization ordinance, annual increases are capped at 4% or at 90% of the rate of inflation, whichever is lower. 

As she campaigns for mayor, Raman touts her work on rent control and promises to continue and extend her defense of renters, though her plans would, at best, slow rent increases, not freeze rents, much less roll them back. Beyond that, the heart of her vision for reducing housing costs is to liberate construction by supporting greater density — an idea viewed warily by many homeowners — and reducing regulatory impediments.

A genuine boost in supply could drive down prices and rents, but market pressures tend to be long-term and unpredictable. If Raman is elected, no one should expect rents to drop right away.

Bass’ affordability plans are similarly long-term, though she can point to some direct action in her tenure. In addition to signing rent stabilization, Bass redirected the Mayor’s Fund to protecting renters, and it has supplied thousands of families with rental assistance and guidance in the face of possible eviction. 

Her support for affordable housing also has helped put more units in the pipeline, and the city has added more than 10,200 during her tenure. It’s an uptick from her predecessors but a trickle of new housing in a city that needs a flood to have a meaningful impact on rents. Bass defends that number, noting that it comes despite the Trump administration’s chaotic tariffs and economic mismanagement.

But it states the obvious to note that if rent control as championed by Raman or eviction protection as practiced by Bass were enough to solve the problem, it would be solved. Instead, the cost of living in Los Angeles remains out of reach for many working people, even after three years of Bass serving as mayor and five years of Raman serving on the council. 

More of the same — or even an expansion of the same programs — seems unlikely to deliver quick relief to those hoping this election might bring it.

Affordability is unlikely to determine the outcome of this campaign, though Raman probably suffers on this issue more than Bass does, if only because expectations of a democratic socialist are higher in this area than for the more traditionally Democratic Bass. At their forum Tuesday night, Bass was much more warmly received, and the audience, a predominantly Jewish crowd at the Skirball Center on L.A.’s Westside, was openly skeptical of Raman’s affiliation with the Democratic Socialists of America.

Rather than embrace her connection to the DSA and highlight the organization’s commitment to making Los Angeles more affordable for working people, Raman seemed to distance herself from it, especially its support for divestment from companies that do business with Israel.

“I have been vocal about places where I’ve disagreed with the DSA on a range of issues,” she said to grumbles from the audience. “I’ve proven myself to be an independent voice during my time on the council.”

She has, and she deserves credit for that. But that independence won’t make Los Angeles more affordable. It will take innovation, creativity and a willingness to try new formulas. 

So far, neither candidate has offered much to suggest that relief is coming soon.

title: Opinion | Bass-Raman LA mayoral race has avoided identity politics
desc: The L.A. mayoral race has not been marked by racial divisions or differences over immigration, assimilation or cultural hegemony.

Photos by Damian Dovarganes, AP Photo and Vivien Killilea, Getty Images This story is part of California Voices, a commentary forum aiming to broaden our understanding of the state and spotlight Californians directly impacted by policy or its absence. Learn more here . The race for mayor of Los Angeles has largely focused on the decision voters face between a liberal incumbent with four years of mixed success and a democratic socialist who might advance a more progressive agenda. If that’s the choice in this election between Mayor Karen Bass and Councilmember Nithya Raman, it is also worth noting what it has not been: In the ethnic and national stew that is Los Angeles, this year’s race has avoided the theater of identity politics that has often shaped its mayoral contests. With one exception , this campaign has not been marked by racial divisions or differences over issues relating to immigration, assimilation or cultural hegemony. That represents a break from much of this city’s recent political history. Tom Bradley, the city’s first Black mayor, held office for five terms. Before moving to politics, Bradley had served as a police officer at the LAPD, navigating one of the most racially entrenched institutions of its time. He never forgot those experiences, and his mayoralty marked and solidified the place of African Americans in Los Angeles leadership, as well as fusing an alliance between Jewish and Black voters. The mayors who have followed often have risen to office against a backdrop of racial divide. Richard Riordan won the support of white voters and many Latinos but never found much support in Black communities. His successor, Jim Hahn, rejiggered the Riordan majority and won by drawing support from Black and moderate-to-conservative white voters — only to lose both when he dumped Police Chief Bernard Parks and opposed San Fernando Valley secession . Antonio Villaraigosa was the first Latino to lead Los Angeles in the modern era, and his election was a triumph for the Latino-labor coalition that united behind him. Eric Garcetti looked like a white guy, but his mother was Mexican; he spoke fluent Spanish and he was popular with many of those who had supported Villaraigosa. And Bass, the mayor now fighting to keep her job, defeated a white, self-financed businessman in the Riordan mold by consolidating support from Black voters and building energy around electing the city’s first woman. That marks a half-century of shifting identity politics, which is natural, perhaps, in a city whose demographics have been fast-evolving over that same period — from a mostly white and Republican anti-labor alternative to San Francisco, to a plurality-Latino metropolis where organized labor is a powerful political force. READ NEXT Commentary LA’s Latino neighborhoods backed Karen Bass in June. Will they stick with her in November? by Jim Newton And yet, there’s been barely a whiff of those tensions or that history in this campaign. Both Bass and Raman enjoy support across ethnic lines, with notably large chunks of the electorate undecided going into the campaign’s final days. The city’s Black voters, of whom there has not been much serious polling, appear to remain firmly in Bass’ camp . Even in that shrinking segment of the L.A. electorate, however, there are signs of younger Black voters coalescing around Raman. Indeed, the only real nod to identity politics in this runoff campaign was telling. During a debate, Raman made a clumsy reference to former LAPD Chief Daryl Gates and the “gold standard” of the police department’s refusal to cooperate with immigration authorities . Her comment, a reference to the department’s Special Order 40 , was clipped. It was also historically suspect since LAPD has long turned over suspects found to be in the country illegally to federal authorities. What Gates did decades ago was prohibit officers from stopping people based solely on suspicion of their immigration status. But Raman’s remark roiled up old antipathies toward the police department and the racial dimensions of that history. In some ways, that was just campaign noise. I did not hear it as suggesting that Gates represented any kind of “gold standard” for policing, and I say that as someone who had issues with Gates, who once challenged me to a fistfight for reporting that he had retired “in disgrace.” It sounded to me like Raman was trying to say that even in the Gates era, the LAPD understood the value of distancing itself from immigration enforcement. Nevertheless, it’s not great politics to insert “Daryl Gates” and “gold standard” into the same sentence, and the words touched a nerve in a certain slice of the electorate. In short, it angered many Black voters who too-often were on the receiving end of racist policing. After the debate, an impromptu community gathering rallied around Bass and demanded that Raman walk back her remark. It featured, for me, friendly and familiar faces. Carl Douglas, the great lawyer who defended O.J. Simpson at Johnnie Cochran’s side, spoke in his trademark stentorian eloquence. Danny Bakewell, the now-graying activist, was gritty and forceful. The crowd chanted “four more years.” All of it felt reminiscent of the 1990s. To her credit, Raman did pull back the comment , however it was initially intended. ELECTION 2026 2026 Voter Guide Get ready for California’s midterm election. This voter guide has everything you need to know But the episode felt out of character with this mayoral election. It stands out in this cycle precisely because the campaign has not been built on such flare-ups, the kind that refresh memories of the deep, destructive racial divisions that once plunged Los Angeles into riots, that threatened the city’s sense of itself as a place of welcome and refuge. That’s not to say that the campaign has avoided division. All campaigns divide. The goal, after all, is to get more voters than the other side, to produce a winner and therefore a loser. In this race, though, the lines of division are not primarily racial and certainly not of gender — not with two women of color contending for the office. Rather, the most palpable divide and predictor has been age, or someone’s time living in Los Angeles. For those who were here when Gates was the chief, when LAPD was regarded as an “occupying army,” when more than 1,000 people a year were being murdered in Los Angeles, the urgency of Raman’s campaign may feel manufactured. It is hard to identify with the idea that the city is in crisis when it seems so much better than it once did. But for newer arrivals, those who have come to the city in recent years in search of its age-old promise, it may feel bleaker. The cost of rent and gas and groceries , the dismaying presence of homeless encampments and the dark threat of immigration raids all seem to block the fulfillment of that dream. Those newer arrivals — Raman herself moved here in 2013 — are more open to the notion that something here is terribly off, that only a fresh take on leadership can bring the city to its fullest potential. Is division by age or length of residence any better than division by race or gender? Probably. All of us were young at some point, and most of us get old, so generational divides have a built-in mechanism for healing in a way that gender and racial divides do not. In the short run, they may decide this race for mayor. And the campaign’s defining divide is also what may keep it competitive. For while Raman is leading in every reputable poll , her support relies on those younger, newer voters, while Bass’ is built on those who have been here longer and have a greater stake in the city’s history. Traditionally, those voters are more dependable, so Raman’s lead, while significant, is not dispositive. A poll of likely voters released this week had the candidates evenly split . This election remains competitive, right to the finish. He never forgot those experiences, and his mayoralty marked and solidified the place of African Americans in Los Angeles leadership, as well as fusing an alliance between Jewish and Black voters.

The mayors who have followed often have risen to office against a backdrop of racial divide. Richard Riordan won the support of white voters and many Latinos but never found much support in Black communities. His successor, Jim Hahn, rejiggered the Riordan majority and won by drawing support from Black and moderate-to-conservative white voters — only to lose both when he dumped Police Chief Bernard Parks and opposed San Fernando Valley secession. 

Antonio Villaraigosa was the first Latino to lead Los Angeles in the modern era, and his election was a triumph for the Latino-labor coalition that united behind him. Eric Garcetti looked like a white guy, but his mother was Mexican; he spoke fluent Spanish and he was popular with many of those who had supported Villaraigosa. And Bass, the mayor now fighting to keep her job, defeated a white, self-financed businessman in the Riordan mold by consolidating support from Black voters and building energy around electing the city’s first woman.

That marks a half-century of shifting identity politics, which is natural, perhaps, in a city whose demographics have been fast-evolving over that same period — from a mostly white and Republican anti-labor alternative to San Francisco, to a plurality-Latino metropolis where organized labor is a powerful political force.

And yet, there’s been barely a whiff of those tensions or that history in this campaign. Both Bass and Raman enjoy support across ethnic lines, with notably large chunks of the electorate undecided going into the campaign’s final days.

The city’s Black voters, of whom there has not been much serious polling, appear to remain firmly in Bass’ camp. Even in that shrinking segment of the L.A. electorate, however, there are signs of younger Black voters coalescing around Raman.

Indeed, the only real nod to identity politics in this runoff campaign was telling. During a debate, Raman made a clumsy reference to former LAPD Chief Daryl Gates and the “gold standard” of the police department’s refusal to cooperate with immigration authorities.

Her comment, a reference to the department’s Special Order 40, was clipped. It was also historically suspect since LAPD has long turned over suspects found to be in the country illegally to federal authorities. What Gates did decades ago was prohibit officers from stopping people based solely on suspicion of their immigration status. But Raman’s remark roiled up old antipathies toward the police department and the racial dimensions of that history.

In some ways, that was just campaign noise. I did not hear it as suggesting that Gates represented any kind of “gold standard” for policing, and I say that as someone who had issues with Gates, who once challenged me to a fistfight for reporting that he had retired “in disgrace.” It sounded to me like Raman was trying to say that even in the Gates era, the LAPD understood the value of distancing itself from immigration enforcement.

Nevertheless, it’s not great politics to insert “Daryl Gates” and “gold standard” into the same sentence, and the words touched a nerve in a certain slice of the electorate. In short, it angered many Black voters who too-often were on the receiving end of racist policing.

After the debate, an impromptu community gathering rallied around Bass and demanded that Raman walk back her remark. It featured, for me, friendly and familiar faces. Carl Douglas, the great lawyer who defended O.J. Simpson at Johnnie Cochran’s side, spoke in his trademark stentorian eloquence. Danny Bakewell, the now-graying activist, was gritty and forceful. The crowd chanted “four more years.” All of it felt reminiscent of the 1990s.

To her credit, Raman did pull back the comment, however it was initially intended. 

But the episode felt out of character with this mayoral election. It stands out in this cycle precisely because the campaign has not been built on such flare-ups, the kind that refresh memories of the deep, destructive racial divisions that once plunged Los Angeles into riots, that threatened the city’s sense of itself as a place of welcome and refuge.

That’s not to say that the campaign has avoided division. All campaigns divide. The goal, after all, is to get more voters than the other side, to produce a winner and therefore a loser.

In this race, though, the lines of division are not primarily racial and certainly not of gender — not with two women of color contending for the office. Rather, the most palpable divide and predictor has been age, or someone’s time living in Los Angeles.

For those who were here when Gates was the chief, when LAPD was regarded as an “occupying army,” when more than 1,000 people a year were being murdered in Los Angeles, the urgency of Raman’s campaign may feel manufactured. It is hard to identify with the idea that the city is in crisis when it seems so much better than it once did.

But for newer arrivals, those who have come to the city in recent years in search of its age-old promise, it may feel bleaker. The cost of rent and gas and groceries, the dismaying presence of homeless encampments and the dark threat of immigration raids all seem to block the fulfillment of that dream. Those newer arrivals — Raman herself moved here in 2013 — are more open to the notion that something here is terribly off, that only a fresh take on leadership can bring the city to its fullest potential.

Is division by age or length of residence any better than division by race or gender? Probably. All of us were young at some point, and most of us get old, so generational divides have a built-in mechanism for healing in a way that gender and racial divides do not.

In the short run, they may decide this race for mayor. And the campaign’s defining divide is also what may keep it competitive. For while Raman is leading in every reputable poll, her support relies on those younger, newer voters, while Bass’ is built on those who have been here longer and have a greater stake in the city’s history.

Traditionally, those voters are more dependable, so Raman’s lead, while significant, is not dispositive. A poll of likely voters released this week had the candidates evenly split.

This election remains competitive, right to the finish.

Mayor-elect Nithya Raman inherits a Los Angeles full of promise and burdened by challenges

By Jim Newton, CalMatters

This commentary was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

Los Angeles, once California’s most reliably Republican stronghold, now faces a future under the leadership of a democratic socialist. Incumbent Mayor Karen Bass has lost her reelection bid to a friend-turned-rival, Councilmember and Mayor-elect Nithya Raman. 

Her election ushers in a new era for California’s largest city, decisively breaking it from the history that preceded it. Raman’s victory was unusual in some respects — she rode a national blue wave that toppled Republicans from Maine to California and, along the way, ousted the liberal, Black woman serving as mayor of Los Angeles — but natural, even overdue, in others. Raman, a 45-year-old Indian immigrant and mother of twins, was carried into office by younger voters and newer arrivals to L.A., those least burdened by the expectations or limitations of the city’s past.

Raman will face significant challenges: Homelessness is a grinding human tragedy that resisted her predecessor’s best efforts; housing is expensive and likely to remain so at least for a while; the 2028 Summer Olympics are fast approaching; the city’s police department and public safety strategies are a source of contention. 

Meanwhile, some of Raman's campaign pronouncements may prove difficult to execute and even contradictory. She has vowed, for instance, to support a smooth run-up to the Games and promised to remove the city’s police chief. These two goals may bump into each other.

Still, she arrives at the post on the heels of a largely positive, uplifting, even joyful campaign. Her election night party at the Greek Theater in Griffith Park was an outpouring of exuberant energy that her supporters hope to carry with them into office.

“Are you ready for an L.A. that loves you back?” she asked those supporters. Their answer was obvious, and their excitement was real.

First, though, what happened to Bass, who will become only the second mayor in modern Los Angeles history to be shown the door by voters after one term. The first, James Hahn, defied his political base — an unusual combination of Valley moderates and Black voters — by opposing Valley secession and denying Police Chief Bernard C. Parks a second term at the helm of the LAPD. That left Hahn in 2005 without allies to face Antonio Villaraigosa in a rematch of their 2001 contest. Hahn was easily defeated.

This race was not so easy for Raman, and Bass did not fold as quickly or decisively as Hahn did. But some noteworthy events conspired with some of Bass’ executive weaknesses to create the conditions for her downfall.

Foremost was one over which she had no control. Dry conditions and furious winds descended upon Los Angeles in January 2025. Once brush and homes began to ignite, nothing could have stopped the inferno that swept across the city — and, simultaneously, over land outside the city, notably in nearby Altadena. The Palisades and Eaton fires were not Bass’ fault, but they were crippling crises that turned a mostly sedate electorate into an enraged one. Her approval ratings plummeted, and she was suddenly vulnerable, especially because she happened to be out of town when the fires erupted. She struggled to regain her footing once she returned.

If it was unfair to blame Bass for the fires, other aspects of her leadership were more susceptible to criticism. She gave police officers a gigantic raise, and the city’s police union became one of her most conspicuous supporters, fueling the critique that she was in cahoots with her backers. She appointed some mediocre deputies and often second-guessed them, delaying decisions on important matters. She frustrated allies by letting problems linger and resisting new ideas in the area of homelessness, for instance. 

Perhaps most importantly, though, she suffered from a politicians’ worst enemy: bad timing. Bass chased off potential rivals in the run-up to her reelection, but Raman jumped in late and then flourished as the national electorate was growing more restive. Rising prices, hostility toward immigrants, a general tone of nastiness in national discourse all were the work of President Donald Trump, whom Raman and Bass loathe equally, but those sources of unhappiness made this a bad time to be an incumbent on the ballot.

Bass conceded defeat Thursday morning. In a statement, she took credit for progress while also acknowledging the mounting votes against her.

“Coming out of the pandemic, when encampments lined our streets and businesses were trying to reopen — we got Angelenos off the streets, made our neighborhoods safer, built more affordable housing and created new opportunities for working families," Bass said. "We stood together through devastating wildfires and protected our immigrant communities when Donald Trump sent federal troops into our streets to spread fear and intimidation. That progress belongs to all of us."

Raman’s campaign, by contrast, was fresh and positive. She successfully positioned herself as an outsider to the mainstream of Los Angeles politics. 

Running both as a member of the council and as the alternative to the status quo gave Raman the luxury of claiming credit for city progress — she boasted of the decline in street homelessness in her district last year — while also distancing herself from the city’s struggles. She did not run a perfect campaign — a few late gaffes gave the Bass camp room for optimism as Election Day approached and the mayor closed the polling gap on the council member.

In the end, however, Bass’ negative ratings — about two-thirds of city voters disapproved of her performance in office — outweighed Raman’s — about half of voters disapproved of hers.

Raman now inherits a city full of promise and potential as well as one burdened by challenges.

Homelessness will top the agenda, and Raman has made herself susceptible to clear accountability: She has promised to reduce street homelessness in the city by 50% over the next two years. That’s a measurable goal, and one she may find hard to meet. Bass, no less committed to solutions in this area, managed to bring down street homelessness about 17% over four years.

But Raman is nothing if not smart, and her background in urban planning and her experience on council give her a fresh perspective on this ancient and frustrating problem. She will certainly be less singularly committed than Bass to Inside Safe, a program that Bass initiated but that has proved very expensive and only incrementally successful. 

Much has been made of Raman’s lack of support from her council colleagues, and it is true that they lined up against her mayoral bid, reflecting a combination of professional disagreements, assessments of her work and flat-out jealousy. There, however, the transition may not be as rough as some suggest. 

Relationships at City Hall are not friendships in the way most people experience friendship. They are commonalities of interest, and the same council members who did not appreciate Raman as a colleague will find ways to mend fences now that they need her. Necessity has a way of papering over differences. 

The issue that may most complicate her new life, however, is public safety. During the campaign, Raman struggled with questions about the LAPD and its leadership. She repeatedly asserted that Chief Jim McDonnell had lost public confidence and that she would seek to replace him. But she never said how she had reached that conclusion or how she would approach replacing him.

At first, she equivocated, saying that the process for firing a chief was complicated by the roles of the council and Police Commission. But that was a dodge, and she knew it. Here’s the process: The mayor appoints the Police Commission and can direct the commission to fire the chief. The chief could appeal to the council, but likely won’t. So, yes, the mayor can fire the chief.

Whether the mayor should fire the chief is another matter. Crime is down significantly since Mayor Bass and Chief McDonnell moved into their positions, so disrupting that progress risks creating a problem where none exists. Moreover, Raman’s insistence that LAPD is doing too much to share information with federal authorities is both historically inaccurate and infuriatingly vague.

Her wisest course there may be to look for an out and to recognize that the police department requires firm civilian oversight. The values she represents as a (politically) young democratic socialist have a place in public safety, but change merely for the sake of politics is unwise.

Los Angeles will be keeping its controversial “mansion tax” just the way it is, thank you very much. On Tuesday morning, L.A.’s city council rejected an eleventh hour proposal to place a re-write of the city’s four-year-old tax on high value real estate sales onto the June 2026 local ballot. The decision, made after a heated session brimming with arcane procedural objections and spirited public comment from tenant activists and union members, effectively quashes the hopes of real estate developers, commercial landlords and a growing caucus of housing construction advocates and Democratic state elected officials who see the highest-in-the-state transfer fee as both an investment killer and an urgent political liability — both in Los Angeles and across California. A sizable majority of the city’s voters approved the tax, known as Measure ULA, in 2022. It places a 4% tax on property sales between $5 million and $10 million and a 5.5% tax on transactions above that. So far, the tax has raised more than $1 billion in revenue dedicated for affordable housing development and support for cash-strapped renters. Any changes to the tax would require sign off from the electorate, which today’s vote ensures won’t come anytime soon. It also kicks a broader multibillion dollar debate over fees on property sales to state lawmakers. Hanging over the debate is the specter of a proposed statewide proposition that would sharply cap municipal transfer taxes , while also restricting other local taxes. That campaign is being organized by the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, which campaigns for lower taxes, and is racing to gather signatures ahead of a late February deadline. If it qualifies, it would appear on the November 2026 ballot. A growing caucus of Democrats and their political allies argue that local opposition to ULA has juiced political support for that more far-reaching anti-tax prop, one they see as a fiscal disaster. Should a statewide anti-tax proposition qualify, many believe that lawmakers will be forced to offer up concessions, in the form of broader statewide restriction on transfer taxes, to convince the backers of the Howard Jarvis measure to remove it from the ballot.
